translations.en: Even as time goes round and round, I want to meet you here again. So we don't get separated, I'll hold this hand.

translations.pt-BR: Mesmo que o tempo gire e gire, quero te encontrar aqui de novo. Para nao nos separarmos, vou segurar esta mao.

literal_meaning.en: go-around + go-around + even-if + again + here + at + meet + want-to / get-separated + not + so-that + this + hand + object + hold + explanatory

grammar_points.name: 〜ても (temo - even if)

explanation.en:
Expresses "even if" or "even though." The speaker acknowledges a condition but says the result stays the same regardless.

How it works:
Take the て-form (te-form) of a verb and add も (mo). It means "even if [verb happens]."

Example from this song:
巡り巡っても (meguri megutte mo, "Even if time goes round and round")

More examples:
- 雨が降っても行く (ame ga futte mo iku, "I'll go even if it rains")
- 高くても買う (takakute mo kau, "I'll buy it even if it's expensive")
- 何回失敗しても諦めない (nankai shippai shite mo akiramenai, "Even if I fail many times, I won't give up")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 巡る (meguru) → 巡って (megutte, te-form) → 巡っても (megutte mo, "even if it goes around")

explanation.en:
Expresses purpose or a wish: "so that [something happens]" or "in order to." It is used when the desired outcome is not directly under the speaker's control.

How it works:
Place ように (you ni) after the dictionary form (positive) or ない-form (negative) of a verb.

Example from this song:
はぐれないように (hagurenai you ni, "So that we don't get separated")

More examples:
- 忘れないようにメモする (wasurenai you ni memo suru, "I'll take notes so I don't forget")
- 聞こえるように大きい声で話す (kikoeru you ni ookii koe de hanasu, "Speak loudly so it can be heard")
- 遅れないように早く出る (okurenai you ni hayaku deru, "Leave early so as not to be late")

grammar_points.name: 〜んだ (nda - explanatory)

explanation.en:
Adds an explanatory or emphatic tone to a statement. It signals that the speaker is giving a reason, making a strong declaration, or emphasizing their resolve.

How it works:
Attach んだ (nda) after the plain form of a verb, adjective, or noun + な. In casual speech, it often sounds like "It's that..." or adds conviction.

Example from this song:
この手をつなぐんだ (kono te o tsunagu nda, "I WILL hold this hand" - emphatic resolve)

More examples:
- 行くんだ (iku nda, "I'm going! / The thing is, I'm going")
- 好きなんだ (suki na nda, "The truth is, I like you")
- どうして泣いてるんだ (doushite naiteru nda, "Why are you crying?")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: つなぐ (tsunagu) + んだ (nda) → つなぐんだ (tsunagu nda, "I will hold [hands] - emphatic")

grammar_points.name: 〜ながら (nagara - while)

explanation.en:
Expresses doing two actions at the same time: "while doing [X], also doing [Y]." The main action comes at the end of the sentence.

How it works:
Take the masu-stem of a verb and add ながら (nagara). The secondary (background) action gets ながら, and the main action follows.

Example from this song:
つなぎ直しながら (tsunaginaoshi nagara, "While reconnecting hands")

More examples:
- 音楽を聴きながら勉強する (ongaku o kiki nagara benkyou suru, "Study while listening to music")
- 歩きながら話す (aruki nagara hanasu, "Talk while walking")
- コーヒーを飲みながら新聞を読む (koohii o nomi nagara shinbun o yomu, "Read the newspaper while drinking coffee")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: つなぎ直す (tsunaginaosu) → つなぎ直し (tsunaginaoshi, masu-stem) + ながら (nagara) → つなぎ直しながら (tsunaginaoshi nagara)

explanation.en:
A conditional meaning "if." It is used when the speaker takes a hypothetical situation as a premise and then states what would follow.

How it works:
Attach なら (nara) after the plain past form of a verb or the dictionary form. It sets up a condition.

Example from this song:
描いたなら (egaita nara, "If you've envisioned [a dream]")

More examples:
- 暇なら映画を見よう (hima nara eiga o miyou, "If you're free, let's watch a movie")
- 日本に行くなら京都がおすすめ (nihon ni iku nara kyouto ga osusume, "If you go to Japan, I recommend Kyoto")
- 分かったなら早くやって (wakatta nara hayaku yatte, "If you understood, do it quickly")

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru - to keep doing)

explanation.en:
An auxiliary verb meaning "to continue doing." Attached to the masu-stem of another verb, it expresses an ongoing, sustained action.

How it works:
Take the masu-stem of a verb and add 続ける (tsuzukeru).

Example from this song:
照らし続けよう (terashi tsuzukeyou, "Let's keep illuminating")

More examples:
- 走り続ける (hashiri tsuzukeru, "to keep running")
- 信じ続ける (shinji tsuzukeru, "to keep believing")
- 練習し続ければ上手になる (renshuu shi tsuzukereba jouzu ni naru, "If you keep practicing, you'll get good")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 照らす (terasu) → 照らし (terashi, masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) → 照らし続けよう (terashi tsuzukeyou, "let's keep shining")

grammar_points.name: 〜はずなのに (hazu nanoni: was supposed to, but...)

explanation.en:
How it works: はず (hazu) means 'supposed to' or 'expected to'. Add なのに (nanoni, 'even though') to express disappointment that reality didn't match expectations. The full pattern is: [verb/adjective] + はず + なのに.

Example from this song: 追いかけていたはずなのに (oikaketeita hazu nanoni) = 'I was supposed to be chasing (but...)' — from 追いかけていた (oikaketeita, 'was chasing') + はず (hazu, 'supposed to') + なのに (nanoni, 'even though')

More examples:
• 届く (todoku, 'to reach') → 届くはずなのに (todoku hazu nanoni, 'it should reach, but...')
• 簡単 (kantan, 'easy') → 簡単なはずなのに (kantan na hazu nanoni, 'it should be easy, but...')

Note: はず alone expresses expectation. Adding なのに adds the contrast — the reality is different from what was expected.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 追いかける (oikakeru, 'to chase') → 追いかけていた (oikaketeita, 'was chasing') + はず (hazu, 'supposed to') + なのに (nanoni, 'but')

grammar_points.name: 〜てしまう (te-shimau: end up doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) and add しまう (shimau). This expresses an action completed fully, often with a feeling of regret or that something happened unintentionally.

Example from this song: 消してしまう (keshite shimau) = 'end up erasing' — from 消す (kesu, 'to erase') → 消して (keshite, te-form) + しまう (shimau)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べてしまう (tabete shimau, 'end up eating it all')
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れてしまう (wasurete shimau, 'end up forgetting')
• 壊す (kowasu, 'to break') → 壊してしまう (kowashite shimau, 'end up breaking')

Note: In casual speech, てしまう contracts to ちゃう (chau), and でしまう to じゃう (jau). So 食べてしまう becomes 食べちゃう (tabechau).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 消す (kesu, 'to erase') → 消して (keshite, te-form) → 消してしまう (keshite shimau, 'end up erasing')

grammar_points.name: 〜ために (tame ni: in order to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place ために (tame ni) after the dictionary form of a verb to express purpose — 'in order to do something'. It can also follow nouns with の (no) to mean 'for the sake of'.

Example from this song: 叶えるために (kanaeru tame ni) = 'in order to make (dreams) come true' — from 叶える (kanaeru, 'to fulfill') + ために (tame ni, 'in order to')

More examples:
• 合格する (goukaku suru, 'to pass') → 合格するために (goukaku suru tame ni, 'in order to pass')
• 日本語 (nihongo, 'Japanese') → 日本語のために (nihongo no tame ni, 'for the sake of Japanese')
• 生きる (ikiru, 'to live') → 生きるために (ikiru tame ni, 'in order to live')

Note: ために with dictionary form = purpose ('in order to'). ために with past tense = cause ('because of'). 合格したために means 'because (I) passed'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 叶える (kanaeru, 'to fulfill') + ために (tame ni, 'in order to') → 叶えるために (kanaeru tame ni, 'in order to fulfill')

grammar_points.name: 〜なくちゃいけない (nakucha ikenai: must do)

explanation.en:
How it works: This is a casual contraction of なくてはいけない (nakutewa ikenai). Take the ない-form of a verb, drop い, add くちゃいけない. Literally 'if I don't do it, it won't do' = 'I must do it'.

Example from this song: 謝らなくちゃいけない (ayamaranakucha ikenai) = 'I must apologize' — from 謝る (ayamaru, 'to apologize') → 謝らない (ayamaranai, negative) → 謝らなくちゃいけない

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べなくちゃいけない (tabenakucha ikenai, 'must eat')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かなくちゃいけない (ikanakucha ikenai, 'must go')
• 勉強する (benkyou suru, 'to study') → 勉強しなくちゃいけない (benkyou shinakucha ikenai, 'must study')

Note: Even shorter casual forms exist: なくちゃ (nakucha) or なきゃ (nakya). So 行かなきゃ (ikanakya) = 'gotta go'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 謝る (ayamaru, 'to apologize') → 謝らない (ayamaranai, negative) → 謝らなくちゃいけない (ayamaranakucha ikenai, 'must apologize')

grammar_points.name: 〜てくる (te-kuru: have been doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) and add くる (kuru, 'to come'). This shows an action that has been building up or continuing from the past toward the present moment.

Example from this song: なくしてきた (nakushite kita) = 'have been losing' — from なくす (nakusu, 'to lose') → なくして (nakushite, te-form) + きた (kita, past of kuru)

More examples:
• 勉強する (benkyou suru, 'to study') → 勉強してきた (benkyou shite kita, 'have been studying')
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩いてきた (aruite kita, 'have been walking')
• 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わってきた (kawatte kita, 'has been changing')

Note: Compare with 〜ていく (te-iku) which shows actions moving away into the future. 〜てくる shows actions coming toward the present from the past.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: なくす (nakusu, 'to lose') → なくして (nakushite, te-form) → なくしてきた (nakushite kita, 'have been losing')

grammar_points.name: 〜たい (tai: want to do)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb stem (masu-stem) and add たい (tai). This expresses wanting to do something. It conjugates like an い-adjective.

Example from this song: 強くなりたい (tsuyoku naritai) = 'want to become strong' — from 強くなる (tsuyoku naru, 'to become strong') → 強くなり (tsuyoku nari, masu-stem) + たい (tai). Also 吐き出したい (hakidashitai) = 'want to spit out'.

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたい (tabetai, 'want to eat')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行きたい (ikitai, 'want to go')
• 話す (hanasu, 'to speak') → 話したい (hanashitai, 'want to speak')

Note: たい is only used for the speaker's own desires (first person). To describe someone else's desire, use たがっている (tagatteiru).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 強くなる (tsuyoku naru, 'to become strong') → 強くなり (tsuyoku nari, masu-stem) → 強くなりたい (tsuyoku naritai, 'want to become strong')

grammar_points.name: 〜ように (you ni: so that; hoping that)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place ように (you ni) after a verb to express a wish, hope, or purpose — 'so that...' or 'hoping that...'. Often used with prayers and wishes.

Example from this song: 分かってくれますように (wakatte kuremasu you ni) = 'I hope you will understand' — from 分かってくれます (wakatte kuremasu, 'you understand for me') + ように (you ni, 'hoping that')

More examples:
• 合格する (goukaku suru, 'to pass') → 合格できますように (goukaku dekimasu you ni, 'I hope I can pass')
• 忘れない (wasurenai, 'not forget') → 忘れないように (wasurenai you ni, 'so that I don't forget')
• 元気になる (genki ni naru, 'to get well') → 元気になりますように (genki ni narimasu you ni, 'I hope you get well')

Note: With ますように it becomes a prayer/wish. With plain form + ように it means 'so that' (purpose). 遅れないように早く出た (okurenai you ni hayaku deta, 'I left early so as not to be late').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 分かってくれます (wakatte kuremasu, 'you understand for me') + ように (you ni, 'hoping that') → 分かってくれますように (wakatte kuremasu you ni, 'I hope you understand')

grammar_points.name: 〜んだ (nda: explanatory)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add んだ (nda) after a verb, adjective, or noun phrase to give an explanatory nuance — 'the fact is that...' or 'you see...'. It signals you're sharing context or explaining something.

Example from this song: 生きてるんだ (ikiterunda) = 'I'm alive, you see' — from 生きてる (ikiteru, 'am living') + んだ (nda). Also 始まってるんだ (hajimatterunda) = 'it has begun, you know'.

More examples:
• 忙しい (isogashii, 'busy') → 忙しいんだ (isogashiinda, 'the thing is, I'm busy')
• 食べた (tabeta, 'ate') → 食べたんだ (tabetanda, 'the thing is, I ate')
• 学生 (gakusei, 'student') → 学生なんだ (gakusei nanda, 'the thing is, I'm a student')

Note: This pattern is extremely common in casual Japanese. After nouns and な-adjectives, it becomes なんだ (nanda). The feminine/softer form is の (no).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 生きてる (ikiteru, 'am living') → 生きてるんだ (ikiterunda, 'I'm alive, you see') / 始まってる (hajimatteru, 'has begun') → 始まってるんだ (hajimatterunda, 'it has begun, you know')

grammar_points.name: 〜ている (continuous state)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach いる (iru) to a verb's te-form to express an ongoing action or resulting state. It's one of the most important grammar patterns in Japanese.

Example from this song: 抱えている (kakaete iru) = 'is carrying/holding' — from 抱える (kakaeru, 'to hold/carry') → 抱えて (kakaete) + いる (iru)

More examples:
• 走っている (hashitte iru, 'is running') — ongoing action — from 走る (hashiru, 'to run')
• 結婚している (kekkon shite iru, 'is married') — resulting state — from 結婚する (kekkon suru, 'to marry')
• 窓が開いている (mado ga aite iru, 'the window is open') — resulting state — from 開く (aku, 'to open')

Note: Whether ている means 'is doing' (ongoing) or 'has done/is in a state' depends on the verb type. Action verbs = ongoing. Change-of-state verbs = resulting state. Casual form: ている → てる.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 抱える (kakaeru, 'to hold') → 抱えて (kakaete) → 抱えている (kakaete iru, 'is holding')

grammar_points.name: 〜のに (even though / if only)

explanation.en:
How it works: のに (noni) expresses 'even though' or 'despite' — it shows a contrast between expectation and reality, often with a feeling of regret or frustration.

Example from this song: The song uses のに to express a gap between what the speaker wanted and what actually happened — 'even though I wanted to say those words...'

More examples:
• 頑張ったのにダメだった (ganbatta noni dame datta, 'even though I tried hard, it was no good')
• せっかく来たのに (sekkaku kita noni, 'even though I came all this way...') — frustration
• 好きなのに言えない (suki na noni ienai, 'even though I like them, I can't say it')

Note: のに at the end of a sentence leaves the conclusion unstated, creating emotional impact: 'and yet...' / 'but...' This trailing のに is very common in songs and emotional speech.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb plain form / i-adj / na-adj + な + のに (noni, 'even though')

grammar_points.name: 〜ば conditional (ba-form)

explanation.en:
How it works: The ば (ba) conditional means 'if.' For godan verbs, change the final -u to -e and add ば. For ichidan verbs, drop る and add れば.

Example from this song: 思い出せば (omoidaseba) = 'if I recall' — from 思い出す (omoidasu, 'to recall') → 思い出せ (omoidase) + ば (ba)

More examples:
• 食べれば (tabereba, 'if you eat') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 行けば (ikeba, 'if you go') — from 行く (iku, 'to go')
• よければ (yokereba, 'if it's good / if you'd like') — from 良い (yoi/ii, 'good')

Note: ば conditional implies natural consequence: 'if X, then Y naturally follows.' Irregular forms: する → すれば (sureba), 来る → 来れば (kureba). For i-adjectives: い → ければ.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 思い出す (omoidasu, 'to recall') → 思い出せば (omoidaseba, 'if I recall')

grammar_points.name: 〜気がする (feel like; sense that)

explanation.en:
How it works: 気がする (ki ga suru) means 'to have a feeling that' or 'to sense that.' It expresses a vague impression or intuition rather than certainty.

Example from this song: The song uses 気がする to express an uncertain feeling — a sense that something might be true without being sure.

More examples:
• 誰かに見られている気がする (dareka ni mirarete iru ki ga suru, 'I feel like someone is watching me')
• 前に会った気がする (mae ni atta ki ga suru, 'I feel like we've met before')
• うまくいく気がする (umaku iku ki ga suru, 'I have a feeling it'll go well')

Note: 気 (ki) means 'spirit/feeling.' The full pattern is: sentence (plain form) + 気がする. It's softer and more uncertain than 思う (omou, 'to think'). Very natural in daily conversation.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb/adjective plain form + 気がする (ki ga suru, 'feel like / sense that')

grammar_points.name: 〜ておく (to do in advance; to leave as is)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach おく (oku) to a verb's te-form to express doing something in preparation or deliberately leaving something in a state. It implies foresight or intentional preservation.

Example from this song: しまっておこう (shimatte okou) = 'let me put it away (for safekeeping)' — from しまう (shimau, 'to put away') → しまって (shimatte) + おこう (okou, volitional of oku)

More examples:
• 予約しておく (yoyaku shite oku, 'make a reservation in advance') — from 予約する (yoyaku suru, 'to reserve')
• メモしておいた (memo shite oita, 'wrote a memo in advance') — past form
• そのままにしておいて (sono mama ni shite oite, 'leave it as it is') — request form

Note: Casual contraction: ておく → とく (toku). Example: 買っとく (kattoku, 'buy in advance'). The volitional form ておこう means 'let me prepare by doing X.'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: しまう (shimau, 'to put away') → しまって (shimatte) → しまっておく (shimatte oku, 'put away for keeps') → しまっておこう (shimatte okou, 'let me put it away')

grammar_points.name: 〜てしまう (regrettable completion)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach しまう (shimau) to a verb's te-form to express complete action, often with regret or that it happened unintentionally.

Example from this song: 失くしてしまった (nakushite shimatta) = 'ended up losing' — from 失くす (nakusu, 'to lose') → 失くして (nakushite) + しまった (shimatta)

More examples:
• 食べてしまった (tabete shimatta, 'ate it all up') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 壊してしまった (kowashite shimatta, 'accidentally broke it') — from 壊す (kowasu, 'to break')
• 言ってしまった (itte shimatta, 'accidentally said it') — from 言う (iu, 'to say')

Note: Casual: てしまう → ちゃう, てしまった → ちゃった. Example: 失くしちゃった (nakushichatta). The nuance can be regret ('unfortunately did') or emphasis on completion ('completely did').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 失くす (nakusu, 'to lose') → 失くして (nakushite) → 失くしてしまった (nakushite shimatta, 'ended up losing')

grammar_points.name: 〜ている (te-iru continuous/resultative)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine a verb's て-form (te-form) with いる (iru) to express an ongoing action or a resulting state. Think of it as the Japanese equivalent of English '-ing' or 'has been'.

Example from this song: 迷っている (mayotte iru) = 'is hesitating' — from 迷う (mayou, 'to hesitate') → 迷って (mayotte, te-form) + いる (iru)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べている (tabete iru, 'is eating')
• 読む (yomu, 'to read') → 読んでいる (yonde iru, 'is reading')
• 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知っている (shitte iru, 'knows' — resultative state)

Note: For -ru verbs (ichidan), drop る and add ている. For -u verbs (godan), use the te-form rules (む→んで, う→って, etc.) then add いる. In casual speech, いる often shortens to る: 迷ってる (mayotteru).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 迷う (mayou, 'to hesitate') → 迷って (mayotte, te-form) → 迷っている (mayotte iru, 'is hesitating')

grammar_points.name: 〜しかない (shika nai — no choice but to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place しか (shika) after a verb in dictionary form and follow with ない (nai). This creates the meaning 'there is nothing but to do X' or 'no choice but to do X'. しか always requires a negative verb.

Example from this song: やるしかない (yaru shika nai) = 'there's no choice but to do it' — from やる (yaru, 'to do') + しか (shika, 'nothing but') + ない (nai, 'not')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くしかない (iku shika nai, 'no choice but to go')
• 待つ (matsu, 'to wait') → 待つしかない (matsu shika nai, 'no choice but to wait')
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じるしかない (shinjiru shika nai, 'no choice but to believe')

Note: しか replaces を or が. You cannot say やるをしかない — just やるしかない.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: やる (yaru, 'to do') + しかない (shika nai, 'nothing but') → やるしかない (yaru shika nai, 'no choice but to do it')

grammar_points.name: 〜んだ (explanatory の + だ)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add んだ (nda) — a contraction of のだ (no da) — after a verb, adjective, or noun to add an explanatory or emphatic nuance. It signals 'the reason is...' or 'the thing is...' It makes your statement sound like you're explaining or justifying something.

Example from this song: ブレるんだ (bureru nda) = 'the thing is, I waver' — from ブレる (bureru, 'to waver') + んだ (nda, explanatory)

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くんだ (iku nda, 'the thing is, I'm going')
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなんだ (suki nanda, 'the thing is, I like it')
• 学生 (gakusei, 'student') → 学生なんだ (gakusei nanda, 'the thing is, I'm a student')

Note: After な-adjectives and nouns, use なんだ (nanda). After verbs and い-adjectives, use んだ (nda) directly.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: ブレる (bureru, 'to waver') + んだ (nda, explanatory) → ブレるんだ (bureru nda, 'the thing is, I waver')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to create a direct command. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with ろ. For -u verbs (godan), change the final う-row syllable to its え-row equivalent.

Example from this song: 掴め (tsukame) = 'Grab it!' — from 掴む (tsukamu, 'to grab') → change む (mu) to め (me)

More examples:
• 攻める (semeru, 'to attack') → 攻めろ (semero, 'Attack!')
• 探る (saguru, 'to search') → 探れ (sagure, 'Search!')
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')

Note: For godan verbs: む→め, く→け, す→せ, つ→て, ぬ→ね, ぶ→べ, る→れ. For ichidan verbs: る→ろ. This form is very direct and strong — common in song lyrics, sports, and anime but rarely used in polite conversation.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 掴む (tsukamu, 'to grab') → 掴め (tsukame, 'Grab!') / 攻める (semeru, 'to attack') → 攻めろ (semero, 'Attack!') / 探る (saguru, 'to search') → 探れ (sagure, 'Search!')

grammar_points.name: 〜ために (tame ni — in order to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ために (tame ni) after a verb in dictionary form to express purpose — 'in order to do X'. For nouns, use noun + のために (no tame ni).

Example from this song: 飛び越えるために (tobikoeru tame ni) = 'in order to leap over' — from 飛び越える (tobikoeru, 'to leap over') + ために (tame ni, 'in order to')

More examples:
• 勝つ (katsu, 'to win') → 勝つために (katsu tame ni, 'in order to win')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べるために (taberu tame ni, 'in order to eat')
• 夢 (yume, 'dream') → 夢のために (yume no tame ni, 'for the sake of a dream')

Note: ために can also express cause/reason with past tense verbs: 雨が降ったために (ame ga futta tame ni, 'because it rained').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 飛び越える (tobikoeru, 'to leap over') + ために (tame ni, 'in order to') → 飛び越えるために (tobikoeru tame ni, 'in order to leap over')

grammar_points.name: 〜たまま (ta mama — while remaining)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use the past tense (た-form) of a verb + まま (mama) to express that a state continues while something else happens. It means 'while still in the state of having done X'.

Example from this song: 抑えたまま (osaeta mama) = 'while keeping it suppressed' — from 抑える (osaeru, 'to suppress') → 抑えた (osaeta, past) + まま (mama, 'as is')

More examples:
• 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand') → 立ったまま (tatta mama, 'while still standing')
• 開ける (akeru, 'to open') → 開けたまま (aketa mama, 'left open')
• 座る (suwaru, 'to sit') → 座ったまま (suwatta mama, 'while still sitting')

Note: まま indicates no change from the described state. 靴を履いたまま寝た (kutsu wo haita mama neta) = 'I slept with my shoes still on'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 抑える (osaeru, 'to suppress') → 抑えた (osaeta, past tense) → 抑えたまま (osaeta mama, 'while keeping suppressed')

grammar_points.name: 〜ば (ba conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to create an 'if' condition. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with れば. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent and add ば.

Example from this song: 過ぎれば (sugireba) = 'if it passes / if you go too far' — from 過ぎる (sugiru, 'to pass/exceed') → 過ぎれば (sugireba, 'if it passes')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行けば (ikeba, 'if you go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べれば (tabereba, 'if you eat')
• 高い (takai, 'expensive') → 高ければ (takakereba, 'if it's expensive')

Note: For い-adjectives, change い to ければ. For godan verbs: く→けば, む→めば, す→せば, つ→てば, ぬ→ねば, ぶ→べば, る→れば.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 過ぎる (sugiru, 'to pass/exceed') → 過ぎれば (sugireba, 'if it passes')

grammar_points.name: 〜ようにする (yō ni suru — as if doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ように (yō ni) after a verb in dictionary form to express manner — 'as if doing X' or 'in such a way that X'. It can describe how an action is performed.

Example from this song: 言い聞かせるように (iikikaseru yō ni) = 'as if telling oneself' — from 言い聞かせる (iikikaseru, 'to tell oneself') + ように (yō ni, 'as if')

More examples:
• 歌う (utau, 'to sing') → 歌うように (utau yō ni, 'as if singing')
• 飛ぶ (tobu, 'to fly') → 飛ぶように (tobu yō ni, 'as if flying')
• 祈る (inoru, 'to pray') → 祈るように (inoru yō ni, 'as if praying')

Note: ように has multiple uses. With する it means 'try to / make sure to': 忘れないようにする (wasurenai yō ni suru, 'make sure not to forget'). Without する, it describes manner.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 言い聞かせる (iikikaseru, 'to tell oneself') + ように (yō ni, 'as if') → 言い聞かせるように (iikikaseru yō ni, 'as if telling oneself')

grammar_points.name: 〜ために (tame ni - for the sake of)

explanation.en:
Expresses purpose or benefit: "for the sake of" or "in order to." It tells you why an action happens or who benefits from it.

How it works:
Place ために (tame ni) after the dictionary form of a verb, or after a noun + の (no).

Example from this song:
君のために朝が来る (kimi no tame ni asa ga kuru, "Morning comes for your sake")

More examples:
- 健康のために運動する (kenkou no tame ni undou suru, "Exercise for your health")
- 合格するために勉強する (goukaku suru tame ni benkyou suru, "Study in order to pass")
- 家族のために働く (kazoku no tame ni hataraku, "Work for the family")

A casual emphatic particle meaning "even" or "no matter what." It stresses that something applies broadly.

How it works:
Attach だって (datte) after a noun. It means "even [noun]" or "[noun] too."

Example from this song:
価値観だっていろいろ (kachikan datte iroiro, "Even values are various")

More examples:
- 誰だって間違う (dare datte machigau, "Anyone can make mistakes")
- 子供だって分かる (kodomo datte wakaru, "Even kids understand")
- 雨だって行く (ame datte iku, "I’ll go even if it rains")

Sentence-ending particles used in casual, masculine speech. They add emphasis, energy, or a tough/playful tone.

How it works:
ぞ (zo) adds strong assertion or warning. ぜ (ze) adds confident emphasis. Both are informal and mostly used by male speakers.

Example from this song:
内緒だぞ (naisho da zo, "It’s a secret!" - playful, rough)

More examples:
- 行くぞ (iku zo, "Let’s go!" - assertive)
- やるぜ (yaru ze, "I’m gonna do it!" - confident)
- すごいぞ (sugoi zo, "That’s amazing!" - excited)

grammar_points.name: 〜てる (teru - continuous/result)

explanation.en:
A casual contraction of ている (te iru), expressing an ongoing action or current state. Extremely common in everyday Japanese.

How it works:
Drop the い (i) from ている (te iru) to get てる (teru).

Example from this song:
笑ってる空 (waratteru sora, "The sky is smiling")

grammar_points.name: 〜てしまう

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach しまう (shimau) to a verb's te-form to express that something was done completely, often with regret or unintentionally. In casual speech, it contracts to ちゃう (chau).

Example from this song: The song uses てしまう to express actions that happened completely or regrettably — things that can't be undone.

More examples:
• 食べてしまった (tabete shimatta, 'ate it all up') — casual: 食べちゃった (tabechatta)
• 忘れてしまう (wasurete shimau, 'will end up forgetting') — casual: 忘れちゃう (wasurechau)
• 壊してしまった (kowashite shimatta, 'accidentally broke it') — casual: 壊しちゃった (kowashichatta)

Note: てしまう → ちゃう, でしまう → じゃう. Past: てしまった → ちゃった, でしまった → じゃった. The casual forms are extremely common in daily speech and song lyrics.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb te-form + しまう (shimau, 'completely / regrettably') → casual: ちゃう (chau)

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて

explanation.en:
How it works: なんて (nante) expresses surprise, disbelief, or emphasis. It can mean 'such a thing as,' 'something like,' or 'how surprising that.' The tone ranges from dismissive to amazed.

Example from this song: The song uses なんて to express disbelief or emotional weight about a situation.

More examples:
• こんなことになるなんて (konna koto ni naru nante, 'to think it would come to this!')
• 君に会えるなんて (kimi ni aeru nante, 'to think I'd get to meet you!')
• 簡単なんて思わなかった (kantan nante omowanakatta, 'I never thought it'd be easy')

Note: なんて replaces particles like は or を and always adds emotional color. In songs, it often expresses the weight of an unexpected realization.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: noun/verb plain form + なんて (nante, 'such a thing as / how surprising')

grammar_points.name: 〜みたい

explanation.en:
How it works: みたい (mitai) means 'like' or 'seems like.' It attaches to nouns, verbs, or adjectives to create comparisons or express appearance. It's the casual version of よう (you).

Example from this song: The song uses みたい to draw comparisons — 'like something' or 'it seems as though.'

More examples:
• 夢みたい (yume mitai, 'like a dream') — from 夢 (yume, 'dream')
• 子供みたいに笑う (kodomo mitai ni warau, 'laugh like a child') — from 子供 (kodomo, 'child')
• 雨が降るみたいだ (ame ga furu mitai da, 'it seems like it'll rain')

Note: みたい after a noun = 'like (noun).' みたい after a verb/adjective = 'seems like.' Add に to use as an adverb: みたいに. Add な to modify a noun: みたいな.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: noun/verb plain form + みたい (mitai, 'like / seems like')

grammar_points.name: 〜たら/なら (conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: たら (tara) is a conditional 'if/when' formed from the past tense + ら. なら (nara) is a conditional 'if (it's the case that)' used for hypothetical situations.

Example from this song: The song uses conditional forms to express hypothetical scenarios — 'if this happened, then...'

More examples:
• 食べたらおいしかった (tabetara oishikatta, 'when I ate it, it was delicious') — たら for 'when'
• 暇なら遊ぼう (hima nara asobou, 'if you're free, let's hang out') — なら for 'if'
• もし宝くじが当たったら (moshi takarakuji ga atattara, 'if I won the lottery') — hypothetical

Note: たら = 'if/when (something happens)' — most versatile. なら = 'if (based on information/supposition)' — focuses on the topic. Both are essential conditionals.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb past (ta-form) + ら (ra) → たら (tara, 'if/when') / noun + なら (nara, 'if it's the case')

grammar_points.name: 〜ている (progressive/state)

explanation.en:
How it works: ている (te iru) after a verb's te-form expresses an ongoing action or resulting state. 持っている means 'to have/possess' (resulting state of having taken hold).

Example from this song: The song uses ている forms to describe ongoing states and actions.

More examples:
• 走っている (hashitte iru, 'is running') — ongoing action
• 知っている (shitte iru, 'knows') — resulting state
• 持っている (motte iru, 'has/possesses') — from 持つ (motsu, 'to hold')

Note: Action verbs + ている = 'is doing.' State-change verbs + ている = 'is in the state of.' 持つ → 持っている means 'possesses' not 'is holding.' Casual: ている → てる.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb te-form + いる (iru, 'to be') → ている (te iru, 'is doing / is in state of')

grammar_points.name: imperative form (命令形)

explanation.en:
How it works: The imperative gives direct commands. For godan verbs (-u), change the final vowel to -e. For ichidan verbs (-ru), replace る with ろ.

Example from this song: 焦がせ (kogase) = 'burn!' — from 焦がす (kogasu, 'to scorch'), godan: す → せ. Also: 渡れ (watare) = 'cross!' — from 渡る (wataru, 'to cross'), godan: る → れ

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'run!')
• 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand') → 立て (tate, 'stand!')
• 起きる (okiru, 'to wake up') → 起きろ (okiro, 'wake up!') — ichidan

Note: Imperatives are poetic and powerful in songs. Irregular: する → しろ (shiro), 来る → 来い (koi). These commands in songs are often self-directed: 'burn! cross! go!'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 焦がす (kogasu, 'to scorch') → 焦がせ (kogase, 'burn!') / 渡る (wataru, 'to cross') → 渡れ (watare, 'cross!')

grammar_points.name: 〜ずに (zu ni: without doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb's negative stem (the ない-form minus ない) and add ずに (zuni) to mean 'without doing X'.

Example from this song: 諦めずに (akiramezuni) = 'without giving up' — from 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up') → 諦め (akirame, negative stem) + ずに (zuni, 'without')

More examples:
• 休む (yasumu, 'to rest') → 休まずに (yasumazuni, 'without resting')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣かずに (nakazuni, 'without crying')
• する (suru, 'to do') → せずに (sezuni, 'without doing') — irregular

Note: For -ru verbs (ichidan), the negative stem is just the stem: 諦める → 諦め. For -u verbs (godan), use the あ-row: 休む → 休ま. This pattern is key to the song's theme of perseverance.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up') → 諦め (akirame, stem) + ずに (zuni, 'without') → 諦めずに (akiramezuni, 'without giving up')

grammar_points.name: 〜てきた (te kita: have been doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add てきた (te kita) after the te-form of a verb to express an action that has continued from the past up to now — 'have been doing X (up until this point)'.

Example from this song: 立ち上がってきた (tachiagatte kita) = 'have been getting back up' — from 立ち上がる (tachiagaru, 'to stand up') → 立ち上がって (tachiagatte, te-form) + きた (kita, 'came')

More examples:
• 頑張る (ganbaru, 'to persevere') → 頑張ってきた (ganbatte kita, 'have been persevering')
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩いてきた (aruite kita, 'have been walking')
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じてきた (shinjite kita, 'have believed all along')

Note: てきた implies looking back at a journey — 'all this time, I've been doing X'. It's emotionally powerful in songs because it acknowledges the accumulated effort. Compare with ていく (future-facing: 'will continue to').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 立ち上がる (tachiagaru, 'to stand up') → 立ち上がって (tachiagatte, te-form) + きた (kita, 'came') → 立ち上がってきた (tachiagatte kita, 'have been getting back up')

grammar_points.name: 〜じゃないか (janai ka: isn't it?; haven't you?)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add じゃないか (janai ka) at the end of a statement to turn it into a rhetorical question for emphasis or encouragement — 'isn't it?' or 'haven't you?'

Example from this song: 立ち上がってきたじゃないか (tachiagatte kita janai ka) = 'haven't you been getting back up?' — an encouraging reminder of past resilience.

More examples:
• すごい (sugoi, 'amazing') → すごいじゃないか (sugoi janai ka, 'isn't that amazing?')
• できた (dekita, 'did it') → できたじゃないか (dekita janai ka, 'you did it, didn't you?')
• 頑張った (ganbatta, 'tried hard') → 頑張ったじゃないか (ganbatta janai ka, 'you tried hard, didn't you?')

Note: じゃないか is encouraging and affirming — 'look, you can/did/are!' It's different from the literal 'isn't it not?' Reading. In this song, it powerfully reminds the listener of their own strength.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 立ち上がってきた (tachiagatte kita, 'have been getting up') + じゃないか (janai ka, 'haven't you?') → 立ち上がってきたじゃないか (tachiagatte kita janai ka, 'you've been getting back up, haven't you?')

grammar_points.name: 〜させて (sasete: let me)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use the causative te-form させて (sasete) to request permission to do something — 'let me do X' or 'allow me to do X'.

Example from this song: いさせて (isasete) = 'let me be here / let me stay' — from いる (iru, 'to be/exist') → いさせる (isaseru, causative) → いさせて (isasete, 'let me be')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かせて (ikasete, 'let me go')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やらせて (yarasete, 'let me do it')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わせて (iwasete, 'let me say')

Note: させて is the causative form used as a request. For -ru verbs: る→させて. For -u verbs: change to あ-row + せて. する→させて, 来る→来させて (kosasete). Adding ください makes it polite: 行かせてください.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: いる (iru, 'to be') → いさせる (isaseru, causative) → いさせて (isasete, 'let me be here')

grammar_points.name: 〜だけは (dake wa: at least)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add だけは (dake wa) after a noun to emphasize 'at least this one thing' — expressing that even if everything else fails, this one thing matters most.

Example from this song: 夢だけは (yume dake wa) = 'at least my dream' — from 夢 (yume, 'dream') + だけは (dake wa, 'at least') — expressing determination to protect this one thing above all.

More examples:
• これ (kore, 'this') → これだけは (kore dake wa, 'at least this')
• 約束 (yakusoku, 'promise') → 約束だけは (yakusoku dake wa, 'at least the promise')
• 言いたいこと (iitai koto, 'what I want to say') → 言いたいことだけは (iitai koto dake wa, 'at least what I want to say')

Note: だけ = 'only'. Adding は after it adds emphasis and contrast — 'as for at least this one thing'. It implies 'everything else may be uncertain, but THIS is certain'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 夢 (yume, 'dream') + だけは (dake wa, 'at least') → 夢だけは (yume dake wa, 'at least my dream')

grammar_points.name: 〜ように (you ni: hoping that)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ように (yō ni) after a verb to express a wish or hope — 'I hope that X' or 'so that X happens'. Often used in prayer-like or wish-like sentences, especially with ありますように.

Example from this song: 多い人生でありますように (ooi jinsei de arimasu yō ni) = 'may life be full' — expressing a heartfelt wish using the formal ありますように pattern.

More examples:
• 叶う (kanau, 'to come true') → 夢が叶いますように (yume ga kanaimasu yō ni, 'I hope my dream comes true')
• うまくいく (umaku iku, 'to go well') → うまくいきますように (umaku ikimasu yō ni, 'I hope it goes well')
• 元気 (genki, 'healthy') → 元気でありますように (genki de arimasu yō ni, 'may you be well')

Note: This ように is specifically for wishes and prayers — different from 'in order to' (purpose). The ます form before ように makes it more formal/prayerful. This is the pattern used at shrines when making wishes.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 多い (ooi, 'many') + 人生 (jinsei, 'life') + でありますように (de arimasu yō ni, 'may it be') → 多い人生でありますように ('may life be abundant')

grammar_points.name: 〜すぎる (sugiru) — too much

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) / Adjective stem + すぎる (sugiru) means "too much ~" or "excessively ~." For い-adjectives (i-adjectives): drop い (i) + すぎる: 高い (takai) → 高すぎる (taka sugiru, "too expensive"). For な-adjectives (na-adjectives): stem + すぎる. すぎる (sugiru) itself conjugates as an ichidan verb.

Example from this song:
小さすぎて (chiisa sugite) — "too small (so...)"
Something is excessively small, leading to a consequence expressed in the next clause.

More examples:
• 食べすぎた (tabe sugita) — "ate too much"
• この映画は長すぎる (kono eiga wa naga sugiru) — "this movie is too long"
• 静かすぎて怖い (shizuka sugite kowai) — "it's so quiet it's scary"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 小さい (chiisai, "small") → 小さ (chiisa, stem) + すぎる (sugiru, "too much") → 小さすぎて (chiisa sugite, te-form, "too small, so...")

grammar_points.name: 〜ている / 〜てる (te iru / teru) — progressive / state

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + いる (iru) expresses ongoing action or resulting state. In casual speech, the い (i) drops: ている (te iru) → てる (teru). This casual contraction is extremely common in everyday spoken Japanese, songs, and informal writing.

Example from this song:
泣いてる (naiteru) — "is crying" (casual)
The casual form captures the immediacy and rawness of the emotion.

More examples:
• 何してる？ (nani shiteru?) — "what are you doing?" (casual)
• もう知ってる (mou shitteru) — "I already know" (casual)
• ずっと待ってた (zutto matteta) — "had been waiting all along" (casual past)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 泣く (naku, "to cry") → 泣いて (naite, te-form) → 泣いている (naite iru, progressive) → 泣いてる (naiteru, casual, "is crying")

grammar_points.name: 〜てく (teku) — going on doing (casual)

explanation.en:
How it works:
てく (teku) is the casual contraction of ていく (te iku), which means an action continues or progresses into the future — moving away from the present. The い (i) is dropped for casual flow. This is extremely common in songs and casual speech.

Example from this song:
ぶっとばしてく (buttobashiteku) — "blasting away" / "keeps knocking out"
The action will keep going forward with relentless energy.

More examples:
• 変わってく (kawatteku) — "keeps changing"
• 消えてく (kieteku) — "fading away"
• 走ってく (hashitteku) — "running off"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: ぶっとばす (buttobasu, "to blast/knock out") → ぶっとばして (buttobashite, te-form) + いく (iku) → ぶっとばしていく (buttobashite iku) → ぶっとばしてく (buttobashiteku, casual, "keeps blasting away")

grammar_points.name: 何も〜ない (nani mo ... nai) — nothing / not anything

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern 何も (nani mo) + negative verb means "nothing" or "not anything." This is part of a broader pattern where question words + も (mo) + negative = total negation: 誰も〜ない (dare mo ... nai, "nobody"), どこも〜ない (doko mo ... nai, "nowhere"), いつも〜ない (itsu mo ... nai, "never"). This is one of the first patterns beginners learn.

Example from this song:
何もない (nani mo nai) — "there is nothing"
A stark declaration of emptiness.

More examples:
• 何も食べていない (nani mo tabete inai) — "I haven't eaten anything"
• 何も心配しないで (nani mo shinpai shinaide) — "don't worry about anything"
• 誰も来なかった (dare mo konakatta) — "nobody came"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 何 (nani, "what") + も (mo) + ない (nai, negative) → 何もない (nani mo nai, "there is nothing")

grammar_points.name: 〜けれど / 〜けど (keredo / kedo) — but / although

explanation.en:
How it works:
けれど (keredo) or its casual form けど (kedo) means "but" or "although." It connects two contrasting clauses. The full form けれども (keredomo) is the most formal, けれど (keredo) is standard, and けど (kedo) is casual. It is one of the most common conjunctions in Japanese.

Example from this song:
無いけれど (nai keredo) — "there isn't, but..."
Despite something being absent, there is still a contrasting reality.

More examples:
• 高いけど美味しい (takai kedo oishii) — "it's expensive but delicious"
• 行きたいけど時間がない (ikitai kedo jikan ga nai) — "I want to go but don't have time"
• 分かってるけど (wakatteru kedo) — "I understand, but..." (trailing off)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 無い (nai, "there isn't") + けれど (keredo, "but") → 無いけれど (nai keredo, "there isn't, but...")

grammar_points.name: 〜ば (conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to form an 'if' condition. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with れば. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent and add ば.

Example from this song: あれば (areba) = 'if there is' — from ある (aru, 'to exist') → あれば (areba, 'if there is'). Also: 迷えば (mayoeba) = 'if you get lost' — from 迷う (mayou, 'to lose one's way') → 迷えば (mayoeba)

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行けば (ikeba, 'if you go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べれば (tabereba, 'if you eat')
• 安い (yasui, 'cheap') → 安ければ (yasukereba, 'if it's cheap')

Note: The ば-conditional often implies a natural or expected consequence: 'if A, then naturally B'. For godan verbs: う→えば, く→けば, す→せば, つ→てば, む→めば, ぶ→べば, ぬ→ねば, る→れば.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: ある (aru, 'to exist') → あれば (areba, 'if there is') / 迷う (mayou, 'to get lost') → 迷えば (mayoeba, 'if you get lost')

grammar_points.name: 〜ながら (while doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach ながら (nagara) to the verb stem (masu-stem) to express doing two actions simultaneously — 'while doing X, also Y'. The main action comes at the end of the sentence.

Example from this song: 傷つきながら (kizutsuki nagara) = 'while getting hurt' — from 傷つく (kizutsuku, 'to get hurt') → 傷つき (kizutsuki, stem) + ながら (nagara, 'while')

More examples:
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩きながら (aruki nagara, 'while walking')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べながら (tabe nagara, 'while eating')
• 聞く (kiku, 'to listen') → 聞きながら (kiki nagara, 'while listening')

Note: The subject must be the same for both actions. You can't say 'while I walk, he eats'. The verb stem is formed by dropping ます from the polite form: 食べます → 食べ.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 傷つく (kizutsuku, 'to get hurt') → 傷つき (kizutsuki, stem) + ながら (nagara, 'while') → 傷つきながら (kizutsuki nagara, 'while getting hurt')

grammar_points.name: 〜ず(に) (without doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb to its negative stem (the ない-form minus ない) and add ず (zu). This means 'without doing X'. Adding に (ni) after is optional and more common in modern Japanese.

Example from this song: 忘れられず (wasurerezu) = 'unable to forget / without being able to forget' — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れられる (wasurerareru, potential: 'can forget') → 忘れられず (wasurerezu, 'without being able to forget')

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べず (tabezu, 'without eating')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わず (iwazu, 'without saying')
• する (suru, 'to do') → せず (sezu, 'without doing') — irregular!

Note: ず is a classical Japanese negative that survives in modern usage. It sounds more literary/poetic than ないで. する → せず is the only irregular form.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れられる (wasurerareru, 'can forget') → 忘れられず (wasurerezu, 'without being able to forget')

grammar_points.name: 意志形 〜よう (volitional)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to express intention or 'let's do'. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with よう. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its お-row equivalent and add う.

Example from this song: 行こう (ikou) = 'let's go' — from 行く (iku, 'to go') → change く (ku) to こ (ko) + う (u) = 行こう (ikou)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べよう (tabeyou, 'let's eat')
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見よう (miyou, 'let's see')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しよう (shiyou, 'let's do it')

Note: For godan verbs: く→こう, す→そう, つ→とう, む→もう, ぶ→ぼう, ぬ→のう, う→おう, る→ろう. The volitional expresses the speaker's will ('I'll do it') or an invitation ('let's do it').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行こう (ikou, 'let's go')

grammar_points.name: 〜にでもなれる (can even become)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine に (ni, 'into') + でも (demo, 'even') + なれる (nareru, 'can become') to express willingness to become something, even something extreme. It shows determination or desperation.

Example from this song: The song expresses the intensity of being willing to become anything — 'I can even become [something extreme]' — showing the singer's resolve.

More examples:
• 鬼 (oni, 'demon') → 鬼にでもなれる (oni ni demo nareru, 'can even become a demon')
• 何 (nani, 'anything') → 何にでもなれる (nani ni demo nareru, 'can become anything')
• 盾 (tate, 'shield') → 盾にでもなれる (tate ni demo nareru, 'can even become a shield')

Note: でも adds the nuance of 'even' — it emphasizes that the subject is willing to go to that extreme. Without でも, it's simply 'can become'. なれる is the potential form of なる (naru, 'to become').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: なる (naru, 'to become') → なれる (nareru, 'can become') → 鬼にでもなれる (oni ni demo nareru, 'can even become a demon')

grammar_points.name: 〜てやる (do forcefully/for someone)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add てやる (te yaru) after the te-form of a verb to express doing something with determination, defiance, or for someone else (in a rough/masculine way). It shows a strong, aggressive resolve.

Example from this song: The song uses てやる to convey fierce determination — 'I'll definitely do it!' with a defiant edge.

More examples:
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見てやる (mite yaru, 'I'll show you / I'll see it through')
• 倒す (taosu, 'to defeat') → 倒してやる (taoshite yaru, 'I'll take you down!')
• 勝つ (katsu, 'to win') → 勝ってやる (katte yaru, 'I'll win, just watch!')

Note: てやる is masculine and assertive. It can mean 'do something for someone' (condescending) or 'I'll definitely do it' (determined). The polite equivalent for doing favors is てあげる (te ageru).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 倒す (taosu, 'to defeat') → 倒して (taoshite, te-form) + やる (yaru, 'do forcefully') → 倒してやる (taoshite yaru, 'I'll take you down!')

grammar_points.name: 〜てしまう (te-shimau accidental/regretful)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach しまう (shimau) to a verb's te-form to express that something has been done completely, often with a feeling of regret or that it happened unintentionally. Think of it as 'ended up doing' or 'unfortunately did.'

Example from this song: 知ってしまった (shitte shimatta) = 'ended up knowing' — from 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知って (shitte) + しまった (shimatta, past of shimau)

More examples:
• 食べてしまった (tabete shimatta, 'ate it all up / accidentally ate it') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 忘れてしまった (wasurete shimatta, 'ended up forgetting') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')
• 壊してしまった (kowashite shimatta, 'broke it by accident') — from 壊す (kowasu, 'to break')

Note: In casual speech, てしまう contracts to ちゃう (chau) and てしまった to ちゃった (chatta). Example: 食べちゃった (tabechatta).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知って (shitte) → 知ってしまった (shitte shimatta, 'ended up knowing')

grammar_points.name: 〜たびに (tabi ni - every time)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach たびに (tabi ni) after a verb in dictionary form or a noun + の to express 'every time' or 'whenever.' It describes a pattern that repeats.

Example from this song: 強がるたびに (tsuyogaru tabi ni) = 'every time I act tough' — from 強がる (tsuyogaru, 'to act tough/bluff')

More examples:
• 会うたびに (au tabi ni, 'every time we meet') — from 会う (au, 'to meet')
• 思い出すたびに (omoidasu tabi ni, 'every time I remember') — from 思い出す (omoidasu, 'to recall')
• 旅のたびに (tabi no tabi ni, 'every trip') — noun + の + たびに

Note: たび (tabi) literally means 'time/occasion.' The pattern always uses the plain/dictionary form of the verb before たびに.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 強がる (tsuyogaru, 'to act tough') + たびに (tabi ni, 'every time') → 強がるたびに (tsuyogaru tabi ni, 'every time I act tough')

grammar_points.name: 〜なくても (nakutemo - even without)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the negative form of a verb (ない-form), change ない to なくても to express 'even without doing' or 'even if not.' It combines negation with the concessive 'even if.'

Example from this song: 言われなくても (iwarenakutemo) = 'even without being told' — from 言われる (iwareru, 'to be told', passive) → 言われない (iwarenai) → 言われなくても (iwarenakutemo)

More examples:
• 食べなくても (tabenakutemo, 'even if you don't eat') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 言わなくてもわかる (iwanakutemo wakaru, 'I understand even without being told') — from 言う (iu, 'to say')
• 高くなくても (takaku nakutemo, 'even if it's not expensive') — from 高い (takai, 'expensive')

Note: For verbs, change ない to なくても. For i-adjectives, change い to くなくても. For na-adjectives/nouns, add じゃなくても (ja nakutemo).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 言われる (iwareru, 'to be told') → 言われない (iwarenai, 'not told') → 言われなくても (iwarenakutemo, 'even without being told')

grammar_points.name: 〜くらい (kurai - to the extent)

explanation.en:
How it works: くらい (kurai) or ぐらい (gurai) after a verb or noun expresses an approximate degree — 'about,' 'to the extent that,' or 'enough to.' It shows how much of something there is.

Example from this song: すくえるくらい (sukueru kurai) = 'to the extent that you could scoop it up' — from すくえる (sukueru, 'can scoop'), describing tears so plentiful they could be scooped

More examples:
• 泣きたいくらい (nakitai kurai, 'to the point where I want to cry') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry')
• 死ぬくらい暑い (shinu kurai atsui, 'hot enough to die') — from 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die')
• 三十分くらい (sanjuppun kurai, 'about 30 minutes') — approximate amount

Note: くらい and ぐらい are interchangeable. When used with verbs, it expresses degree. When used with numbers, it means 'approximately.'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: すくえる (sukueru, 'can scoop') + くらい (kurai, 'to the extent') → すくえるくらい (sukueru kurai, 'enough to scoop up')

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて (nante - something like)

explanation.en:
How it works: なんて (nante) expresses surprise, disbelief, or dismissiveness about something. It can mean 'something like,' 'such a thing as,' or 'how surprising that.' The tone depends on context.

Example from this song: 幸せなんて (shiawase nante) = 'something like happiness' — expresses that happiness feels distant, unattainable, or surprising

More examples:
• 嘘なんて (uso nante, 'something like a lie / I can't believe it's a lie') — from 嘘 (uso, 'lie')
• できるなんて思わなかった (dekiru nante omowanakatta, 'I never thought I could do it') — surprise
• 彼が来るなんて (kare ga kuru nante, 'that he would come!') — disbelief

Note: なんて can replace は or を in a sentence. It always adds an emotional nuance — either 'I can't believe' or 'something as trivial as.'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 幸せ (shiawase, 'happiness') + なんて (nante, 'something like') → 幸せなんて (shiawase nante, 'something like happiness')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていた (te-ita past progressive)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine a verb's te-form with いた (ita) to describe an action that was ongoing in the past. It translates to 'was doing' in English.

Example from this song: 奏でていた (kanadete ita) = 'was playing (music)' — from 奏でる (kanaderu, 'to play an instrument/perform music')

More examples:
• 走っていた (hashitte ita, 'was running') — from 走る (hashiru, 'to run')
• 考えていた (kangaete ita, 'was thinking') — from 考える (kangaeru, 'to think')
• 雪が降っていた (yuki ga futte ita, 'it was snowing') — from 降る (furu, 'to fall')

Note: ている (te iru) = present continuous ('is doing'). ていた (te ita) = past continuous ('was doing'). In casual speech, ていた shortens to てた (teta).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 奏でる (kanaderu, 'to play music') → 奏でて (kanadete) → 奏でていた (kanadete ita, 'was playing')

grammar_points.name: 〜たら (tara: if; when)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add たら (tara) to the past tense form (た-form) of a verb to create a conditional — 'if/when X happens'. It's the most common and versatile conditional form.

Example from this song: 歩いたら (aruitara) = 'if/when you walk' — from 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩いた (aruita, past) + ら (ra) = 歩いたら (aruitara)

More examples:
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見たら (mitara, 'if you see')
• 着く (tsuku, 'to arrive') → 着いたら (tsuitara, 'when you arrive')
• いい天気 (ii tenki, 'nice weather') → いい天気だったら (ii tenki dattara, 'if the weather is nice')

Note: たら often implies discovering something: 開けたら猫がいた (aketara neko ga ita, 'when I opened it, there was a cat'). It's the go-to conditional for beginners — it works in almost any situation.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩いた (aruita, past) + ら (ra) → 歩いたら (aruitara, 'if/when you walk')

grammar_points.name: 〜のままに (no mama ni: as it is; following)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + のままに (no mama ni) to express following something without resistance — 'as X dictates' or 'following the flow of X'. まま means 'as is' and に indicates manner.

Example from this song: 衝動のままに (shoudou no mama ni) = 'following the impulse / as the impulse dictates' — from 衝動 (shoudou, 'impulse') + の (no) + ままに (mama ni, 'as is')

More examples:
• 心 (kokoro, 'heart') → 心のままに (kokoro no mama ni, 'following your heart')
• 気持ち (kimochi, 'feeling') → 気持ちのままに (kimochi no mama ni, 'as your feelings dictate')
• 流れ (nagare, 'flow') → 流れのままに (nagare no mama ni, 'going with the flow')

Note: ままに implies surrendering control and letting something guide you. Without に, まま means the state remains unchanged: そのまま (sono mama, 'as it is').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 衝動 (shoudou, 'impulse') + の (no) + ままに (mama ni, 'following') → 衝動のままに (shoudou no mama ni, 'following the impulse')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to create a direct command. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with ろ.

Example from this song: 笑え (warae) = 'Laugh!', 泣け (nake) = 'Cry!', 叫べ (sakebe) = 'Shout!', 走れ (hashire) = 'Run!' — a series of commands rallying the listener.

More examples:
• 歌う (utau, 'to sing') → 歌え (utae, 'Sing!')
• 生きる (ikiru, 'to live') → 生きろ (ikiro, 'Live!')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しろ (shiro, 'Do it!')

Note: This song stacks multiple imperatives for powerful effect. Each godan verb simply changes its ending: う→え, く→け, ぶ→べ, る→れ. This pattern is very common in motivational rock songs.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 笑う (warau, 'to laugh') → 笑え (warae, 'Laugh!') / 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣け (nake, 'Cry!') / 叫ぶ (sakebu, 'to shout') → 叫べ (sakebe, 'Shout!') / 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')

grammar_points.name: 〜かな (kana: I wonder)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add かな (kana) at the end of a sentence to express wondering or uncertainty — 'I wonder if...' It's softer and more reflective than か (ka) alone.

Example from this song: 差すかな (sasu kana) = 'I wonder if it shines through' — from 差す (sasu, 'to shine/point') + かな (kana, 'I wonder')

More examples:
• 大丈夫 (daijoubu, 'okay') → 大丈夫かな (daijoubu kana, 'I wonder if it's okay')
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来るかな (kuru kana, 'I wonder if they'll come')
• いい (ii, 'good') → いいのかな (ii no kana, 'I wonder if it's alright')

Note: かな is used when talking to yourself or thinking aloud. Adding の before かな (のかな) adds more of an explanatory nuance. かな is gender-neutral, while かしら (kashira) is the traditional feminine equivalent.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 差す (sasu, 'to shine') + かな (kana, 'I wonder') → 差すかな (sasu kana, 'I wonder if it shines through')

grammar_points.name: 〜くらい (kurai: to the extent of)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add くらい (kurai) or ぐらい (gurai) after a word to express degree or extent — 'so much that' or 'to the point of'. It quantifies the intensity.

Example from this song: 痛いくらい強い (itai kurai tsuyoi) = 'strong to the point of being painful' — from 痛い (itai, 'painful') + くらい (kurai, 'to the extent of') + 強い (tsuyoi, 'strong')

More examples:
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣くくらい嬉しい (naku kurai ureshii, 'so happy I could cry')
• 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die') → 死ぬくらい好き (shinu kurai suki, 'I like it so much I could die')
• 一時間 (ichijikan, 'one hour') → 一時間くらい (ichijikan kurai, 'about one hour')

Note: くらい has two uses: 1) expressing extent/degree (this song), 2) expressing approximation — 'about/approximately'. Context makes the meaning clear.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 痛い (itai, 'painful') + くらい (kurai, 'to the extent of') + 強い (tsuyoi, 'strong') → 痛いくらい強い (itai kurai tsuyoi, 'strong to the point of pain')

grammar_points.name: 〜てる (teru: progressive contraction)

explanation.en:
How it works: In casual speech, 〜ている (te iru, progressive/resultative) is shortened to 〜てる (teru). This is extremely common in everyday Japanese and in songs.

Example from this song: 生きてる (ikiteru) = 'is living / is alive' — from 生きている (ikite iru, 'is living') → contracted to 生きてる (ikiteru)

More examples:
• 食べている (tabete iru, 'is eating') → 食べてる (tabeteru)
• 知っている (shitte iru, 'knows') → 知ってる (shitteru)
• 待っている (matte iru, 'is waiting') → 待ってる (matteru)

Note: This contraction happens in all tenses: てる (present), てた (past = ていた), てない (negative = ていない). Understanding this contraction is essential for understanding casual Japanese and song lyrics.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 生きている (ikite iru, 'is living') → 生きてる (ikiteru, 'is alive' — casual contraction)

grammar_points.name: 〜なきゃ (nakya: gotta; must)

explanation.en:
How it works: This is the most casual contraction of なければならない (nakereba naranai, 'must do'). Take the ない-form, drop い, change to なきゃ. It means 'gotta' or 'have to'.

Example from this song: 勝ち取らなきゃ (kachitoranakya) = 'gotta win/seize' — from 勝ち取る (kachitoru, 'to win/seize') → 勝ち取らない (kachitoranai) → 勝ち取らなきゃ (kachitoranakya)

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かなきゃ (ikanakya, 'gotta go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べなきゃ (tabenakya, 'gotta eat')
• 起きる (okiru, 'to wake up') → 起きなきゃ (okinakya, 'gotta wake up')

Note: Contraction chain: なければならない → なくてはいけない → なくちゃいけない → なくちゃ → なきゃ. Each step gets more casual. なきゃ is what you'd hear in everyday anime dialogue.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 勝ち取る (kachitoru, 'to seize') → 勝ち取らない (kachitoranai, negative) → 勝ち取らなきゃ (kachitoranakya, 'gotta seize')

grammar_points.name: Imperative form (命令形)

explanation.en:
How it works: For godan verbs, change the final -u to -e. For ichidan verbs, replace る with ろ. This creates a strong, direct command.

Example from this song: 断ち切れ (tachikire) = 'Cut it off!' — from 断ち切る (tachikiru, 'to sever') → 断ち切れ. Also 叫べ (sakebe) = 'Shout!' and 出し切れ (dashikire) = 'Give it all!'

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べろ (tabero, 'Eat!')
• 頑張る (ganbaru, 'to do your best') → 頑張れ (ganbare, 'Do your best!')

Note: The imperative is particularly powerful in this song as a rallying cry for freedom. 頑張れ (ganbare, 'Do your best!') is one of the most commonly heard imperatives in Japanese culture.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 断ち切る (tachikiru, 'to sever') → 断ち切れ (tachikire, 'Cut it off!') / 叫ぶ (sakebu, 'to shout') → 叫べ (sakebe, 'Shout!')

grammar_points.name: 〜ちゃう (chau: end up doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: This is the casual contraction of てしまう (te shimau). て + しまう → ちゃう, で + しまう → じゃう. It expresses completion, often with regret or an unintended outcome.

Example from this song: 渡っちゃう (watacchau) = 'end up crossing' — from 渡る (wataru, 'to cross') → 渡って (watatte) + しまう (shimau) → 渡っちゃう (watacchau)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べちゃう (tabechau, 'end up eating')
• 飲む (nomu, 'to drink') → 飲んじゃう (nonjau, 'end up drinking')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やっちゃう (yacchau, 'end up doing it')

Note: In this song, the 'ending up' nuance is more about determination than regret — 'I'll just go ahead and cross!' The context determines whether ちゃう sounds regretful or boldly decisive.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 渡る (wataru, 'to cross') → 渡って (watatte, te-form) + しまう (shimau) → 渡っちゃう (watacchau, 'end up crossing')

grammar_points.name: 〜次第 (shidai: depending on)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach 次第 (shidai) to a noun to mean 'depending on' or 'up to'. It can also attach to verb masu-stem to mean 'as soon as'.

Example from this song: 自分次第 (jibun shidai) = 'up to yourself / depends on you' — from 自分 (jibun, 'oneself') + 次第 (shidai, 'depending on')

More examples:
• 天気 (tenki, 'weather') → 天気次第 (tenki shidai, 'depending on the weather')
• 気持ち (kimochi, 'feelings') → 気持ち次第 (kimochi shidai, 'depends on how you feel')
• 届く (todoku, 'to arrive') → 届き次第 (todoki shidai, 'as soon as it arrives')

Note: Noun + 次第 = 'depends on'. Verb masu-stem + 次第 = 'as soon as'. 結果次第 (kekka shidai, 'depending on the results'). This is a common business/formal expression that also appears in motivational contexts.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 自分 (jibun, 'oneself') + 次第 (shidai, 'depending on') → 自分次第 (jibun shidai, 'up to yourself')

grammar_points.name: 〜んだ (nda: explanatory)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add んだ (nda) after a verb or adjective to provide explanatory emphasis — 'the fact is...' or 'it's that...'. It signals emotional weight or background context.

Example from this song: 決めるんだ (kimerunda) = 'I'm going to decide, you hear!' — from 決める (kimeru, 'to decide') + んだ (nda). Also 変わるんだ (kawarunda) = 'things will change!'

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くんだ (ikunda, 'I'm going!')
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じるんだ (shinjirunda, 'I believe in it!')
• 終わった (owatta, 'ended') → 終わったんだ (owattanda, 'it's over, you see')

Note: In this song's context, んだ adds determination and conviction. It turns a simple statement into a declaration. 俺が変えるんだ (ore ga kaerunda, 'I'm the one who'll change things!').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 決める (kimeru, 'to decide') → 決めるんだ (kimerunda, 'I'm going to decide!') / 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わるんだ (kawarunda, 'things will change!')

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて (nante: such a thing as)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place なんて (nante) after a noun or phrase to express surprise, dismissal, or emphasis about something unexpected — 'such a thing as' or 'something like'.

Example from this song: 先立つものなんてなくたって (sakidatsu mono nante nakutatte) = 'even without something like money upfront' — from 先立つもの (sakidatsu mono, 'money/resources upfront') + なんて (nante, 'such a thing as') + なくたって (nakutatte, 'even without')

More examples:
• 不可能 (fukanou, 'impossible') → 不可能なんてない (fukanou nante nai, 'there's no such thing as impossible')
• 嘘 (uso, 'lie') → 嘘なんて！ (uso nante!, 'A lie! — shocked')
• お金 (okane, 'money') → お金なんて関係ない (okane nante kankei nai, 'money doesn't matter')

Note: なんて is emotionally charged. It can dismiss (そんなのなんて, 'something like that — trivial'), express shock (まさかなんて, 'to think that...'), or rebel (ルールなんて, 'rules? Who cares!').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 先立つもの (sakidatsu mono, 'money upfront') + なんて (nante, 'such a thing as') + なくたって (nakutatte, 'even without') → 'even without something like money'

grammar_points.name: 〜にも...ない (not even / no one can)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine a question word (誰/dare = who, 何/nani = what, どこ/doko = where) with にも (ni mo) and a negative verb. This creates absolute negation — 'no one', 'nothing', 'nowhere'.

Example from this song: 誰にも見れない (dare ni mo mirenai) = 'no one can see' — from 誰 (dare, 'who') + にも (ni mo, 'even to') + 見れない (mirenai, 'cannot see')

More examples:
• 何も食べない (nani mo tabenai, 'eat nothing / don't eat anything')
• どこにも行かない (doko ni mo ikanai, 'don't go anywhere')
• 誰にも言わない (dare ni mo iwanai, 'won't tell anyone')

Note: The particle も (mo) combined with a negative verb creates total negation. Without the negative, も means 'also/even'. 誰にも (dare ni mo) + positive = 'to everyone'; + negative = 'to no one'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 誰 (dare, 'who') + にも (ni mo, 'even to') + 見れない (mirenai, 'cannot see') = 誰にも見れない (dare ni mo mirenai, 'no one can see')

grammar_points.name: 〜ても concessive (even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) of a verb and add も (mo). This creates 'even if' — the outcome remains the same regardless of the condition.

Example from this song: とられても (toraretemo) = 'even if taken away' — from とられる (torareru, 'to be taken', passive) → とられて (torarete, te-form) + も (mo)

More examples:
• 失敗する (shippai suru, 'to fail') → 失敗しても (shippai shitemo, 'even if I fail')
• 雨が降る (ame ga furu, 'it rains') → 雨が降っても (ame ga futtemo, 'even if it rains')
• 難しい (muzukashii, 'difficult') → 難しくても (muzukashikutemo, 'even if it's difficult')

Note: This is one of the most common concessive patterns in Japanese. For い-adjectives, change い to くても. For な-adjectives/nouns, use でも (demo).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: とられる (torareru, 'to be taken') → とられて (torarete, te-form) → とられても (toraretemo, 'even if taken away')

grammar_points.name: 〜きれない (can't completely)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add きれない (kirenai). This means 'cannot completely do' or 'unable to do all of'. きる (kiru) as an auxiliary means 'to do completely'.

Example from this song: 押さえきれない (osae kirenai) = 'can't hold back completely' — from 押さえる (osaeru, 'to hold back') → 押さえ (osae, masu-stem) + きれない (kirenai, 'can't completely')

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べきれない (tabe kirenai, 'can't eat it all')
• 数える (kazoeru, 'to count') → 数えきれない (kazoe kirenai, 'too many to count')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言いきれない (ii kirenai, 'can't say everything')

Note: The positive form きる (kiru) means 'to do completely': 食べきる (tabe kiru, 'eat it all'). The negative きれない expresses the impossibility of completing the action.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 押さえる (osaeru, 'to hold back') → 押さえ (osae, masu-stem) + きれない (kirenai, 'can't completely') → 押さえきれない (osae kirenai, 'can't completely hold back')

grammar_points.name: 〜から (because)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place から (kara) at the end of a clause to express a reason — 'because'. It follows verbs, adjectives, or nouns (with だ/da).

Example from this song: The lyrics use から to explain motivations and reasons for the speaker's feelings and actions.

More examples:
• 暑い (atsui, 'hot') → 暑いから (atsui kara, 'because it's hot')
• 好きだ (suki da, 'like') → 好きだから (suki da kara, 'because I like it')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くから (iku kara, 'because I'm going')

Note: から is more subjective and personal compared to ので (node), which sounds more objective and polite. In casual speech, から is much more common. The reason comes before から, and the result follows.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [reason clause] + から (kara, 'because') → [result clause]

grammar_points.name: 〜ほど...ない (not to the extent)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use ほど (hodo, 'to the extent') with a negative verb to say 'not as much as' or 'not to the point of'. It sets an upper limit that isn't reached.

Example from this song: The lyrics use this pattern to express that something doesn't reach a certain degree or intensity.

More examples:
• 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die') → 死ぬほどではない (shinu hodo dewa nai, 'not to the point of dying')
• 彼 (kare, 'he') → 彼ほど強くない (kare hodo tsuyokunai, 'not as strong as him')
• 昨日 (kinou, 'yesterday') → 昨日ほど寒くない (kinou hodo samukunai, 'not as cold as yesterday')

Note: ほど alone means 'to the extent that': 泣くほど嬉しい (naku hodo ureshii, 'so happy I could cry'). Adding ない makes it 'not to that extent'. This is useful for softened comparisons.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [noun/verb] + ほど (hodo, 'to the extent') + [negative] = 'not as much as...'

grammar_points.name: 〜ぬ archaic negative

explanation.en:
How it works: Replace the modern negative ending ない (nai) with ぬ (nu). This is the classical Japanese negative, used in literary contexts, poetry, and song lyrics for a dramatic or elevated tone.

Example from this song: 知らぬ (shiranu) = 'not knowing' — from 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知らない (shiranai, modern negative) → 知らぬ (shiranu, archaic negative)

More examples:
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見えぬ (mienu, 'cannot see')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わぬ (iwanu, 'do not say')
• 消える (kieru, 'to disappear') → 消えぬ (kienu, 'does not disappear')

Note: ぬ is the attributive form (can modify nouns directly). The base form is ず (zu): 知らず (shirazu, 'without knowing'). Both appear in anime songs for poetic gravity.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知らない (shiranai, modern negative) → 知らぬ (shiranu, archaic negative, 'not knowing')

grammar_points.name: 〜なくていい (nakute ii: don't have to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the negative て-form (なくて, nakute) and add いい (ii, 'good') to express 'you don't have to do X' — giving permission not to do something.

Example from this song: 強がらなくていい (tsuyo garanakute ii) = 'you don't have to pretend to be strong' — from 強がる (tsuyogaru, 'to act tough') → 強がらなくて (tsuyo garanakute, negative te-form) + いい (ii, 'fine')

More examples:
• 我慢する (gaman suru, 'to endure') → 我慢しなくていい (gaman shinakute ii, 'you don't have to endure it')
• 隠す (kakusu, 'to hide') → 隠さなくていい (kakusanakute ii, 'you don't have to hide it')
• 急ぐ (isogu, 'to hurry') → 急がなくていい (isoganakute ii, 'you don't have to hurry')

Note: This is a comforting, liberating expression — 'it's okay, you don't need to'. Very common in emotional moments. The song's title 'Let it Out' matches this grammar perfectly — stop holding back.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 強がる (tsuyogaru, 'to act tough') → 強がらない (tsuyo garanai, negative) → 強がらなくて (tsuyo garanakute) + いい (ii, 'fine') → 強がらなくていい (tsuyo garanakute ii, 'you don't have to act tough')

grammar_points.name: 〜たり〜たり (tari tari: doing things like)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add たり (tari) to the past form of two or more verbs, usually ending with する, to list representative actions — 'doing things like X and Y'. It implies there are more actions too.

Example from this song: 失くしたり拾ったり (nakushitari hirottari) = 'losing things and picking them up (among other things)' — from 失くす (nakusu, 'to lose') → 失くしたり and 拾う (hirou, 'to pick up') → 拾ったり

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') / 飲む (nomu, 'to drink') → 食べたり飲んだりする (tabetari nondari suru, 'doing things like eating and drinking')
• 笑う (warau, 'to laugh') / 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 笑ったり泣いたりする (warattari naitari suru, 'laughing and crying')
• 読む (yomu, 'to read') / 書く (kaku, 'to write') → 読んだり書いたりする (yondari kaitari suru, 'reading and writing and such')

Note: Formation: past form + り. 食べた → 食べたり. 飲んだ → 飲んだり. The たり list is incomplete by nature — it implies 'and other things'. Usually ends with する but not always in casual speech.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 失くす (nakusu, 'to lose') → 失くしたり (nakushitari) / 拾う (hirou, 'to pick up') → 拾ったり (hirottari) → 失くしたり拾ったり (nakushitari hirottari, 'losing and picking up and such')

grammar_points.name: 〜ちゃう (chau: end up doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Replace てしまう (te shimau) with ちゃう (chau) in casual speech. It expresses that something happened completely, often unintentionally or regrettably.

Example from this song: 泣いちゃう (naichau) = 'end up crying' — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣いて (naite, te-form) + しまう (shimau) → casual: 泣いちゃう (naichau)

More examples:
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れちゃう (wasurechau, 'end up forgetting')
• 壊す (kowasu, 'to break') → 壊しちゃう (kowashichau, 'accidentally break')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べちゃう (tabechau, 'end up eating')

Note: Contraction rules: てしまう → ちゃう, でしまう → じゃう. Past: ちゃった/じゃった. 泣いちゃう often carries a cute, helpless nuance — 'I just can't help crying'. Very natural in everyday speech.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣いて (naite, te-form) + しまう (shimau) → 泣いちゃう (naichau, 'end up crying' — casual contraction)

grammar_points.name: 〜よう (you: volitional / let's)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to the volitional form to express intention ('I'll do X') or invitation ('let's do X'). For -ru verbs: drop る, add よう. For -u verbs: change final syllable to お-row + う.

Example from this song: 変えよう (kaeyou) = 'let's change it' — from 変える (kaeru, 'to change') → 変えよう (kaeyou). Also: 作ろう (tsukurou) = 'let's make' and 探そう (sagasou) = 'let's search'

More examples:
• 始める (hajimeru, 'to start') → 始めよう (hajimeyou, 'let's start')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行こう (ikou, 'let's go')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しよう (shiyou, 'let's do it')

Note: Ichidan: る→よう. Godan: く→こう, す→そう, つ→とう, む→もう. The song uses multiple volitional forms to create an uplifting, action-oriented mood: 'let's change, let's create, let's search!'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 変える (kaeru, 'to change') → 変えよう (kaeyou, 'let's change') / 作る (tsukuru, 'to make') → 作ろう (tsukurou, 'let's make') / 探す (sagasu, 'to search') → 探そう (sagasou, 'let's search')

grammar_points.name: 〜かもしれない (kamoshirenai: might)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add かもしれない (kamoshirenai) after a verb, adjective, or noun to express possibility or uncertainty — 'it might be' or 'perhaps'. It indicates the speaker isn't sure.

Example from this song: 来るかもしれない (kuru kamoshirenai) = 'it might come' — expressing the uncertain hope that something may arrive.

More examples:
• 雨 (ame, 'rain') → 雨かもしれない (ame kamoshirenai, 'it might rain')
• 遅い (osoi, 'late') → 遅いかもしれない (osoi kamoshirenai, 'it might be late')
• 間違い (machigai, 'mistake') → 間違いかもしれない (machigai kamoshirenai, 'it might be a mistake')

Note: Casual forms: かもしれない → かもしれん → かも. Just かも is very common in speech: 雨かも (ame kamo, 'it might rain'). It expresses less certainty than だろう (darou, 'probably').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 来る (kuru, 'to come') + かもしれない (kamoshirenai, 'might') → 来るかもしれない (kuru kamoshirenai, 'it might come')

grammar_points.name: 〜ないでいる (naide iru: to remain not doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use the negative て-form ないで (naide, 'without doing') + いる (iru, 'to be') to express deliberately maintaining a state of NOT doing something — 'to remain without doing X'.

Example from this song: 変わらないでいよう (kawaranaide iyou) = 'let's stay unchanged / let's remain as we are' — from 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わらないで (kawaranaide, 'without changing') + いよう (iyou, volitional of いる, 'let's be')

More examples:
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れないでいる (wasurenaide iru, 'to remain not forgetting')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣かないでいる (nakanaide iru, 'to hold back tears')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わないでいる (iwanaide iru, 'to keep not saying it')

Note: This pattern implies a conscious choice to maintain a state. 変わらないでいよう is a beautiful wish — choosing together to stay as you are. The volitional いよう makes it an invitation.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わらないで (kawaranaide, 'without changing') + いよう (iyou, 'let's be') → 変わらないでいよう (kawaranaide iyou, 'let's stay unchanged')

grammar_points.name: 〜の方が (no hou ga: the ... one is more)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use A の方が (no hou ga) + adjective to express that A has MORE of that quality. It's the comparison pattern — 'A is more [adj] (than B)'.

Example from this song: 嘘の方がずっと痛かった (uso no hou ga zutto itakatta) = 'the lie was far more painful' — from 嘘 (uso, 'lie') + の方が (no hou ga, 'is more') + ずっと (zutto, 'far more') + 痛かった (itakatta, 'was painful')

More examples:
• こっち (kocchi, 'this one') → こっちの方がいい (kocchi no hou ga ii, 'this one is better')
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩いた方がいい (aruita hou ga ii, 'it's better to walk')
• 夏 (natsu, 'summer') → 夏の方が好き (natsu no hou ga suki, 'I like summer more')

Note: For nouns: A の方が. For verbs (advice): た-form + 方がいい = 'you should'. ずっと (zutto, 'much more') intensifies the comparison. This song's line powerfully says lies hurt MORE than the truth.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 嘘 (uso, 'lie') + の方が (no hou ga, 'is more') + ずっと (zutto, 'far') + 痛かった (itakatta, 'was painful') → 嘘の方がずっと痛かった (uso no hou ga zutto itakatta, 'the lie was far more painful')
