grammar_points.name: 〜故に (yue ni - because of)

explanation.en:
A literary and formal way to say "because of" or "due to." It sounds much more elegant than the everyday から (kara) or ので (node). You will mostly find it in written Japanese, poetry, and song lyrics.

How it works:
Attach 故に (yue ni) after a verb in past tense, a noun, or a na-adjective + な. It marks the reason or cause for what follows.

Example from this song:
愛した故に芽生えた悪の花 (aishita yue ni mebaeta aku no hana, "Because I loved, a flower of evil bloomed")

More examples:
- 若さ故に (wakasa yue ni, "because of youth")
- 知らなかった故に (shiranakatta yue ni, "because I did not know")
- 彼女が好きだった故に (kanojo ga suki datta yue ni, "because I liked her")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 愛する (aisuru) → 愛した (aishita) → 愛した故に (aishita yue ni)

grammar_points.name: 〜であろう (de arou - probably is/will be)

explanation.en:
A formal way to express conjecture or probability, similar to "will probably be" or "is likely." This is the volitional form of である (de aru), which is the formal equivalent of だ (da). You will encounter it in literature, formal speeches, and dramatic lyrics.

How it works:
Place であろう (de arou) after a noun or na-adjective stem. It replaces だろう (darou) in formal/literary registers.

Example from this song:
これから先訪れるであろう全てを (korekara saki otozureru de arou subete o, "Everything that will likely come from here on")

More examples:
- 困難であろう (konnan de arou, "it will probably be difficult")
- 彼は天才であろう (kare wa tensai de arou, "he is probably a genius")
- 正しいであろう判断 (tadashii de arou handan, "a judgment that is probably correct")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: である (de aru) → であろう (de arou, volitional conjecture)

grammar_points.name: 〜ワケにはいかない (wake ni wa ikanai - cannot do)

explanation.en:
Expresses that something "cannot be done" due to social, moral, or situational reasons. It is stronger than できない (dekinai, "cannot") because it implies the speaker feels a moral or social obligation not to do something.

How it works:
Attach ワケにはいかない (wake ni wa ikanai) after the dictionary form of a verb. The verb describes the action that is unacceptable.

Example from this song:
誰にも邪魔させるワケにはいかないから (dare ni mo jama saseru wake ni wa ikanai kara, "Because I cannot allow anyone to get in the way")

More examples:
- ここで諦めるワケにはいかない (koko de akirameru wake ni wa ikanai, "I cannot give up here")
- 嘘をつくワケにはいかない (uso o tsuku wake ni wa ikanai, "I cannot tell a lie")
- 友達を裏切るワケにはいかない (tomodachi o uragiru wake ni wa ikanai, "I cannot betray my friend")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 邪魔する (jama suru) → 邪魔させる (jama saseru, causative) + ワケにはいかない (wake ni wa ikanai)

grammar_points.name: 〜させる (saseru - causative form)

explanation.en:
The causative form expresses "make someone do" or "let someone do" something. It is one of the key verb conjugations in Japanese.

How it works:
For ichidan (ru-) verbs: drop る (ru) and add させる (saseru).
For godan (u-) verbs: change the last vowel to the あ (a) column and add せる (seru).

Example from this song:
誰にも邪魔させるワケにはいかない (dare ni mo jama saseru wake ni wa ikanai, "I cannot let anyone interfere")

More examples:
- 子供を遊ばせる (kodomo o asobaseru, "to let the child play")
- 食べさせる (tabesaseru, "to make/let someone eat")
- 先生が学生に本を読ませた (sensei ga gakusei ni hon o yomaseta, "The teacher made the students read a book")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 邪魔する (jama suru) → 邪魔させる (jama saseru, causative)

grammar_points.name: 〜てあげる (te ageru - do for someone)

explanation.en:
Expresses doing something as a favor for someone else. It adds a "giving" nuance to the action, meaning "I will do [this] for you."

How it works:
Take the て-form (te-form) of a verb and add あげる (ageru). The subject does the action for the benefit of another person.

Example from this song:
いつか僕が見せてあげる光り輝く世界を (itsuka boku ga misete ageru hikari kagayaku sekai o, "Someday I will show you a brilliantly shining world")

More examples:
- 教えてあげる (oshiete ageru, "I will teach you")
- 手伝ってあげた (tetsudatte ageta, "I helped them out")
- 作ってあげよう (tsukutte ageyou, "Let me make it for you")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 見せる (miseru) → 見せて (misete) → 見せてあげる (misete ageru)

grammar_points.name: 〜合う (au - mutual/reciprocal action)

explanation.en:
When attached to a verb stem, 合う (au) indicates that two or more people do an action to/for each other. It turns a one-way action into a mutual, reciprocal one.

How it works:
Take the masu-stem of a verb (remove ます) and add 合う (au). This creates a compound verb meaning "do X together/to each other."

Example from this song:
交わし合った革命の契り (kawashi atta kakumei no chigiri, "The revolutionary oath we exchanged together")

More examples:
- 助け合う (tasuke au, "to help each other")
- 話し合う (hanashi au, "to discuss together")
- 愛し合う (aishi au, "to love each other")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 交わす (kawasu) → 交わし (kawashi, masu-stem) + 合う (au) → 交わし合う (kawashi au)

grammar_points.name: 〜なき (literary negation, 'without')

explanation.en:
How it works: なき (naki) is the classical/literary form of ない (nai, 'without/not'), used to modify nouns. It gives a poetic, timeless quality.

Example from this song: 終わりなき (owari naki) = 'endless / without end' — from 終わり (owari, 'end') + なき (naki, literary 'without')

More examples:
• 果てなき旅 (hate naki tabi, 'an endless journey') — from 果て (hate, 'end')
• 名もなき花 (na mo naki hana, 'a nameless flower') — from 名 (na, 'name')
• 限りなき愛 (kagiri naki ai, 'limitless love') — from 限り (kagiri, 'limit')

Note: なき is the literary equivalent of ない used as an adjective. Modern Japanese would say 終わりのない (owari no nai). なき appears in song titles, poetry, and formal writing for its elegance.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 終わり (owari, 'end') + なき (naki, literary 'without') → 終わりなき (owari naki, 'endless / without end')

grammar_points.name: 〜かけて (on the verge of)

explanation.en:
How it works: かける (kakeru) attached to a verb's masu-stem means 'about to,' 'on the verge of,' or 'half-done.' It expresses an incomplete or starting action.

Example from this song: 掴みかけて (tsukami kakete) = 'on the verge of grasping' — from 掴む (tsukamu, 'to grasp') → 掴み (tsukami, stem) + かけて (kakete)

More examples:
• 死にかける (shini kakeru, 'nearly die') — from 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die')
• 言いかけて止めた (ii kakete yameta, 'started to say but stopped') — from 言う (iu, 'to say')
• 食べかけのパン (tabe kake no pan, 'half-eaten bread') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')

Note: 〜かけ as a noun modifier means 'half-done': 読みかけの本 (yomikake no hon, 'half-read book'). The て-form かけて connects to the next action: 'was on the verge of X, and then...'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 掴む (tsukamu, 'to grasp') → 掴み (tsukami, stem) + かけて (kakete, 'on the verge of') → 掴みかけて (tsukami kakete, 'on the verge of grasping')

grammar_points.name: けして〜ない (never)

explanation.en:
How it works: けして (keshite) or 決して (keshite) combined with a negative verb means 'never' or 'by no means.' It creates an emphatic absolute negation.

Example from this song: The song uses けして...ない to express something that will absolutely never happen — an unbreakable resolve.

More examples:
• 決して忘れない (keshite wasurenai, 'I will never forget') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')
• 決して諦めない (keshite akiramenai, 'I will never give up') — from 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up')
• 決して許さない (keshite yurusanai, 'I will never forgive') — from 許す (yurusu, 'to forgive')

Note: 決して must always pair with a negative form. Never use it with positive verbs. It's stronger than ぜんぜん〜ない (zenzen ~nai, 'not at all'). 決して expresses firm determination.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 決して (keshite, 'never') + verb negative form → 決して〜ない (keshite ~nai, 'absolutely never')

grammar_points.name: 〜ずに (without doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: ずに (zu ni) is the classical negative te-form meaning 'without doing.' Replace ない with ず and add に to connect to the next action.

Example from this song: 逸らさずに (sorasazu ni) = 'without averting (one's gaze)' — from 逸らす (sorasu, 'to avert') → 逸らさない (sorasanai) → 逸らさず (sorasazu) + に (ni)

More examples:
• 食べずに寝た (tabezu ni neta, 'slept without eating') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 迷わずに進む (mayowazu ni susumu, 'advance without hesitating') — from 迷う (mayou, 'to hesitate')
• 諦めずに頑張る (akiramezu ni ganbaru, 'keep trying without giving up')

Note: ずに = literary ないで. Exception: する → せずに (sezu ni), not しずに. ず can also stand alone without に in literary contexts: 言わず語らず (iwazu katarazu, 'without saying or telling').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 逸らす (sorasu, 'to avert') → 逸らさない (sorasanai) → 逸らさず (sorasazu) + に (ni) → 逸らさずに (sorasazu ni, 'without averting')

grammar_points.name: 〜ために (for the sake of)

explanation.en:
How it works: ために (tame ni) expresses purpose ('in order to') or benefit ('for the sake of'). After a verb dictionary form, it means 'in order to do.' After a noun + の, it means 'for the sake of.'

Example from this song: The song uses ために to express what the speaker is striving for — the purpose behind their actions.

More examples:
• 合格するために勉強する (goukaku suru tame ni benkyou suru, 'study in order to pass')
• 家族のために働く (kazoku no tame ni hataraku, 'work for the family')
• 健康のために走る (kenkou no tame ni hashiru, 'run for health')

Note: Verb + ために = 'in order to (do).' Noun + のために = 'for the sake of (noun).' Compare with ように, which is for non-volitional results.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb dictionary form + ために (tame ni, 'in order to') / noun + の + ために (no tame ni, 'for the sake of')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていく (continuing into the future)

explanation.en:
How it works: ていく (te iku) expresses an action or change continuing from now into the future. It shows forward progression through time.

Example from this song: 生きていく (ikite iku) = 'will go on living' — from 生きる (ikiru, 'to live') → 生きて (ikite) + いく (iku, 'to go')

More examples:
• 強くなっていく (tsuyoku natte iku, 'getting stronger and stronger')
• 変わっていく (kawatte iku, 'keeps changing over time') — from 変わる (kawaru, 'to change')
• 学んでいく (manande iku, 'will continue learning') — from 学ぶ (manabu, 'to learn')

Note: ていく shows future-directed change. てくる shows past-to-present change. 生きていく is a powerful expression meaning 'I will go on living' — often used to express determination in the face of difficulty.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 生きる (ikiru, 'to live') → 生きて (ikite) + いく (iku, 'to go') → 生きていく (ikite iku, 'will go on living')

grammar_points.name: 〜たら conditional

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the past tense (た-form) of a verb and add ら (ra). This creates a conditional meaning 'if' or 'when'. It's the most versatile conditional in Japanese.

Example from this song: はばたいたら (habataitara) = 'if I spread my wings' — from はばたく (habataku, 'to flap wings') → はばたいた (habataita, past) + ら (ra)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたら (tabetara, 'if/when I eat')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行ったら (ittara, 'if/when I go')
• 安い (yasui, 'cheap') → 安かったら (yasukattara, 'if it's cheap')

Note: たら is the most conversational conditional. It works for hypothetical, real, and one-time conditions. It also implies a time sequence — 'when X happens, then Y'. Compare: ば (more hypothetical), と (natural/automatic result), なら (topic-based).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: はばたく (habataku, 'to flap wings') → はばたいた (habataita, past) → はばたいたら (habataitara, 'if I spread my wings')

grammar_points.name: 〜のは...だ (emphasis/focus)

explanation.en:
How it works: Wrap a clause with のは...だ to emphasize or focus on a specific element. のは nominalizes the clause ('the one who...', 'the thing that...'), and だ concludes. This is like English cleft sentences: 'It is X that...'.

Example from this song: The lyrics use this pattern to focus attention on what truly matters in the speaker's journey.

More examples:
• 教えてくれたのは先生だ (oshiete kureta no wa sensei da, 'it was the teacher who taught me')
• 一番大切なのは友達だ (ichiban taisetsu na no wa tomodachi da, 'what's most important is friends')
• 泣いたのは嬉しかったからだ (naita no wa ureshikatta kara da, 'the reason I cried is because I was happy')

Note: This is a focus/emphasis construction, not just a statement. It draws attention to the specific element between のは and だ.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [clause] + のは (no wa, nominalizer + topic) ... だ (da, 'it is') = emphasis pattern

grammar_points.name: 〜ず literary negative

explanation.en:
How it works: Replace the negative ない (nai) ending with ず (zu). This is the classical negative conjunctive form, meaning 'without doing' or 'not doing'. It's equivalent to modern ないで (naide).

Example from this song: 覚えられず (oboerarazu) = 'unable to remember' — from 覚えられる (oboerareru, 'can remember') → 覚えられない (oboerarenai) → 覚えられず (oboerarazu, literary negative)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べず (tabezu, 'without eating')
• 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知らず (shirazu, 'without knowing')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わず (iwazu, 'without saying')

Note: ず is the conjunctive form (connects to the next clause). ぬ is the attributive form (modifies nouns). Both are classical negatives. する becomes せず (sezu). You'll encounter ず frequently in anime lyrics and proverbs.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 覚えられる (oboerareru, 'can remember') → 覚えられない (oboerarenai, modern negative) → 覚えられず (oboerarazu, 'unable to remember')

grammar_points.name: 〜はじめる (begin to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add はじめる (hajimeru, 'to begin'). This creates a compound verb meaning 'to begin doing something'.

Example from this song: つかみはじめた (tsukami hajimeta) = 'began to grasp' — from つかむ (tsukamu, 'to grasp') → つかみ (tsukami, masu-stem) + はじめた (hajimeta, past of hajimeru)

More examples:
• 降る (furu, 'to fall') → 降りはじめる (furi hajimeru, 'begin to fall — rain starting')
• 読む (yomu, 'to read') → 読みはじめる (yomi hajimeru, 'begin to read')
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かりはじめる (wakari hajimeru, 'begin to understand')

Note: Compare with 〜だす (dasu), which also means 'begin to' but implies a more sudden or unexpected start. はじめる is a gradual, intentional beginning.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: つかむ (tsukamu, 'to grasp') → つかみ (tsukami, masu-stem) + はじめる (hajimeru, 'to begin') → つかみはじめた (tsukami hajimeta, 'began to grasp')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていく (gradual change/departure)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) and add いく (iku, 'to go'). This expresses a gradual change moving away from the present or an action continuing into the future.

Example from this song: 変わっていく (kawatte iku) = 'keep changing (going forward)' — from 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わって (kawatte, te-form) + いく (iku)

More examples:
• 消える (kieru, 'to disappear') → 消えていく (kiete iku, 'gradually disappear')
• 強くなる (tsuyoku naru, 'to become strong') → 強くなっていく (tsuyoku natte iku, 'keep getting stronger')
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れていく (wasurete iku, 'gradually forget')

Note: 〜ていく (moving away/forward) vs. 〜てくる (approaching/building up). Think of it as direction: いく = away from now, くる = toward now.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わって (kawatte, te-form) → 変わっていく (kawatte iku, 'keep changing')

grammar_points.name: 〜ほど (to the extent that)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place ほど (hodo) after a verb or noun to indicate degree — 'to the extent that' or 'the more... the more...'. It shows how much of something there is.

Example from this song: The lyrics use ほど to express the intensity of feelings and experiences.

More examples:
• 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die') → 死ぬほど疲れた (shinu hodo tsukareta, 'tired enough to die — exhausted')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣くほど嬉しい (naku hodo ureshii, 'so happy I could cry')
• 食べる (taberu) + ほど → 食べれば食べるほど (tabereba taberu hodo, 'the more you eat, the more...')

Note: The pattern [verb-ば] [same verb-dictionary] + ほど means 'the more you do, the more...'. This is very common: 知れば知るほど (shireba shiru hodo, 'the more you know, the more...').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [verb/noun] + ほど (hodo, 'to the extent that')

grammar_points.name: 〜ことは...ない (never/won't)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place ことは (koto wa) after a verb's dictionary form and follow with ない (nai). This creates a firm statement: 'I will never do X' or 'there is no doing X'.

Example from this song: The lyrics use this pattern to express a firm resolve — there's something the speaker absolutely won't do.

More examples:
• 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up') → 諦めることはない (akirameru koto wa nai, 'there's no giving up / I won't give up')
• 後悔する (koukai suru, 'to regret') → 後悔することはない (koukai suru koto wa nai, 'there's nothing to regret')
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れることはない (wasureru koto wa nai, 'I'll never forget')

Note: This sounds more reflective and decisive than simply using ない. It turns the action into an abstract concept (こと = 'the act of') and negates it entirely.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [verb dictionary form] + ことはない (koto wa nai, 'there is no doing X / will never X')

grammar_points.name: 〜ておく

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) and add おく (oku, 'to place'). This means doing something in advance or in preparation for later. The idea is 'placing' the action's result for future use.

Example from this song: 呼んでおいた (yonde oita) = 'called (in advance)' — from 呼ぶ (yobu, 'to call') → 呼んで (yonde, te-form) + おいた (oita, past of oku)

More examples:
• 買う (kau, 'to buy') → 買っておく (katte oku, 'buy in advance')
• 調べる (shiraberu, 'to check') → 調べておく (shirabete oku, 'check beforehand')
• 準備する (junbi suru, 'to prepare') → 準備しておく (junbi shite oku, 'prepare in advance')

Note: In casual speech, ておく contracts to とく (toku): 買っとく (kattoku, 'buy ahead of time'). Past: 買っといた (kattoita). This contraction is very common.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 呼ぶ (yobu, 'to call') → 呼んで (yonde, te-form) → 呼んでおいた (yonde oita, 'called in advance')

grammar_points.name: 〜ちゃう / 〜じゃう

explanation.en:
How it works: These are casual contractions of 〜てしまう (te shimau) and 〜でしまう (de shimau). They express completion with regret, or something happening unintentionally.

Example from this song: つまんなくなっちゃう (tsumannaku nacchau) = 'end up getting bored' — from つまらなくなる (tsumaranaku naru, 'to become boring') → つまんなくなって (tsumannaku natte) + しまう (shimau) → なっちゃう (nacchau)

More examples:
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れちゃう (wasurechau, 'end up forgetting')
• 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die') → 死んじゃう (shinjau, 'end up dying')
• 壊れる (kowareru, 'to break') → 壊れちゃう (kowarechau, 'end up breaking')

Note: て + しまう = ちゃう. で + しまう = じゃう. Past: ちゃった/じゃった. These contractions are the default in casual speech — using the full てしまう sounds somewhat formal.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: つまらなくなる (tsumaranaku naru, 'to become boring') → つまんなくなっちゃう (tsumannaku nacchau, 'end up getting bored')

grammar_points.name: 〜そうで〜ない

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add そう (sou, 'looks like') + で (de, connecting) + the potential negative. This expresses frustrated expectation — 'it seems like it would X, but it won't/can't'.

Example from this song: 壊れそうで壊せない (kowaresou de kowasenai) = 'seems like it would break but I can't break it' — from 壊れる (kowareru, 'to break') → 壊れそう (kowaresou, 'looks like it'll break') + で + 壊せない (kowasenai, 'can't break')

More examples:
• 届く (todoku, 'to reach') → 届きそうで届かない (todokisou de todokanai, 'seems within reach but can't reach')
• できる (dekiru, 'can do') → できそうでできない (dekisou de dekinai, 'seems doable but can't do it')

Note: This pattern captures a relatable frustration — something that appears possible but isn't. It's a powerful emotional expression in song lyrics.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 壊れる (kowareru, 'to break') → 壊れそう (kowaresou, 'seems breakable') + で (de) + 壊せない (kowasenai, 'can't break') = 壊れそうで壊せない (kowaresou de kowasenai, 'seems breakable but can't break')

grammar_points.name: 〜んだ (explanatory)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add んだ (nda) after a statement to give explanatory nuance — 'you see...' or 'the thing is...'. It signals emotional emphasis or background context.

Example from this song: 痛いんだ (itainda) = 'it hurts, you see' — from 痛い (itai, 'painful') + んだ (nda, explanatory)

More examples:
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなんだ (suki nanda, 'the thing is, I like it')
• 行きたい (ikitai, 'want to go') → 行きたいんだ (ikitainda, 'the thing is, I want to go')
• 分からない (wakaranai, 'don't understand') → 分からないんだ (wakaranainda, 'the thing is, I don't understand')

Note: After い-adjectives and verbs, just add んだ. After な-adjectives and nouns, add なんだ. This is among the most common patterns in casual Japanese — you'll hear it constantly in anime.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 痛い (itai, 'painful') → 痛いんだ (itainda, 'it hurts, you see')

grammar_points.name: 〜ても (even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) and add も (mo). This means 'even if' — the result holds true regardless of the condition.

Example from this song: もがいても (mogaitemo) = 'even if you struggle' — from もがく (mogaku, 'to struggle') → もがいて (mogaite, te-form) + も (mo)

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走っても (hashittemo, 'even if I run')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣いても (naitemo, 'even if I cry')
• 高い (takai, 'expensive') → 高くても (takakutemo, 'even if it's expensive')

Note: With question words, it becomes 'no matter': 何をしても (nani o shitemo, 'no matter what I do'), どこへ行っても (doko e ittemo, 'no matter where I go').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: もがく (mogaku, 'to struggle') → もがいて (mogaite, te-form) → もがいても (mogaitemo, 'even if you struggle')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative)

explanation.en:
How it works: For godan (u-verbs), change the final -u to -e. For ichidan (ru-verbs), replace る with ろ. This creates a direct, forceful command.

Example from this song: 切り開け (kirihirake) = 'Carve it open!' — from 切り開く (kirihiraku, 'to carve open') → change く (ku) to け (ke)

More examples:
• 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand') → 立て (tate, 'Stand!')
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見ろ (miro, 'Look!')

Note: The imperative is strong and masculine. It's common in anime songs, sports, and emotional outbursts. For polite requests, use てください (te kudasai) instead. Negative imperative: [dictionary form] + な (na) = 'Don't!'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 切り開く (kirihiraku, 'to carve open') → 切り開け (kirihirake, 'Carve it open!')

grammar_points.name: 〜すぎる (too much)

explanation.en:
How it works: For い-adjectives, drop い and add すぎる (sugiru). For verbs, use the masu-stem + すぎる. This expresses 'too much' of a quality or action.

Example from this song: 青すぎた (ao sugita) = 'was too blue' — from 青い (aoi, 'blue') → drop い, add すぎた (sugita, past of sugiru) → 青すぎた

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べすぎる (tabe sugiru, 'eat too much')
• 高い (takai, 'expensive') → 高すぎる (taka sugiru, 'too expensive')
• 飲む (nomu, 'to drink') → 飲みすぎる (nomi sugiru, 'drink too much')

Note: すぎる itself is an ichidan verb, so it conjugates: すぎた (past), すぎない (negative), すぎて (te-form). 食べすぎて気持ち悪い (tabe sugite kimochi warui, 'ate too much and feel sick').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 青い (aoi, 'blue') → 青すぎた (ao sugita, 'was too blue')

grammar_points.name: 〜くらい / ぐらい (to the extent)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place くらい (kurai) or ぐらい (gurai) after a verb or noun to express degree — 'to the extent of' or 'about/approximately'.

Example from this song: 息もできないくらい (iki mo dekinai kurai) = 'to the extent of not being able to breathe' — from 息もできない (iki mo dekinai, 'can't even breathe') + くらい (kurai, 'to the extent')

More examples:
• 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die') → 死ぬくらい痛い (shinu kurai itai, 'hurts so much I could die')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣くくらい嬉しい (naku kurai ureshii, 'so happy I could cry')
• 3時間 (san jikan, '3 hours') → 3時間くらい (san jikan kurai, 'about 3 hours')

Note: くらい and ぐらい are interchangeable. With verbs, it means 'to the extent that'. With numbers, it means 'approximately'. Both are very common in everyday Japanese.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 息もできない (iki mo dekinai, 'can't even breathe') + くらい (kurai, 'to the extent') → 息もできないくらい (iki mo dekinai kurai, 'to the extent of not being able to breathe')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていく (moving away/continuing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) and add いく (iku, 'to go'). This expresses an action continuing into the future or gradually moving away.

Example from this song: 遠ざかっていく (toozakatte iku) = 'moving farther away' — from 遠ざかる (toozakaru, 'to move away') → 遠ざかって (toozakatte, te-form) + いく (iku)

More examples:
• 薄れる (usureru, 'to fade') → 薄れていく (usurete iku, 'gradually fading')
• 離れる (hanareru, 'to separate') → 離れていく (hanarete iku, 'drifting apart')
• 大きくなる (ookiku naru, 'to grow big') → 大きくなっていく (ookiku natte iku, 'keep growing bigger')

Note: In this song, the image of something moving further away creates a sense of loss. ていく captures that gradual, irreversible movement away from the speaker.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 遠ざかる (toozakaru, 'to move away') → 遠ざかって (toozakatte, te-form) → 遠ざかっていく (toozakatte iku, 'moving farther away')

grammar_points.name: 意向形 (volitional)

explanation.en:
How it works: For godan verbs, change the final -u to -ou. For ichidan verbs, replace る with よう. For する, it becomes しよう (shiyou). This expresses 'let's do' or 'I shall do'.

Example from this song: しよう (shiyou) = 'let's do' — from する (suru, 'to do') → しよう (shiyou)

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行こう (ikou, 'let's go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べよう (tabeyou, 'let's eat')
• 始める (hajimeru, 'to begin') → 始めよう (hajimeyou, 'let's begin')

Note: The volitional can express invitation ('let's...'), personal resolve ('I shall...'), or suggestion ('why don't we...'). In songs, it often conveys determination and forward movement.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: する (suru, 'to do') → しよう (shiyou, 'let's do')

grammar_points.name: 〜たら (if/when)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the た-form (past tense) and add ら (ra). This creates a versatile conditional meaning 'if' or 'when'.

Example from this song: 気づいたら (kizuitara) = 'when I realized' — from 気づく (kizuku, 'to realize') → 気づいた (kizuita, past) + ら (ra)

More examples:
• 終わる (owaru, 'to end') → 終わったら (owattara, 'when it ends')
• 帰る (kaeru, 'to go home') → 帰ったら (kaettara, 'when I get home')
• 安い (yasui, 'cheap') → 安かったら (yasukattara, 'if it were cheap')

Note: たら is the most conversational conditional. It can express both hypothetical and actual conditions, and implies time sequence — the condition must be met before the result. 家に帰ったら電話して (ie ni kaettara denwa shite, 'call me when you get home').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 気づく (kizuku, 'to realize') → 気づいた (kizuita, past) → 気づいたら (kizuitara, 'when I realized')

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて (things like)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place なんて (nante) after a noun or phrase to express a dismissive or surprised tone — 'things like' or 'something trivial like'. It minimizes or shows surprise about what precedes it.

Example from this song: 悲しみなんて (kanashimi nante) = 'things like sadness (are trivial)' — from 悲しみ (kanashimi, 'sadness') + なんて (nante, 'things like')

More examples:
• 嘘 (uso, 'a lie') → 嘘なんて (uso nante, 'things like lies — as if!')
• できない (dekinai, 'can't do') → できないなんて (dekinai nante, 'to think you can't do it!')
• 彼 (kare, 'he') → 彼なんて (kare nante, 'someone like him — dismissive')

Note: なんて can be dismissive (下に見る), surprised (意外), or self-deprecating. Context determines the emotion. 私なんて (watashi nante, 'someone like me') is humble/self-deprecating.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 悲しみ (kanashimi, 'sadness') + なんて (nante, 'things like') → 悲しみなんて (kanashimi nante, 'things like sadness — trivial')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative)

explanation.en:
How it works: For godan verbs, change the final -u to -e. For ichidan verbs, replace る with ろ. This creates a direct, powerful command.

Example from this song: 燃やせ (moyase) = 'Burn!' — from 燃やす (moyasu, 'to burn') → change す (su) to せ (se). Also 鳴らせ (narase) = 'Ring!' and 叫べ (sakebe) = 'Shout!'

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見ろ (miro, 'Look!')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言え (ie, 'Say it!')

Note: This song uses imperatives heavily for intensity — multiple commands stacked together create an overwhelming feeling of urgency. In anime, the imperative is the go-to form for battle cries and rally calls.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 燃やす (moyasu, 'to burn') → 燃やせ (moyase, 'Burn!') / 鳴らす (narasu, 'to ring') → 鳴らせ (narase, 'Ring!') / 叫ぶ (sakebu, 'to shout') → 叫べ (sakebe, 'Shout!')

grammar_points.name: 〜のならば (if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place のならば (no naraba) after a verb to express a formal conditional — 'if it is the case that...'. This is a more formal/literary version of のなら (no nara).

Example from this song: 願うのならば (negau no naraba) = 'if you wish' — from 願う (negau, 'to wish') + のならば (no naraba, 'if it is that')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くのならば (iku no naraba, 'if you are going')
• 戦う (tatakau, 'to fight') → 戦うのならば (tatakau no naraba, 'if you are to fight')
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じるのならば (shinjiru no naraba, 'if you believe')

Note: Formality scale: なら (casual) < のなら (standard) < のならば (formal/literary). ならば adds gravitas, making it common in epic anime songs and dramatic speeches.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 願う (negau, 'to wish') + のならば (no naraba, 'if it is that') → 願うのならば (negau no naraba, 'if you wish')

grammar_points.name: 〜のよう (like)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place のよう (no you) after a noun to create a simile — 'like X' or 'similar to X'. It can be followed by に (ni) for adverbial use or な (na) to modify nouns.

Example from this song: 雲のよう (kumo no you) = 'like a cloud' — from 雲 (kumo, 'cloud') + のよう (no you, 'like')

More examples:
• 夢 (yume, 'dream') → 夢のような (yume no you na, 'dream-like')
• 子供 (kodomo, 'child') → 子供のように (kodomo no you ni, 'like a child')
• 花 (hana, 'flower') → 花のように美しい (hana no you ni utsukushii, 'beautiful like a flower')

Note: のよう + な = modifies a noun (夢のような話, 'a dream-like story'). のよう + に = modifies a verb (鳥のように飛ぶ, 'fly like a bird'). みたい (mitai) is the casual equivalent.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 雲 (kumo, 'cloud') + のよう (no you, 'like') → 雲のよう (kumo no you, 'like a cloud')

grammar_points.name: 〜んだろう (probably)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine the explanatory ん (n) with だろう (darou, conjecture). This creates 'you probably...' or 'I wonder if...'. It's the explanatory version of だろう.

Example from this song: 気付いているんだろう (kizuiteiru ndarou) = 'you've probably noticed' — from 気付いている (kizuiteiru, 'have noticed') + んだろう (ndarou, 'probably')

More examples:
• 知っている (shitteiru, 'know') → 知ってるんだろう (shitterundarou, 'you probably know')
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなんだろう (suki nandarou, 'you probably like it')
• 辛い (tsurai, 'painful') → 辛いんだろう (tsuraiundarou, 'it's probably painful')

Note: Without ん: だろう = simple conjecture ('probably'). With ん: んだろう = reflective wondering with explanatory nuance ('I suppose the reason is...'). Common in introspective song lyrics.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 気付いている (kizuiteiru, 'have noticed') + んだろう (ndarou, 'probably') → 気付いているんだろう (kizuiteiru ndarou, 'you've probably noticed')

grammar_points.name: 〜きる (completely)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add きる (kiru, 'to cut'). As an auxiliary, it means 'to do completely' or 'to do thoroughly'. The negative きれない means 'can't fully do'.

Example from this song: 満たし切る (mitashi kiru) = 'to fully satisfy' — from 満たす (mitasu, 'to satisfy') → 満たし (mitashi, masu-stem) + 切る (kiru)

More examples:
• 使う (tsukau, 'to use') → 使い切る (tsukai kiru, 'use up completely')
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走り切る (hashiri kiru, 'run the whole way')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言い切る (ii kiru, 'state definitively')

Note: きる adds a sense of completion and totality. 疲れ切った (tsukare kitta, 'completely exhausted'). The negative きれない is also very common: やりきれない (yari kirenai, 'can't bear it / too much to handle').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 満たす (mitasu, 'to satisfy') → 満たし (mitashi, masu-stem) + 切る (kiru, 'completely') → 満たし切る (mitashi kiru, 'to fully satisfy')

grammar_points.name: Japanese-English code-switching

explanation.en:
How it works: This song mixes Japanese lyrics with English phrases ('run away', 'shout out', 'catch the fire'). Code-switching in J-rock adds energy and international appeal, with English often used for hooks and emotional peaks.

Example from this song: English phrases like 'run away' and 'shout out' appear alongside Japanese verses, creating a dynamic bilingual energy.

More examples of anime songs with code-switching:
• ONE OK ROCK — extensive English-Japanese mixing
• MY FIRST STORY — bilingual choruses
• MAN WITH A MISSION — English verses with Japanese bridges

Note: English words in Japanese songs are typically pronounced with Japanese phonology: 'shout out' becomes シャウトアウト (shauto auto). This katakana-English (和製英語/wasei eigo) is an important part of modern Japanese.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: N/A — code-switching is a stylistic choice, not a grammar conjugation

grammar_points.name: 〜合う (au: mutual action)

explanation.en:
How it works: 合う (au, 'to meet/match') attaches to a verb stem as a compound suffix meaning 'to do something mutually' or 'to each other.' It turns a one-way action into a reciprocal one.

Example from this song: 呼び合う (yobiau) = 'to call each other' — from 呼ぶ (yobu, 'to call') → 呼び (yobi, stem) + 合う (au). Also: 分かち合う (wakachiau) = 'to share with each other'

More examples:
• 助け合う (tasukeau, 'to help each other') — from 助ける (tasukeru, 'to help')
• 話し合う (hanashiau, 'to discuss / talk with each other') — from 話す (hanasu, 'to talk')
• 愛し合う (aishiau, 'to love each other') — from 愛する (aisuru, 'to love')

Note: This suffix always implies reciprocity — both parties are doing the action. It's formed from the verb's masu-stem (drop ます) + 合う. Very common in emotional and relational contexts.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 呼ぶ (yobu, 'to call') → 呼び (yobi, stem) + 合う (au, 'mutually') → 呼び合う (yobiau, 'to call each other')

grammar_points.name: 〜ないでいて (naide ite: please remain not doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: ないでいて (naide ite) is a request to stay in a state of NOT doing something. It combines ないで (naide, 'without doing') with いて (ite, te-form of いる, 'to be/stay').

Example from this song: 忘れないでいて (wasurenaide ite) = 'please keep not forgetting / please continue to remember' — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れないで (wasurenaide) + いて (ite)

More examples:
• 泣かないでいて (nakanaide ite, 'please don't cry / stay not crying') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry')
• 怒らないでいて (okoranaide ite, 'please stay calm / don't be angry') — from 怒る (okoru, 'to get angry')
• そばにいて (soba ni ite, 'please stay by my side') — from いる (iru, 'to be')

Note: ないでいて emphasizes maintaining a state, while ないで alone is just 'please don't.' The いて adds duration — 'keep being in the state of not doing X.'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れない (wasurenai) → 忘れないで (wasurenaide, 'without forgetting') + いて (ite, 'stay') → 忘れないでいて (wasurenaide ite, 'please keep remembering')

grammar_points.name: 〜ぬように (nu you ni: so as not to)

explanation.en:
How it works: ぬ (nu) is the classical/literary negative form (equivalent to ない), and ように (you ni) means 'so that.' Together, ぬように means 'so as not to' — expressing purpose of prevention.

Example from this song: 色褪せぬように (iroasenu you ni) = 'so that it won't fade' — from 色褪せる (iroaseru, 'to fade in color') → 色褪せ (iroase, stem) + ぬ (nu, negative) + ように (you ni)

More examples:
• 忘れぬように (wasurenu you ni, 'so as not to forget') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')
• 消えぬように (kienu you ni, 'so that it won't disappear') — from 消える (kieru, 'to disappear')
• 朽ちぬように (kuchinu you ni, 'so it won't decay') — from 朽ちる (kuchiru, 'to decay')

Note: ぬ is the literary equivalent of ない. It's common in songs, poetry, and formal writing. Modern equivalent: 色褪せないように (iroasenai you ni). ぬ gives a more elegant, timeless feeling.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 色褪せる (iroaseru, 'to fade') → 色褪せ (iroase, stem) + ぬ (nu, literary negative) + ように (you ni, 'so that') → 色褪せぬように (iroasenu you ni, 'so as not to fade')

grammar_points.name: 〜ならば (naraba: if)

explanation.en:
How it works: ならば (naraba) is the formal version of なら (nara), meaning 'if it is the case that.' It adds formality and weight to the conditional.

Example from this song: 会えるなら (aeru nara) = 'if I can meet you' — from 会える (aeru, 'can meet', potential of 会う) + なら (nara, 'if')

More examples:
• 可能ならば (kanou naraba, 'if it's possible') — from 可能 (kanou, 'possible')
• 行くならば早く (iku naraba hayaku, 'if you're going, go quickly')
• 君がそう言うならば (kimi ga sou iu naraba, 'if you say so') — from 言う (iu, 'to say')

Note: なら is casual, ならば is formal/literary. Both express the same conditional meaning. In songs, ならば gives a more dramatic or poetic feeling than plain なら.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 会える (aeru, 'can meet') + なら (nara, 'if') → 会えるなら (aeru nara, 'if I can meet you')

grammar_points.name: 〜だけの (dake no: only)

explanation.en:
How it works: だけ (dake) means 'only' or 'just,' and adding の (no) lets it modify a noun. Together, だけの means 'only for' or 'exclusively belonging to.'

Example from this song: 僕らだけの名前 (bokura dake no namae) = 'a name that belongs only to us' — from 僕ら (bokura, 'we/us') + だけの (dake no) + 名前 (namae, 'name')

More examples:
• 二人だけの秘密 (futari dake no himitsu, 'a secret just between the two of us') — from 二人 (futari, 'two people')
• 自分だけの世界 (jibun dake no sekai, 'a world all your own') — from 自分 (jibun, 'oneself')
• 今日だけの特別 (kyou dake no tokubetsu, 'special for today only') — from 今日 (kyou, 'today')

Note: だけ alone limits quantity ('only X'). だけの modifies the following noun to express exclusivity. It creates a warm, intimate feeling when used with relationships.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 僕ら (bokura, 'we') + だけ (dake, 'only') + の (no) + 名前 (namae, 'name') → 僕らだけの名前 (bokura dake no namae, 'a name only for us')

grammar_points.name: 〜のに (even though)

explanation.en:
How it works: のに (noni) at the end of a clause expresses 'even though' or 'despite the fact that.' It conveys contrast, disappointment, or frustration that reality doesn't match expectations.

Example from this song: はえてんのに (haeten noni) = 'even though I have (wings)' — from はえている (haete iru, 'wings are growing') → casual contraction はえてん (haeten) + のに (noni). Despite having wings in dreams, the speaker can't fly.

More examples:
• 約束したのに来なかった (yakusoku shita noni konakatta, 'even though we promised, they didn't come')
• 勉強したのに落ちた (benkyou shita noni ochita, 'even though I studied, I failed')
• 高いのにおいしくない (takai noni oishikunai, 'even though it's expensive, it's not tasty')

Note: のに at the end of a sentence often leaves the conclusion unstated, creating a feeling of 'and yet...' This is common in emotional or poetic contexts.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: はえる (haeru, 'to grow') → はえている (haete iru, 'have grown') → はえてん (haeten, casual) + のに (noni, 'even though')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていった (went on doing / faded away)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine a verb's te-form with いった (itta, past of いく) to express an action that moved away or progressed over time in the past. It shows something gradually happening and going away.

Example from this song: 消えていった (kiete itta) = 'faded away / disappeared gradually' — from 消える (kieru, 'to disappear') → 消えて (kiete) + いった (itta)

More examples:
• 走っていった (hashitte itta, 'ran off/away') — from 走る (hashiru, 'to run')
• 変わっていった (kawatte itta, 'gradually changed over time') — from 変わる (kawaru, 'to change')
• 忘れていった (wasurete itta, 'gradually forgot') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')

Note: ていく (te iku) = going forward from now. ていった (te itta) = went forward in the past. The emphasis is on movement away from the speaker or progression through time.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 消える (kieru, 'to disappear') → 消えて (kiete) → 消えていった (kiete itta, 'faded away')

grammar_points.name: 〜てん (casual contraction of ている)

explanation.en:
How it works: てん (ten) is an ultra-casual spoken contraction of ている (te iru, 'is doing'). The いる gets compressed: ている → てる → てん. This is common in song lyrics and very informal speech.

Example from this song: はえてん (haeten) = 'have (wings)' — from はえている (haete iru, 'wings are growing') → はえてる (haeteru) → はえてん (haeten)

More examples:
• 知ってん (shitten, 'I know') — from 知っている (shitte iru)
• 食べてん (tabeten, 'am eating') — from 食べている (tabete iru)
• 待ってん (matten, 'am waiting') — from 待っている (matte iru)

Note: This contraction is regional (common in Kansai dialect) and very casual. The standard casual contraction is てる (teru). てん (ten) is one step more casual and is frequently heard in song lyrics.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: はえる (haeru, 'to grow') → はえている (haete iru, 'is growing') → はえてる (haeteru) → はえてん (haeten, ultra-casual)

grammar_points.name: 〜まま (as it is; unchanged state)

explanation.en:
How it works: まま (mama) indicates a state that remains unchanged. After past-tense verbs, it means something was left in that completed state.

Example from this song: しまったまま (shimatta mama) = 'left in the state of being put away/closed' — from しまう (shimau, 'to put away') → しまった (shimatta, past) + まま (mama)

More examples:
• 座ったまま (suwatta mama, 'while still sitting') — from 座る (suwaru, 'to sit')
• 電気をつけたまま寝た (denki o tsuketa mama neta, 'slept with the lights on') — from つける (tsukeru, 'to turn on')
• そのまま (sono mama, 'as it is / leave it like that')

Note: Verb past tense + まま = 'left in that state.' Noun + の + まま = 'remaining as that noun.' This pattern often implies the state is noteworthy or unexpected.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: しまう (shimau, 'to put away') → しまった (shimatta, past) + まま (mama, 'as is') → しまったまま (shimatta mama, 'left put away')

grammar_points.name: 〜なら (if; in the case of)

explanation.en:
How it works: なら (nara) is a conditional meaning 'if' that focuses on a topic or hypothetical supposition. Add it after a plain form verb, noun, or adjective.

Example from this song: The song uses なら to express a hypothetical condition — 'if that's the case, then...'

More examples:
• 明日なら大丈夫 (ashita nara daijoubu, 'if it's tomorrow, it's fine') — noun + なら
• 君なら出来る (kimi nara dekiru, 'if it's you, you can do it') — expressing confidence
• 安いなら買う (yasui nara kau, 'if it's cheap, I'll buy it')

Note: なら is softer than ば (ba) and often used when responding to what someone said. It means 'if what you said is true' or 'if we're talking about X.'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: noun/verb plain form + なら (nara, 'if')

grammar_points.name: 〜を超えて (to surpass; beyond)

explanation.en:
How it works: を超えて (o koete) means 'going beyond' or 'surpassing.' 超える (koeru) means 'to exceed,' and in te-form it connects to the next action or description.

Example from this song: 限界を超えて (genkai o koete) = 'surpassing the limits' — from 限界 (genkai, 'limit') + を (o) + 超えて (koete, 'exceeding')

More examples:
• 国境を超えて (kokkyou o koete, 'crossing borders') — from 国境 (kokkyou, 'national border')
• 想像を超えた (souzou o koeta, 'exceeded imagination') — from 想像 (souzou, 'imagination')
• 時を超えて (toki o koete, 'transcending time') — from 時 (toki, 'time')

Note: 超える (koeru) is a versatile verb. を超えて in te-form often connects to what happens after surpassing: 限界を超えて飛び出そう (genkai o koete tobidasou, 'let's break past our limits and leap out').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 超える (koeru, 'to surpass') → 超えて (koete, te-form) → 限界を超えて (genkai o koete, 'surpassing the limits')

grammar_points.name: 〜ながら (while doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: ながら (nagara) attaches to a verb's masu-stem to express doing two actions simultaneously: 'while doing X, also doing Y.'

Example from this song: 揺らめきながら (yurameki nagara) = 'while flickering' — from 揺らめく (yurameku, 'to flicker') → 揺らめき (yurameki, stem) + ながら (nagara)

More examples:
• 音楽を聴きながら勉強する (ongaku o kiki nagara benkyou suru, 'study while listening to music')
• 歩きながら話す (aruki nagara hanasu, 'talk while walking')
• 泣きながら笑う (naki nagara warau, 'laugh while crying')

Note: The main action is the second verb (after ながら). The ながら verb is the background/simultaneous action. Both actions are done by the same person.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 揺らめく (yurameku, 'to flicker') → 揺らめき (yurameki, stem) + ながら (nagara, 'while') → 揺らめきながら (yurameki nagara, 'while flickering')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていく (continuing/progressing)

explanation.en:
How it works: ていく (te iku) expresses an action or change that continues from now into the future, or progresses away from the current point.

Example from this song: 変えていった (kaete itta) = 'kept changing (over time)' — from 変える (kaeru, 'to change') → 変えて (kaete) + いった (itta, past of iku)

More examples:
• 成長していく (seichou shite iku, 'keeps growing') — from 成長する (seichou suru, 'to grow')
• 忘れていく (wasurete iku, 'gradually forgetting') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')
• 強くなっていく (tsuyoku natte iku, 'getting stronger and stronger')

Note: ていく = future/away direction. てくる = past-to-present/toward direction. Past tense ていった means this progression happened over time in the past.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 変える (kaeru, 'to change') → 変えて (kaete) → 変えていった (kaete itta, 'kept changing over time')

grammar_points.name: 〜としても (even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: としても (to shite mo) means 'even if' or 'even assuming that.' It presents a hypothetical condition and says the result holds regardless.

Example from this song: The song uses としても to express that even in a hypothetical worst case, something still holds true.

More examples:
• 雨だとしても行く (ame da to shite mo iku, 'I'll go even if it rains')
• 失敗したとしても後悔しない (shippai shita to shite mo koukai shinai, 'even if I fail, I won't regret it')
• 嘘だとしても嬉しい (uso da to shite mo ureshii, 'even if it's a lie, I'm happy')

Note: としても is more formal/hypothetical than ても. ても is 'even if (it happens),' while としても is 'even assuming/supposing that.'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb/noun + としても (to shite mo, 'even assuming that')

grammar_points.name: 〜かな (I wonder)

explanation.en:
How it works: かな (kana) is a sentence-ending particle expressing wondering or uncertainty. It's like thinking out loud: 'I wonder if...'

Example from this song: The song uses かな to express the singer's inner wondering and uncertainty about a situation.

More examples:
• 大丈夫かな (daijoubu kana, 'I wonder if it's OK')
• 明日は晴れるかな (ashita wa hareru kana, 'I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow')
• 好きなのかな (suki na no kana, 'I wonder if I like them')

Note: かな is softer and more introspective than か (ka, question marker). It's used for self-directed wondering, not direct questions to others. Very common in songs for expressing inner thoughts.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: plain form + かな (kana, 'I wonder')

grammar_points.name: 〜次第 (depends on; up to)

explanation.en:
How it works: 次第 (shidai) after a noun means 'depends on' or 'up to.' It indicates that the outcome is determined by the stated factor.

Example from this song: 自分次第 (jibun shidai) = 'up to myself / depends on me' — from 自分 (jibun, 'oneself') + 次第 (shidai)

More examples:
• 天気次第 (tenki shidai, 'depends on the weather') — from 天気 (tenki, 'weather')
• やり方次第 (yarikata shidai, 'depends on how you do it') — from やり方 (yarikata, 'method')
• 気持ち次第 (kimochi shidai, 'depends on your feelings') — from 気持ち (kimochi, 'feelings')

Note: Noun + 次第 is a very empowering expression. 自分次第 means 'it's all up to me' — a common motivational phrase. 次第 can also mean 'as soon as' with verb stems: 届き次第 (todoki shidai, 'as soon as it arrives').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 自分 (jibun, 'oneself') + 次第 (shidai, 'depends on') → 自分次第 (jibun shidai, 'up to myself')

grammar_points.name: 〜たら (if/when conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: たら (tara) is a conditional meaning 'if' or 'when.' Form it by adding ら to the past tense (ta-form) of a verb or adjective.

Example from this song: 埋められたら (umeraretara) = 'if I could fill (the gap)' — from 埋める (umeru, 'to fill') → potential: 埋められる (umerareru) → past: 埋められた (umerareta) + ら (ra)

More examples:
• 食べたら (tabetara, 'if/when you eat') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 安かったら買う (yasukattara kau, 'if it's cheap, I'll buy it') — from 安い (yasui, 'cheap')
• 暇だったら来て (hima dattara kite, 'if you're free, come over') — from 暇 (hima, 'free')

Note: たら is the most versatile conditional — it works for hypothetical ('if'), temporal ('when'), and counterfactual ('if only'). It's often the safest conditional to use when unsure.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 埋める (umeru, 'to fill') → 埋められる (umerareru, potential) → 埋められた (umerareta, past) + ら (ra) → 埋められたら (umeraretara, 'if I could fill')

grammar_points.name: 〜くらいなら (kurai nara: rather than)

explanation.en:
How it works: くらいなら (kurai nara) means 'rather than (doing X)' — it expresses that the speaker would prefer an extreme alternative over the stated option.

Example from this song: 殺られるくらいなら (yarareru kurai nara) = 'rather than being killed/beaten' — from 殺られる (yarareru, 'to be done in/killed', passive) + くらいなら

More examples:
• 負けるくらいなら死んだ方がいい (makeru kurai nara shinda hou ga ii, 'I'd rather die than lose')
• 嘘をつくくらいなら黙る (uso o tsuku kurai nara damaru, 'rather than lie, I'll stay quiet')
• 待つくらいなら自分でやる (matsu kurai nara jibun de yaru, 'rather than wait, I'll do it myself')

Note: くらいなら literally means 'if it's to the extent of...' — the speaker finds the stated action so unacceptable that they'd prefer an alternative. It's dramatic and emphatic.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 殺られる (yarareru, 'to be beaten') + くらいなら (kurai nara, 'rather than') → 殺られるくらいなら (yarareru kurai nara, 'rather than be beaten')

grammar_points.name: 〜すぎる (sugiru: too much)

explanation.en:
How it works: すぎる (sugiru, 'to exceed') attaches to verb stems or adjective stems to express 'too much.' For verbs: masu-stem + すぎる. For i-adjectives: drop い + すぎる.

Example from this song: 若すぎる (wakasugiru) = 'too young' — from 若い (wakai, 'young') → 若 (waka) + すぎる (sugiru)

More examples:
• 食べすぎる (tabesugiru, 'to eat too much') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 高すぎる (takasugiru, 'too expensive') — from 高い (takai, 'expensive')
• 静かすぎる (shizuka sugiru, 'too quiet') — na-adjective + すぎる

Note: すぎる conjugates as an ichidan verb: すぎた (sugita, past), すぎない (suginai, negative). This is one of the most frequently used grammar patterns — 暑すぎる！(atsusugiru, 'it's too hot!').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 若い (wakai, 'young') → 若 (waka, drop い) + すぎる (sugiru, 'too much') → 若すぎる (wakasugiru, 'too young')

grammar_points.name: 〜なよ (na yo: don't do!)

explanation.en:
How it works: な (na) after a verb's dictionary form is a casual negative command: 'don't do X!' Adding よ (yo) makes it slightly softer or more emphatic depending on tone.

Example from this song: 隠すなよ (kakusu na yo) = 'don't hide it!' — from 隠す (kakusu, 'to hide') + な (na, 'don't') + よ (yo)

More examples:
• 泣くな (naku na, 'don't cry!') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry')
• 心配するなよ (shinpai suru na yo, 'don't worry!') — from 心配する (shinpai suru, 'to worry')
• 諦めるな (akirameru na, 'don't give up!') — from 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up')

Note: Dictionary form + な is the rough masculine prohibition form. It's very common in anime and songs. Don't confuse with the な that makes na-adjectives (静かな = quiet).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 隠す (kakusu, 'to hide') + な (na, 'don't') + よ (yo, emphasis) → 隠すなよ (kakusu na yo, 'don't hide it!')

grammar_points.name: 〜にだって (ni datte: even by)

explanation.en:
How it works: にだって (ni datte) combines に (ni, 'by') with だって (datte, 'even'). It emphasizes that even the stated agent or means can or can't do something.

Example from this song: テロリストにだって消せない (terorisuto ni datte kesenai) = 'even a terrorist can't erase it' — emphasizing that not even the most extreme agent can destroy it

More examples:
• 誰にだって秘密がある (dare ni datte himitsu ga aru, 'even anyone has secrets / everyone has secrets')
• 子供にだってわかる (kodomo ni datte wakaru, 'even a child can understand')
• 親にだって言えない (oya ni datte ienai, 'can't tell even my parents')

Note: だって adds the nuance of 'even.' It's more emphatic than でも. にだって specifically emphasizes 'even by (this agent).' It's a punk/rebellious way to make a strong point.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: テロリスト (terorisuto, 'terrorist') + に (ni, 'by') + だって (datte, 'even') → テロリストにだって (terorisuto ni datte, 'even by a terrorist') + 消せない (kesenai, 'can't erase')

grammar_points.name: 〜てくれ (te kure: do it for me! / please do)

explanation.en:
How it works: くれ (kure) is the imperative of くれる (kureru, 'to do for me'). Attach it to a verb's te-form for a rough/casual request: 'do this for me!'

Example from this song: 聞いてくれ (kiite kure) = 'listen to me!' — from 聞く (kiku, 'to listen') → 聞いて (kiite) + くれ (kure)

More examples:
• 見てくれ (mite kure, 'look at this!') — from 見る (miru, 'to see')
• 信じてくれ (shinjite kure, 'believe me!') — from 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe')
• 待ってくれ (matte kure, 'wait for me!') — from 待つ (matsu, 'to wait')

Note: てくれ is more direct/rough than てください. It's masculine and common in punk, rock, and emotional contexts. Adding よ softens it slightly: 聞いてくれよ (kiite kure yo).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 聞く (kiku, 'to listen') → 聞いて (kiite) → 聞いてくれ (kiite kure, 'listen to me!')

grammar_points.name: 〜じまう (jimau: end up doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: じまう (jimau) is the rough casual contraction of でしまう (de shimau). It expresses unintended or regrettable completion. Used after verbs whose te-form ends in で.

Example from this song: 死んじまう (shinjimau) = 'end up dying' — from 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die') → 死んで (shinde) + しまう (shimau) → contracted: 死んじまう (shinjimau)

More examples:
• 飲んじまった (nonjimatta, 'ended up drinking it') — from 飲む (nomu, 'to drink')
• 壊れちまう (kowarechimau, 'gonna end up breaking') — from 壊れる (kowareru, 'to break')
• やっちまった (yacchimatta, 'I messed up / did it') — from やる (yaru, 'to do')

Note: The contraction pattern: てしまう → ちまう/ちゃう, でしまう → じまう/じゃう. じまう is rougher and more masculine than じゃう. Very common in punk/rock lyrics.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die') → 死んで (shinde) + しまう (shimau) → 死んじまう (shinjimau, 'end up dying')

grammar_points.name: 〜ことで

explanation.en:
How it works: ことで (koto de) means 'by doing ~' — it indicates the means or method by which something is achieved. こと (koto) nominalizes the verb, and で (de) marks the means.

Example from this song: The song uses ことで to express how something is achieved — 'by (doing this action), (this result happens).'

More examples:
• 練習することで上手になる (renshuu suru koto de jouzu ni naru, 'by practicing, you get better')
• 話すことで気持ちが楽になる (hanasu koto de kimochi ga raku ni naru, 'by talking, you feel better')
• 読むことで世界が広がる (yomu koto de sekai ga hirogaru, 'by reading, your world expands')

Note: こと turns a verb into a noun (nominalizer). Adding で means 'by means of that action.' This is useful for explaining cause-and-effect or methods.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb dictionary form + ことで (koto de, 'by doing')

grammar_points.name: 〜さえ(も)

explanation.en:
How it works: さえ (sae) means 'even,' emphasizing an extreme or unexpected case. Adding も (mo) intensifies it further. It implies 'if even this extreme thing is true, then everything else surely is too.'

Example from this song: The song uses さえ to emphasize something surprising — 'even (this thing you wouldn't expect)...'

More examples:
• 名前さえ知らない (namae sae shiranai, 'don't even know the name') — most basic info is unknown
• 子供さえもできる (kodomo sae mo dekiru, 'even children can do it') — emphasizing ease
• 立つことさえできない (tatsu koto sae dekinai, 'can't even stand') — extreme inability

Note: さえ replaces が or を. さえも is more emphatic than さえ alone. Pattern: noun + さえ or verb te-form + さえ. It creates dramatic emphasis.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: noun + さえ (sae, 'even') / さえも (sae mo, 'even')

grammar_points.name: 〜てくれる

explanation.en:
How it works: くれる (kureru) after a verb's te-form indicates someone does something for the speaker's benefit. It expresses gratitude.

Example from this song: The song uses てくれる to acknowledge someone doing something beneficial — there's warmth and thankfulness in this expression.

More examples:
• 教えてくれた (oshiete kureta, 'taught me') — from 教える (oshieru, 'to teach')
• 信じてくれる (shinjite kureru, 'believes in me') — from 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe')
• 来てくれてありがとう (kite kurete arigatou, 'thanks for coming') — from 来る (kuru, 'to come')

Note: てくれる is uniquely Japanese — it marks that an action was received as a favor. Without it, the sentence is neutral. With it, gratitude is built into the grammar itself.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb te-form + くれる (kureru, 'does for me')

grammar_points.name: 〜なけりゃ (casual conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: なけりゃ (nakerya) is the casual spoken contraction of なければ (nakereba), meaning 'if not.' It's common in songs, anime, and informal speech.

Example from this song: The song uses なけりゃ as a casual 'if not' — expressing what needs to happen or what would go wrong without something.

More examples:
• 行かなけりゃ (ikanakerya, 'if I don't go') — from 行く (iku, 'to go')
• やらなけりゃダメだ (yaranakerya dame da, 'you gotta do it') — from やる (yaru, 'to do')
• 食べなけりゃ死ぬ (tabenakerya shinu, 'if you don't eat, you'll die')

Note: Contraction chain: なければ → なけりゃ → なきゃ. なきゃ is even more casual. All three mean 'if not' / 'must.' なけりゃならない = 'must do' (casual of なければならない).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb negative stem + なければ (nakereba, 'if not') → なけりゃ (nakerya, casual) → なきゃ (nakya, ultra-casual)

grammar_points.name: volitional form 〜よう/〜おう

explanation.en:
How it works: The volitional form expresses 'let's do' or 'I shall do.' For godan verbs, change -u to -ou. For ichidan verbs, replace る with よう.

Example from this song: 進んでいこう (susunde ikou) = 'let's move forward' — from 進む (susumu, 'to advance') + ていく (te iku) → volitional: いこう (ikou)

More examples:
• 食べよう (tabeyou, 'let's eat') — from 食べる (taberu, ichidan)
• 頑張ろう (ganbarou, 'let's do our best') — from 頑張る (ganbaru, godan)
• 始めよう (hajimeyou, 'let's begin') — from 始める (hajimeru, ichidan)

Note: The volitional can express suggestion ('let's') or personal resolve ('I shall'). In songs, it often expresses determination: 進んでいこう conveys 'let's keep moving forward together!'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 進む (susumu, 'to advance') → 進んで (susunde) + いく (iku) → いこう (ikou, volitional) → 進んでいこう (susunde ikou, 'let's move forward')

grammar_points.name: 〜ことさえも

explanation.en:
How it works: ことさえも (koto sae mo) combines the nominalizer こと (koto) with the emphatic particle さえも (sae mo, 'even'). It means 'even the act of doing X.'

Example from this song: The song uses ことさえも to emphasize that even the action itself is noteworthy or surprising.

More examples:
• 歩くことさえも辛い (aruku koto sae mo tsurai, 'even just walking is painful')
• 笑うことさえも忘れた (warau koto sae mo wasureta, 'even forgot how to laugh')
• 生きることさえも怖い (ikiru koto sae mo kowai, 'even living itself is scary')

Note: こと turns the verb into a noun ('the act of doing'). さえも adds 'even.' Together: 'even the very act of X.' This creates strong dramatic emphasis — if even this fundamental action is affected, the situation is extreme.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: verb dictionary form + こと (koto, 'the act of') + さえも (sae mo, 'even') → ことさえも (koto sae mo, 'even the act of')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (meireikei) — imperative form

explanation.en:
How it works:
The imperative form is used for direct, strong commands. For godan (u-verb) verbs, change the final -u to -e: 出す (dasu) → 出せ (dase). For ichidan (ru-verb) verbs, drop る (ru) and add ろ (ro): 食べる (taberu) → 食べろ (tabero). This form sounds forceful and is common in anime, sports, and song lyrics. It is too blunt for polite conversation.

Example from this song:
曝け出せ (sarake dase) — "lay bare!" / "expose everything!"
A rallying cry to hold nothing back.

More examples:
• 走れ (hashire) — "run!"
• 立て (tate) — "stand up!"
• 諦めるな (akirameru na) — "don't give up!" (negative imperative with な)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 曝け出す (sarake dasu, "to expose/lay bare") → 曝け出せ (sarake dase, imperative, "lay bare!")

grammar_points.name: 〜てゆく / 〜ていく (te yuku / te iku) — gradual change into the future

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + いく (iku) or ゆく (yuku) expresses an action or change that continues moving forward into the future. Think of it as "going on doing ~" or "continuing to ~." The form ゆく (yuku) is more literary and poetic; いく (iku) is standard. In casual speech, ていく (te iku) contracts to てく (teku).

Example from this song:
変えて行く (kaete iku) — "will keep changing" / "will go on changing"
The singer declares they will keep transforming things going forward.

More examples:
• 強くなっていく (tsuyoku natte iku) — "keep getting stronger"
• 忘れていく (wasurete iku) — "gradually forgetting"
• 夢を叶えていく (yume o kanaete iku) — "keep making dreams come true"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 変える (kaeru, "to change") → 変えて (kaete, te-form) → 変えて行く (kaete iku, "will keep changing")

grammar_points.name: 〜すら (sura) — even (emphatic)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The particle すら (sura) means "even" and is more emphatic and literary than さえ (sae). It highlights an extreme or unexpected example to make a stronger point. The pattern is Noun + すら (sura). If even this extreme case is true, then everything else certainly is too. It is often found in written Japanese and song lyrics.

Example from this song:
忘れた事すら (wasureta koto sura) — "even the fact of forgetting"
The singer emphasizes that even the act of forgetting itself has significance.

More examples:
• 自分の名前すら忘れた (jibun no namae sura wasureta) — "I forgot even my own name"
• 彼女は挨拶すらしなかった (kanojo wa aisatsu sura shinakatta) — "she didn't even greet me"
• 一円すら持っていない (ichi-en sura motte inai) — "I don't have even one yen"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れた事 (wasureta koto, "the fact of forgetting") + すら (sura, "even") → 忘れた事すら (wasureta koto sura, "even the fact of forgetting")

grammar_points.name: 〜かけた (kaketa) — on the verge of / half-done

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + かける (kakeru) means "to be on the verge of doing ~" or "to have started doing ~ but not finished." In the past tense: かけた (kaketa). It captures the moment just before something happens, or an action that was begun but interrupted.

Example from this song:
崩れかけた (kuzure kaketa) — "was about to collapse" / "half-collapsed"
Something was on the brink of falling apart.

More examples:
• 死にかけた (shini kaketa) — "nearly died"
• 言いかけてやめた (ii kakete yameta) — "started to say something but stopped"
• 食べかけのりんご (tabe kake no ringo) — "a half-eaten apple"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 崩れる (kuzureru, "to collapse") → 崩れ (kuzure, masu-stem) → 崩れかけた (kuzure kaketa, "was about to collapse")

grammar_points.name: 可能形 (kanoukei) — potential form 〜える/〜られる

explanation.en:
How it works:
The potential form expresses ability — "can do ~" or "be able to ~." For godan (u-verb) verbs: change the final -u to -e and add る (ru): 会う (au) → 会える (aeru). For ichidan (ru-verb) verbs: drop る (ru) and add られる (rareru): 食べる (taberu) → 食べられる (taberareru). In casual speech, ichidan verbs often drop the ら (ra): 食べれる (tabereru).

Example from this song:
出会えた (deaeta) — "was able to meet"
The singer expresses gratitude for having been able to encounter someone special.

More examples:
• 日本語が話せる (nihongo ga hanaseru) — "I can speak Japanese"
• 一人で行ける (hitori de ikeru) — "I can go alone"
• 信じられない (shinjirarenai) — "I can't believe it"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 出会う (deau, "to encounter") → 出会える (deaeru, potential) → 出会えた (deaeta, past potential, "was able to meet")

grammar_points.name: 〜ようとして (you to shite) — trying to

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb volitional form + とする (to suru) means "to try to ~" or "to be about to ~." The て-form version, ようとして (you to shite), connects this attempt to what happens next. It captures the moment of effort or intention, often when the attempt is difficult or interrupted.

Example from this song:
見つけ出そうとして (mitsuke dasou to shite) — "trying to find"
The singer is making an effort to discover something.

More examples:
• 逃げようとしたが、捕まった (nigeyou to shita ga, tsukamatta) — "tried to escape but was caught"
• ドアを開けようとしている (doa o akeyou to shite iru) — "is trying to open the door"
• 立ち上がろうとして転んだ (tachiagaro to shite koronda) — "tried to stand up and fell"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 見つけ出す (mitsuke dasu, "to find out") → 見つけ出そう (mitsuke dasou, volitional) → 見つけ出そうとして (mitsuke dasou to shite, "trying to find")

grammar_points.name: 〜ようとする (you to suru) — try to / about to

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb volitional form + とする (to suru) means "to try to ~" or "to be about to ~." The volitional form expresses intention (行こう, ikou, "let's go"), and adding とする (to suru) shows the attempt or the moment just before the action. It captures effort and intention, especially when the outcome is uncertain.

Example from this song:
挑もうとする (idomou to suru) — "trying to challenge"
The singer is making an effort to face a difficult challenge head-on.

More examples:
• 逃げようとしたが捕まった (nigeyou to shita ga tsukamatta) — "tried to escape but was caught"
• 寝ようとしている (neyou to shite iru) — "is trying to sleep"
• 立ち上がろうとする (tachiagaro to suru) — "tries to stand up"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 挑む (idomu, "to challenge") → 挑もう (idomou, volitional) → 挑もうとする (idomou to suru, "trying to challenge")

grammar_points.name: 〜のようで (no you de) — it seems like / is like

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Noun + のようで (no you de) means "it seems like ~" or "it's like ~" and is used to describe something by comparison. The で (de) here is the て-form of だ (da), allowing you to connect this comparison to another clause. It is a softer, more descriptive version of のように (no you ni).

Example from this song:
The singer describes their experience by comparing it to familiar things — making abstract feelings concrete.

More examples:
• 夢のようで信じられない (yume no you de shinjirarenai) — "it's like a dream and I can't believe it"
• 映画のようで面白かった (eiga no you de omoshirokatta) — "it was like a movie and was interesting"
• 嵐のようで激しかった (arashi no you de hageshikatta) — "it was like a storm and was intense"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Noun + の (no) + ようで (you de) → "it's like ~ and..."

grammar_points.name: 〜たびに (tabi ni) — each time / every time

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb dictionary form + たびに (tabi ni) means "each time ~" or "every time ~." It describes a recurring trigger — whenever the first action occurs, the second action follows. It has a slightly literary or reflective tone, making it common in songs and storytelling.

Example from this song:
増えるたびに (fueru tabi ni) — "each time it increases"
Every time something grows or accumulates, the singer notices a change.

More examples:
• 会うたびに綺麗になる (au tabi ni kirei ni naru) — "you get prettier every time we meet"
• この歌を聞くたびに泣く (kono uta o kiku tabi ni naku) — "I cry every time I hear this song"
• 旅をするたびに新しい発見がある (tabi o suru tabi ni atarashii hakken ga aru) — "every time I travel, there are new discoveries"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 増える (fueru, "to increase") + たびに (tabi ni) → 増えるたびに (fueru tabi ni, "each time it increases")

grammar_points.name: 〜とか〜とか (toka ... toka) — things like ~ and ~

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern X + とか (toka) + Y + とか (toka) lists examples casually — "things like X and Y." It implies there are other items too, but you are just mentioning a few. It is more casual than や (ya) and very common in everyday speech. You can list verbs, nouns, or even sentences.

Example from this song:
The singer casually lists different experiences or feelings as examples of what they go through.

More examples:
• サッカーとかバスケとか好き (sakkaa toka basuke toka suki) — "I like things like soccer and basketball"
• 映画を見るとか本を読むとか (eiga o miru toka hon o yomu toka) — "things like watching movies and reading books"
• 東京とか大阪とかに行きたい (toukyou toka oosaka toka ni ikitai) — "I want to go to places like Tokyo and Osaka"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: X + とか (toka) + Y + とか (toka) → "things like X and Y"

grammar_points.name: 〜ではなくて (de wa nakute) — not ~ but rather

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Noun + ではなくて (de wa nakute) means "not ~ but rather ~." It negates one thing and then presents the alternative. ではない (de wa nai) is the negative of だ (da, copula), and the て-form なくて (nakute) connects it to the next clause. In casual speech, では (de wa) contracts to じゃ (ja): じゃなくて (ja nakute).

Example from this song:
The singer contrasts two ideas — rejecting one interpretation and offering another.

More examples:
• 問題は能力ではなくて努力だ (mondai wa nouryoku de wa nakute doryoku da) — "the issue is not ability but effort"
• 犬じゃなくて猫が好き (inu ja nakute neko ga suki) — "I like cats, not dogs" (casual)
• 怒っているのではなくて心配している (okotte iru no de wa nakute shinpai shite iru) — "I'm not angry, I'm worried"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Noun + ではなくて (de wa nakute) → "not ~ but rather ~" / casual: じゃなくて (ja nakute)

grammar_points.name: 〜んだ (n da) — explanatory emphasis

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + んだ (n da) adds explanatory nuance — "the thing is ~" or "it's that ~." It is the casual form of のだ (no da). It signals that you are explaining a reason, giving context, or emphasizing something. It is extremely common in spoken Japanese and song lyrics. Without it, a statement is just a fact; with it, it becomes an explanation.

Example from this song:
The singer uses んだ (n da) to share personal revelations — explaining their inner feelings to the listener.

More examples:
• 実は日本に住んでいるんだ (jitsu wa nihon ni sunde iru n da) — "the thing is, I live in Japan"
• 疲れたんだ (tsukareta n da) — "the thing is, I'm tired" (explaining why)
• どうしたんだ (doushita n da) — "what happened?" (seeking explanation)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb/Adjective plain form + ん (n) + だ (da) → "the thing is ~" / "it's that ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜てしまう (te shimau) — completion / regret

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + しまう (shimau) expresses that something was completed, often with regret or unintended consequences. Casual forms: てしまう (te shimau) → ちゃう (chau), でしまう (de shimau) → じゃう (jau). It can also express "just go ahead and do it" when combined with ば (ba): しまえばいい (shimaeba ii).

Example from this song:
忘れてしまえばいい (wasurete shimaeba ii) — "if you just forget, it'll be fine"
The singer suggests that forgetting completely would solve the pain.

More examples:
• 食べてしまった (tabete shimatta) — "ate it all" (regret)
• やっちゃえ (yacchae) — "just do it!" (casual, encouraging)
• 壊してしまった (kowashite shimatta) — "ended up breaking it"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れる (wasureru, "to forget") → 忘れて (wasurete, te-form) → 忘れてしまう (wasurete shimau, "end up forgetting") → 忘れてしまえば (wasurete shimaeba, conditional, "if you just forget")

grammar_points.name: 〜ば conditional (ba) — if

explanation.en:
How it works:
The 〜ば (ba) form creates a conditional meaning "if ~." For godan (u-verb) verbs: change -u to -e + ば (ba). For ichidan (ru-verb) verbs: drop る (ru) + れば (reba). For い-adjectives (i-adjectives): drop い (i) + ければ (kereba). It often pairs with いい (ii, "good") to mean "if you just ~ it'll be fine."

Example from this song:
しまえばいい (shimaeba ii) — "if you just (do it completely), it's fine"
Encouragement to take decisive action.

More examples:
• 聞けばわかる (kikeba wakaru) — "if you ask, you'll understand"
• 安ければ買う (yasukereba kau) — "if it's cheap, I'll buy it"
• 練習すればうまくなる (renshuu sureba umaku naru) — "if you practice, you'll get better"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: しまう (shimau, "to finish") → しまえ (shimae, ba-stem) → しまえば (shimaeba, conditional, "if you finish") → しまえばいい (shimaeba ii, "if you just finish, it's fine")

grammar_points.name: 〜てくれる (te kureru) — someone does a favor for me

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + くれる (kureru) expresses that someone did something for the speaker's benefit. It carries appreciation and gratitude. Past tense: くれた (kureta). This is one of the most important patterns for expressing thankfulness in Japanese.

Example from this song:
守ってくれた (mamotte kureta) — "protected (me)"
Someone protected the singer, and the singer is deeply grateful.

More examples:
• 教えてくれてありがとう (oshiete kurete arigatou) — "thank you for teaching me"
• 信じてくれた人 (shinjite kureta hito) — "the person who believed in me"
• 迎えに来てくれた (mukae ni kite kureta) — "came to pick me up (for my sake)"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 守る (mamoru, "to protect") → 守って (mamotte, te-form) → 守ってくれた (mamotte kureta, "protected me (with gratitude)")

grammar_points.name: 〜ている / 〜てる (te iru / teru) — progressive / state

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + いる (iru) expresses ongoing action or resulting state. In casual speech, いる (iru) contracts to る (ru): している (shite iru) → してる (shiteru). The んだ (n da) often follows to add explanatory emphasis: 守ってるんだ (mamotteru n da, "the thing is, I'm protecting").

Example from this song:
守ってるんだ (mamotteru n da) — "I'm protecting (you), you see"
The singer reveals they have been protecting someone all along.

More examples:
• 今、食べてる (ima, tabeteru) — "I'm eating right now" (casual)
• ずっと待ってたんだ (zutto matteteta n da) — "I've been waiting all along, you know"
• もう知ってるよ (mou shitteru yo) — "I already know"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 守る (mamoru, "to protect") → 守って (mamotte, te-form) → 守っている (mamotte iru, progressive) → 守ってる (mamotteru, casual) → 守ってるんだ (mamotteru n da, "I'm protecting, you see")

grammar_points.name: 〜んだ (n da) — explanatory emphasis

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + んだ (n da) is casual のだ (no da). It adds explanatory emphasis — "the thing is ~" or "it's that ~." Without it, you are just stating a fact. With it, you are explaining, justifying, or emphasizing. This is essential for natural conversation.

Example from this song:
わかってたんだ (wakatteta n da) — "the thing is, I understood all along"
The singer reveals an inner truth — they knew the whole time.

More examples:
• 体調が悪いんだ (taichou ga warui n da) — "the thing is, I'm not feeling well" (explaining why)
• 本当に好きなんだ (hontou ni suki nan da) — "I really do love (you)" (emphasis)
• 何があったんだ (nani ga atta n da) — "what happened?" (demanding explanation)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: わかっていた (wakatte ita, "understood") → わかってた (wakatteta, casual contraction) + ん (n) + だ (da) → わかってたんだ (wakatteta n da, "the thing is, I understood")

grammar_points.name: 〜に来る (ni kuru) — come to do

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + に来る (ni kuru) means "to come in order to do ~." It expresses purpose of movement — someone comes with the specific intention of performing an action. Past tense: に来た (ni kita, "came to do").

Example from this song:
伝えに来た (tsutae ni kita) — "came to tell (you)"
The singer traveled specifically to deliver a message.

More examples:
• 遊びに来て (asobi ni kite) — "come hang out" / "come visit"
• 日本語を勉強しに来た (nihongo o benkyou shi ni kita) — "came to study Japanese"
• 助けに来たよ (tasuke ni kita yo) — "I came to help!"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 伝える (tsutaeru, "to tell") → 伝え (tsutae, masu-stem) + に (ni, purpose) + 来た (kita, "came") → 伝えに来た (tsutae ni kita, "came to tell")
