grammar_points.name: 〜はずのない (hazu no nai) — should not have / impossible that

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb た-form (ta-form) + はずのない (hazu no nai) means "should not have ~" or "it's impossible that ~." はず (hazu) expresses expectation, and のない (no nai) negates it — the expectation was that it could not happen, yet it did. This expresses surprise at something unexpected.

Example from this song:
交わしたはずのない (kawashita hazu no nai) — "shouldn't have exchanged"
The singer is surprised by a connection or promise that logically should not exist.

More examples:
• ここに置いたはずのない鍵 (koko ni oita hazu no nai kagi) — "a key that shouldn't have been placed here"
• 会ったはずのない人 (atta hazu no nai hito) — "a person I shouldn't have met"
• 知っているはずのない情報 (shitte iru hazu no nai jouhou) — "information they shouldn't know"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 交わす (kawasu, "to exchange") → 交わした (kawashita, past) → 交わしたはずのない (kawashita hazu no nai, "shouldn't have exchanged")

grammar_points.name: 〜ようとする (you to suru) — try to / about to

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb volitional form + とする (to suru) means "to try to ~" or "to be about to ~." It captures the moment of effort or intention. The volitional form shows will or desire, and とする (to suru) frames it as an attempt.

Example from this song:
奪おうとする (ubaou to suru) — "tries to steal"
Someone is making an attempt to take something away.

More examples:
• 逃げようとしたが失敗した (nigeyou to shita ga shippai shita) — "tried to escape but failed"
• 何かを言おうとしている (nanika o iou to shite iru) — "is trying to say something"
• 立ち上がろうとする (tachiagaro to suru) — "tries to stand up"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 奪う (ubau, "to steal") → 奪おう (ubaou, volitional) → 奪おうとする (ubaou to suru, "tries to steal")

grammar_points.name: 〜だって (datte) — even / no matter

explanation.en:
How it works:
The particle だって (datte) after a noun means "even ~" or "no matter ~." It is the casual equivalent of でも (demo) in this usage. With question words, it means "no matter what/who/when": 誰だって (dare datte, "anyone / no matter who"). It sounds defiant and emphatic.

Example from this song:
どんな瞬間だって (donna shunkan datte) — "no matter what moment"
Every single moment counts — there are no exceptions.

More examples:
• 誰だって失敗する (dare datte shippai suru) — "anyone can fail"
• いつだって味方だよ (itsu datte mikata da yo) — "I'm always on your side"
• 何だってできる (nan datte dekiru) — "you can do anything"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: どんな瞬間 (donna shunkan, "what kind of moment") + だって (datte, "no matter") → どんな瞬間だって (donna shunkan datte, "no matter what moment")

grammar_points.name: 〜ちゃう (chau) — casual completion / regret

explanation.en:
How it works:
ちゃう (chau) is the casual contraction of てしまう (te shimau), which expresses completion — often with regret or something unintended. Similarly, じゃう (jau) is the contraction of でしまう (de shimau). This is extremely common in everyday speech and songs. Past tense: ちゃった (chatta).

Example from this song:
考えちゃって (kangaechatte) — "end up thinking"
The singer can't help but think about something — the thought happens uncontrollably.

More examples:
• 食べちゃった (tabechatta) — "ate it all" (oops)
• 忘れちゃった (wasurechatta) — "accidentally forgot"
• 好きになっちゃった (suki ni nacchatta) — "ended up falling in love"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 考える (kangaeru, "to think") → 考えて (kangaete, te-form) → 考えてしまう (kangaete shimau) → 考えちゃう (kangaechau, casual) → 考えちゃって (kangaechatte, te-form, "end up thinking")

grammar_points.name: 〜より (yori) — more than / rather than

explanation.en:
How it works:
The particle より (yori) means "more than ~" or "rather than ~" and is used for comparisons. The pattern is B + より (yori) + A + が + adjective, meaning "A is more [adjective] than B." It can also stand alone meaning "rather than ~."

Example from this song:
The singer compares different things or paths, expressing a preference or making a value judgment.

More examples:
• 犬より猫が好き (inu yori neko ga suki) — "I like cats more than dogs"
• 昨日より暑い (kinou yori atsui) — "hotter than yesterday"
• 言葉より行動だ (kotoba yori koudou da) — "actions (matter) more than words"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: B + より (yori, "more than") + A → "A is more than B"

grammar_points.name: 〜んだ (n da) — explanatory emphasis

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + んだ (n da) is the casual form of のだ (no da). It adds explanatory nuance — "the thing is ~" or "it's that ~." It signals you are providing context, reason, or emphasis rather than simply stating a fact. Essential for natural-sounding Japanese.

Example from this song:
迎えにいくんだ (mukae ni iku n da) — "I'm going to greet (you)" (with determination)
The んだ (n da) adds resolve — this is not just a statement but a declaration.

More examples:
• 明日テストがあるんだ (ashita tesuto ga aru n da) — "the thing is, I have a test tomorrow"
• 本当に好きなんだ (hontou ni suki nan da) — "I really do like (you)"
• どこに行くんだ (doko ni iku n da) — "where are you going?" (seeking explanation)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 迎えに行く (mukae ni iku, "to go greet") + ん (n) + だ (da) → 迎えにいくんだ (mukae ni iku n da, "I'm going to greet — that's what I'm doing")

grammar_points.name: 〜で (de - means/instrument)

explanation.en:
The particle で (de) indicates the means, tool, or method by which an action is done. It answers "by what means?"

How it works:
Place で (de) after the noun that represents the tool or method.

Example from this song:
全部、携帯で (zenbu, keitai de, "Everything, by cell phone")

More examples:
- 電車で行く (densha de iku, "Go by train")
- 筆で書く (fude de kaku, "Write with a brush")
- 日本語で話す (nihongo de hanasu, "Speak in Japanese")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 携帯 (keitai, "cell phone") + で (de) → 携帯で (keitai de, "by cell phone")

grammar_points.name: 〜を追い越す (o oikosu - to overtake)

explanation.en:
A compound verb meaning "to overtake" or "to pass by." Combines 追い (oi, "chase") + 越す (kosu, "cross over").

How it works:
Use を (o) to mark the object being overtaken, then 追い越す (oikosu).

Example from this song:
風を追い越して (kaze o oikoshite, "Overtaking the wind")

More examples:
- 車を追い越す (kuruma o oikosu, "to overtake a car")
- 時代を追い越す (jidai o oikosu, "to surpass the era")
- 先輩を追い越した (senpai o oikoshita, "surpassed my senior")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 風 (kaze) + を (o) + 追い越す (oikosu) → 風を追い越して (kaze o oikoshite, "overtaking the wind")

grammar_points.name: 〜ながら (nagara - while)

explanation.en:
Expresses doing two actions simultaneously: "while doing [X], also doing [Y]."

How it works:
Take the masu-stem of a verb and add ながら (nagara). The background action gets ながら; the main action follows.

Example from this song:
背を向け合いながら (se o mukeai nagara, "While turning our backs to each other")

More examples:
- 音楽を聴きながら勉強する (ongaku o kiki nagara benkyou suru, "Study while listening to music")
- 歩きながら食べる (aruki nagara taberu, "Eat while walking")
- 笑いながら泣いていた (warai nagara naite ita, "Was crying while laughing")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 向け合う (mukeau) → 向け合い (mukeai) + ながら (nagara) → 向け合いながら (mukeai nagara)

grammar_points.name: 〜たい (tai - want to)

explanation.en:
Expresses desire: "want to [do something]." One of the most-used patterns in everyday Japanese.

How it works:
Remove ます (masu) from the polite form, add たい (tai).

Example from this song:
君への想いを今すぐ伝えたい (kimi e no omoi o ima sugu tsutaetai, "I want to convey my feelings for you right now")

More examples:
- 食べたい (tabetai, "want to eat")
- 日本に行きたい (nihon ni ikitai, "want to go to Japan")
- 会いたかった (aitakatta, "I wanted to see you")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 伝える (tsutaeru) → 伝え (tsutae, masu-stem) + たい (tai) → 伝えたい (tsutaetai)

grammar_points.name: 〜今すぐ (ima sugu - right now)

explanation.en:
Means "right now" or "immediately." Combines 今 (ima, "now") + すぐ (sugu, "immediately") for urgency.

How it works:
Place 今すぐ (ima sugu) before the verb to emphasize immediacy.

Example from this song:
今すぐ伝えたい (ima sugu tsutaetai, "I want to convey right now")

More examples:
- 今すぐ行きたい (ima sugu ikitai, "I want to go right now")
- 今すぐ電話して (ima sugu denwa shite, "Call right now")
- 今すぐ会いたい (ima sugu aitai, "I want to see you right now")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 今 (ima) + すぐ (sugu) → 今すぐ伝えたい (ima sugu tsutaetai, "want to convey right now")

grammar_points.name: 〜まま (as it is)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place まま (mama) after a verb (past or negative form) to express that a state remains unchanged — 'as it is' or 'while still in that condition'.

Example from this song: わからないまま (wakaranai mama) = 'remaining not understanding' — from わからない (wakaranai, 'don't understand') + まま (mama, 'as is')

More examples:
• 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand') → 立ったまま (tatta mama, 'while still standing')
• 電気をつける (denki o tsukeru, 'turn on light') → つけたまま (tsuketa mama, 'left turned on')
• 食べない (tabenai, 'not eat') → 食べないまま (tabenai mama, 'without eating')

Note: Negative + まま = a state that hasn't changed (still not doing). Past + まま = a state left as is (did it and left it). Both imply the state persists.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: わからない (wakaranai, 'don't understand') + まま (mama, 'as is') → わからないまま (wakaranai mama, 'remaining not understanding')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていく (continuing away)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) and add いく (iku, 'to go'). This shows an action continuing forward into the future, or gradually moving away from the present.

Example from this song: 振り払っていく (furiharatte iku) = 'keep shaking off' — from 振り払う (furiharau, 'to shake off') → 振り払って (furiharatte, te-form) + いく (iku)

More examples:
• 消える (kieru, 'to disappear') → 消えていく (kiete iku, 'gradually disappear')
• 強くなる (tsuyoku naru, 'become strong') → 強くなっていく (tsuyoku natte iku, 'keep getting stronger')
• 進む (susumu, 'to advance') → 進んでいく (susunde iku, 'keep moving forward')

Note: ていく = forward/away direction. てくる = toward/approaching direction. This directional pair is fundamental to understanding progressive actions in Japanese.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 振り払う (furiharau, 'to shake off') → 振り払って (furiharatte, te-form) → 振り払っていく (furiharatte iku, 'keep shaking off')

grammar_points.name: 〜ば (conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: For godan verbs, change the final -u to -eba. For ichidan verbs, drop る and add れば. This creates the conditional 'if' — a general or hypothetical condition.

Example from this song: いれば (ireba) = 'if you are here' — from いる (iru, 'to be') → drop る, add れば → いれば. Also 触れれば (furereba) = 'if I touch' — from 触れる (fureru, 'to touch') → 触れれば

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行けば (ikeba, 'if you go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べれば (tabereba, 'if you eat')
• 安い (yasui, 'cheap') → 安ければ (yasukereba, 'if it's cheap')

Note: The ば conditional is often used for general truths and hypotheticals. It pairs well with いい (ii): 行けばいい (ikeba ii, 'you should just go'). It's one of four Japanese conditionals (ば, たら, なら, と).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: いる (iru, 'to be') → いれば (ireba, 'if you are here') / 触れる (fureru, 'to touch') → 触れれば (furereba, 'if I touch')

grammar_points.name: 〜たい (want to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add たい (tai). This expresses the speaker's desire to do something. It conjugates like an い-adjective.

Example from this song: 感じたい (kanjitai) = 'want to feel' — from 感じる (kanjiru, 'to feel') → 感じ (kanji, masu-stem) + たい (tai)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたい (tabetai, 'want to eat')
• 会う (au, 'to meet') → 会いたい (aitai, 'want to meet')
• 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知りたい (shiritai, 'want to know')

Note: たい is for the speaker's own desires (first person). For third person, use たがっている (tagatteiru): 彼は食べたがっている (kare wa tabetagatteiru, 'he wants to eat'). Past: たかった (takatta, 'wanted to').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 感じる (kanjiru, 'to feel') → 感じ (kanji, masu-stem) → 感じたい (kanjitai, 'want to feel')

grammar_points.name: 〜ても (even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) and add も (mo). This creates 'even if' — a concessive meaning where the result holds true regardless of the condition.

Example from this song: 纏っても (matottemo) = 'even if wrapped in' — from 纏う (matou, 'to wear/wrap') → 纏って (matotte, te-form) + も (mo)

More examples:
• 失敗する (shippai suru, 'to fail') → 失敗しても (shippai shitemo, 'even if I fail')
• 寒い (samui, 'cold') → 寒くても (samukutemo, 'even if it's cold')
• 雨 (ame, 'rain') → 雨でも (ame demo, 'even if it rains')

Note: ても is the go-to concessive pattern in Japanese. It's one of the most common grammar points across all JLPT levels because of its versatility and frequency in both speech and writing.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 纏う (matou, 'to wrap') → 纏って (matotte, te-form) → 纏っても (matottemo, 'even if wrapped in')

grammar_points.name: 〜ように (you ni) — as if / in such a way

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Noun + のように (no you ni) or Verb + ように (you ni) means "as if ~" or "in such a way that ~." It creates comparisons (similes) or expresses purpose. When it follows a noun, you need の (no) before ように (you ni). It modifies the verb that comes after it.

Example from this song:
The singer uses this pattern to compare their actions and feelings to vivid images — running like the wind, shining like a star.

More examples:
• 風のように走る (kaze no you ni hashiru) — "run like the wind"
• 夢を見ているように (yume o mite iru you ni) — "as if dreaming"
• 死ぬように眠った (shinu you ni nemutta) — "slept as if dead"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Noun + の (no) + ように (you ni) → "like ~" / Verb plain + ように (you ni) → "as if ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜ながら (nagara) — while doing / despite

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + ながら (nagara) has two meanings: (1) doing two actions simultaneously — "while doing ~," and (2) expressing contradiction — "despite ~" or "although ~." The second meaning is more formal. Both meanings are very common in everyday Japanese.

Example from this song:
The singer describes doing things simultaneously — experiencing pain while still pushing forward.

More examples:
• 音楽を聴きながら勉強する (ongaku o kiki nagara benkyou suru) — "study while listening to music"
• 歩きながら話す (aruki nagara hanasu) — "talk while walking"
• 知っていながら黙っていた (shitte i nagara damatte ita) — "stayed silent despite knowing" (contradiction)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + ながら (nagara) → "while doing ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜てゆく (te yuku) — progressive movement away (literary)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + ゆく (yuku) is the literary and poetic version of ていく (te iku). It expresses gradual change, fading, or movement away from the current moment. ゆく (yuku) is the classical form of 行く (iku, "to go"). Because it sounds more elegant and emotional, it appears frequently in songs, poems, and novels.

Example from this song:
失ってゆく (ushinatte yuku) — "gradually losing"
Things are slipping away one by one over time.

More examples:
• 消えてゆく (kiete yuku) — "fading away"
• 過ぎてゆく時間 (sugite yuku jikan) — "time passing by"
• 離れてゆく (hanarete yuku) — "drifting apart"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 失う (ushinau, "to lose") → 失って (ushinatte, te-form) → 失ってゆく (ushinatte yuku, "gradually losing")

grammar_points.name: 〜てきた (te kita) — have been doing (up to now)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + きた (kita) expresses an action that has been continuing from the past up to the present moment. It conveys accumulated experience or ongoing change. きた (kita) is the past tense of くる (kuru, "to come"), so think of it as the action "coming" toward the present.

Example from this song:
裏切ってきた (uragitte kita) — "have been betraying"
A pattern of betrayal that has continued over time up to now.

More examples:
• ずっと頑張ってきた (zutto ganbatte kita) — "have been working hard all along"
• 日本語を勉強してきた (nihongo o benkyou shite kita) — "have been studying Japanese"
• たくさんの人に出会ってきた (takusan no hito ni deatte kita) — "have met many people (over time)"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 裏切る (uragiru, "to betray") → 裏切って (uragitte, te-form) → 裏切ってきた (uragitte kita, "have been betraying")

grammar_points.name: 命令形 〜ろ (ro) — imperative for ru-verbs

explanation.en:
How it works:
For ichidan (ru-verb) verbs, the imperative (command form) is made by dropping る (ru) and adding ろ (ro). For godan (u-verb) compound verbs like 走り抜ける (hashiri nukeru, "to run through"), the same rule applies to the final verb. This form is direct and forceful — a battle cry or rallying command.

Example from this song:
走り抜けろ (hashiri nukero) — "run through it!" / "break through!"
A raw command to push through every obstacle.

More examples:
• 食べろ (tabero) — "eat!" (blunt command)
• 起きろ (okiro) — "wake up!"
• 逃げろ (nigero) — "run away!" / "flee!"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 走り抜ける (hashiri nukeru, "to run through") → 走り抜けろ (hashiri nukero, imperative, "run through it!")

grammar_points.name: 〜も〜も (mo ... mo) — both ... and ...

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern X + も (mo) + Y + も (mo) means "both X and Y" or "X as well as Y." It emphasizes that multiple things share the same quality or are included equally. It can also be used with negatives to mean "neither X nor Y" when followed by a negative verb.

Example from this song:
The singer lists multiple things that are equally important or equally lost, using も...も to give them equal weight.

More examples:
• 日本語も英語も話せる (nihongo mo eigo mo hanaseru) — "can speak both Japanese and English"
• 時間もお金もない (jikan mo okane mo nai) — "have neither time nor money"
• 父も母も元気です (chichi mo haha mo genki desu) — "both my father and mother are well"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: X + も (mo) + Y + も (mo) → "both X and Y"

grammar_points.name: 〜て form (te-form connection)

explanation.en:
How it works: The て-form (te-form) is one of the most essential Japanese conjugations. It connects actions in sequence, shows means/method, and links to auxiliary verbs. For godan verbs, the ending changes based on the final consonant.

Example from this song: 目指して (mezashite) = 'aiming for (and...)' — from 目指す (mezasu, 'to aim for') → 目指して (mezashite, te-form)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べて (tabete)
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行って (itte)
• 読む (yomu, 'to read') → 読んで (yonde)

Note: Te-form rules for godan verbs: す→して, く→いて, ぐ→いで, む/ぶ/ぬ→んで, つ/る/う→って. Exception: 行く → 行って (not 行いて). For ichidan verbs, just replace る with て. Mastering the te-form unlocks many grammar patterns.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 目指す (mezasu, 'to aim for') → 目指して (mezashite, te-form, 'aiming for')

grammar_points.name: 〜ず (classical negative)

explanation.en:
How it works: Replace the negative ない (nai) with ず (zu). This is the classical/literary negative conjunctive form, meaning 'without doing'. It's equivalent to modern ないで (naide).

Example from this song: 構わず (kamawazu) = 'without caring' — from 構う (kamau, 'to care/mind') → 構わない (kamawanai, negative) → 構わず (kamawazu)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べず (tabezu, 'without eating')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わず (iwazu, 'without saying')
• する (suru, 'to do') → せず (sezu, 'without doing')

Note: する → せず (not しず) is an irregular form to memorize. ず is common in written Japanese, formal speech, proverbs, and anime lyrics. 振り向かず進む (furimukazu susumu, 'advance without looking back').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 構う (kamau, 'to care') → 構わない (kamawanai, negative) → 構わず (kamawazu, 'without caring')

grammar_points.name: 〜がままに (as one pleases)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place がままに (ga mama ni) after the dictionary form of a verb to express 'as one pleases' or 'according to'. It suggests following something naturally without resistance.

Example from this song: 信じるがままに (shinjiru ga mama ni) = 'as one believes / following what you believe' — from 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') + がままに (ga mama ni, 'as one pleases')

More examples:
• 思う (omou, 'to think') → 思うがままに (omou ga mama ni, 'as one thinks/wishes')
• 感じる (kanjiru, 'to feel') → 感じるがままに (kanjiru ga mama ni, 'as one feels')
• 流れる (nagareru, 'to flow') → 流れるがままに (nagareru ga mama ni, 'as it flows')

Note: This is a literary/formal expression. It conveys a philosophical acceptance — acting according to one's nature or instinct. 心のままに (kokoro no mama ni, 'as your heart wishes') is a related simpler pattern.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') + がままに (ga mama ni, 'as one pleases') → 信じるがままに (shinjiru ga mama ni, 'following what you believe')

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて (dismissive emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place なんて (nante) after a noun or phrase to add a dismissive or emphatic tone — 'things like' or 'something trivial like'. It shows the speaker's attitude toward what precedes it.

Example from this song: The lyrics use なんて to dismiss obstacles or conventional thinking, reinforcing the song's rebellious spirit.

More examples:
• 常識 (joushiki, 'common sense') → 常識なんて (joushiki nante, 'things like common sense — who needs it')
• 限界 (genkai, 'limit') → 限界なんてない (genkai nante nai, 'there's no such thing as limits')
• 失敗 (shippai, 'failure') → 失敗なんて怖くない (shippai nante kowakunai, 'I'm not afraid of something like failure')

Note: なんて can express dismissal, surprise, or defiance depending on context. In songs about freedom and determination (like GO!!!), it usually expresses defiance against limitations.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [noun/phrase] + なんて (nante, 'things like — dismissive') = dismissive emphasis

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: For godan verbs, change the final -u to -e. For ichidan verbs, replace る with ろ. This creates a direct, forceful command. An alternative masculine form uses ろ for godan verbs too in some dialects.

Example from this song: 見極めろ (mikiwamero) = 'Discern!' — from 見極める (mikiwameru, 'to discern') → 見極めろ (mikiwamero). Also 切り開け (kirihirake) = 'Carve open!' — from 切り開く (kirihiraku) → 切り開け

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行け (ike, 'Go!')
• 起きる (okiru, 'to wake up') → 起きろ (okiro, 'Wake up!')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しろ (shiro, 'Do it!')

Note: The imperative is the quintessential anime battle-cry form. FLOW's GO!!! is full of these commands, creating an infectious energy. 走れ (hashire, 'Run!') and 行け (ike, 'Go!') are among the most iconic anime imperatives.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 見極める (mikiwameru, 'to discern') → 見極めろ (mikiwamero, 'Discern!') / 切り開く (kirihiraku, 'to carve open') → 切り開け (kirihirake, 'Carve open!')

grammar_points.name: 〜だろう (conjecture/confirmation seeking)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add だろう (darou) after a verb, adjective, or noun to express conjecture — 'probably' or 'I think'. With rising intonation, it seeks confirmation — 'right?'

Example from this song: The lyrics use だろう to both speculate and challenge — 'you know that, right?' or 'it's probably true, isn't it?'

More examples:
• 雨が降る (ame ga furu, 'it'll rain') → 雨が降るだろう (ame ga furu darou, 'it'll probably rain')
• 大丈夫 (daijoubu, 'OK') → 大丈夫だろう (daijoubu darou, 'it'll probably be fine')
• 知っている (shitteiru, 'know') → 知ってるだろう (shitteru darou, 'you know, right?')

Note: だろう is casual. でしょう (deshou) is the polite form. In anime, だろう with assertive tone = 'right?!' (challenging). With soft tone = 'probably' (speculation). でしょう with rising tone = 'isn't it?' (seeking agreement).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [verb/adjective/noun] + だろう (darou, 'probably / right?')

grammar_points.name: 〜てくぜ (gonna do it - masculine)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine the て-form + いく (iku, 'to go') + ぜ (ze, masculine emphasis particle). This creates an energetic, masculine declaration — 'I'm gonna keep doing it!' The いく often contracts away.

Example from this song: The song uses this pattern to express determined forward momentum with a rough, energetic masculine tone.

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行ってくぜ (ittekuze, 'I'm heading out!')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やってくぜ (yattekuze, 'I'm gonna do it!')
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走ってくぜ (hashittekuze, 'I'm gonna run!')

Note: ぜ (ze) is a rough masculine sentence-ending particle that adds energy and assertion. It's less aggressive than ぞ (zo). Common in shonen anime and J-rock. Think Naruto saying 行くってばよ (ikuttebayo) — similarly energetic but different particle.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [te-form] + いく (iku, 'to go') + ぜ (ze, masculine emphasis) → てくぜ (tekuze, 'gonna do it!')

grammar_points.name: 〜でいて (please be/stay)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use で (de, state marker) + いて (ite, te-form of いる, 'to be') to request someone to remain in a certain state — 'please stay/be [adjective]'. Often used with adjectives and な-adjectives.

Example from this song: The song asks someone to stay a certain way — 'please remain as you are' — using でいて to express the wish for continued existence in that state.

More examples:
• 元気 (genki, 'healthy') → 元気でいて (genki de ite, 'please stay healthy')
• そのまま (sono mama, 'as is') → そのままでいて (sono mama de ite, 'please stay as you are')
• 優しい (yasashii, 'kind') → 優しくいて (yasashiku ite, 'please stay kind')

Note: For な-adjectives and nouns, use で: 元気でいて. For い-adjectives, use the く-form: 優しくいて. Adding ください makes it more polite: 元気でいてください.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 元気 (genki, 'healthy') + で (de, state) + いて (ite, 'be') → 元気でいて (genki de ite, 'please stay healthy')

grammar_points.name: 〜てしまう (end up doing, regrettably)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add てしまう (te shimau) after the te-form of a verb to express that something happened completely, often with regret or that it was unintentional. In casual speech, it contracts to ちゃう (chau) or じゃう (jau).

Example from this song: 忘れちゃう (wasurechau) = 'end up forgetting (regrettably)' — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れて (wasurete, te-form) + しまう (shimau) → casual: 忘れちゃう (wasurechau)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べてしまう (tabete shimau, 'end up eating it all') → 食べちゃう (tabechau)
• 壊す (kowasu, 'to break') → 壊してしまう (kowashite shimau, 'accidentally break') → 壊しちゃう (kowashichau)
• 飲む (nomu, 'to drink') → 飲んでしまう (nonde shimau) → 飲んじゃう (nonjau)

Note: Contraction rules: てしまう → ちゃう, でしまう → じゃう. Past tense: ちゃった/じゃった. てしまう can also express completion without regret in some contexts.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れて (wasurete) + しまう (shimau) → 忘れてしまう (wasurete shimau, 'end up forgetting') → 忘れちゃう (wasurechau, casual)

grammar_points.name: 〜たくなる (come to want to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the たい (tai, 'want to') form of a verb, change い to く, then add なる (naru, 'to become'). This expresses a spontaneous feeling arising — 'come to want to do X'.

Example from this song: 泣きたくなる (nakitaku naru) = 'come to want to cry' — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣きたい (nakitai, 'want to cry') → 泣きたく (nakitaku) + なる (naru, 'become') = 泣きたくなる (nakitaku naru)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたくなる (tabetaku naru, 'come to want to eat')
• 帰る (kaeru, 'to return') → 帰りたくなる (kaeritaku naru, 'come to want to go home')
• 会う (au, 'to meet') → 会いたくなる (aitaku naru, 'come to want to see someone')

Note: This describes feelings that arise naturally, not deliberate decisions. たい conjugates like an い-adjective: たい → たく (adverb form) + なる.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣きたい (nakitai, 'want to cry') → 泣きたく (nakitaku) + なる (naru, 'become') → 泣きたくなる (nakitaku naru, 'come to want to cry')

grammar_points.name: 〜なくても (even without doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the negative form of a verb (ない), change it to なくて (nakute), then add も (mo, 'even'). This means 'even if you don't do X' or 'even without doing X'.

Example from this song: 見回さなくても (miwasanakutemo) = 'even without looking around' — from 見回す (miwasu, 'to look around') → 見回さない (miwasanai, 'don't look around') → 見回さなくても (miwasanakutemo, 'even without looking around')

More examples:
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わなくても (iwanakutemo, 'even without saying')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べなくても (tabenakutemo, 'even without eating')
• 心配する (shinpai suru, 'to worry') → 心配しなくても (shinpai shinakutemo, 'even without worrying')

Note: なくても often implies 'it's fine / it'll be okay even without doing X'. Compare with なくてもいい (nakutemo ii, 'it's okay not to').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 見回す (miwasu, 'to look around') → 見回さない (miwasanai, 'don't look around') → 見回さなくても (miwasanakutemo, 'even without looking around')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to create a direct command. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with ろ.

Example from this song: 歌え (utae) = 'Sing!' — from 歌う (utau, 'to sing') → change う (u) to え (e) = 歌え (utae)

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')
• 起きる (okiru, 'to wake up') → 起きろ (okiro, 'Wake up!')
• 頑張る (ganbaru, 'to do your best') → 頑張れ (ganbare, 'Do your best!')

Note: The imperative is very forceful. In this song, it's used as encouragement — 歌え means 'Sing!' in an inspiring way. Godan: う→え. Ichidan: る→ろ. The special verbs: する→しろ, 来る→来い (koi).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 歌う (utau, 'to sing') → 歌え (utae, 'Sing!')

grammar_points.name: 〜んだよ (explanatory emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add んだよ (nda yo) at the end of a sentence to strongly explain or emphasize something. ん (n) is the contracted explanatory の (no), だ (da) is the copula, and よ (yo) adds assertive emphasis.

Example from this song: The song uses んだよ to assert emotional truths with feeling — 'that's the way it is!' or 'I'm telling you that...'.

More examples:
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなんだよ (suki nandayo, 'I'm telling you, I like it!')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くんだよ (iku ndayo, 'I'm going, you know!')
• 大丈夫 (daijoubu, 'fine') → 大丈夫なんだよ (daijoubu nandayo, 'I'm telling you, it's fine!')

Note: んだよ is casual and direct. It's warmer than plain よ because の/ん adds the feeling of 'let me explain why'. After な-adjectives and nouns, add な before んだよ.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 好き (suki, 'like') + なんだよ (nandayo, 'I'm telling you') → 好きなんだよ (suki nandayo, 'I'm telling you, I like it!')

grammar_points.name: 〜てくれる (someone does for me)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add てくれる (te kureru) after the te-form of a verb to express that someone did something for the speaker's benefit. It carries gratitude — 'they did X for me'.

Example from this song: 笑ってくれた (waratte kureta) = 'you laughed for me / you smiled at me' — from 笑う (warau, 'to laugh/smile') → 笑って (waratte, te-form) + くれた (kureta, past of kureru, 'did for me')

More examples:
• 教える (oshieru, 'to teach') → 教えてくれた (oshiete kureta, 'taught me')
• 待つ (matsu, 'to wait') → 待ってくれた (matte kureta, 'waited for me')
• 聞く (kiku, 'to listen') → 聞いてくれた (kiite kureta, 'listened to me')

Note: くれる shows the action comes toward you (someone does it for your benefit). Compare with あげる (ageru, doing for someone else) and もらう (morau, receiving the action).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 笑う (warau, 'to laugh') → 笑って (waratte, te-form) + くれた (kureta, 'did for me') → 笑ってくれた (waratte kureta, 'smiled for me')

grammar_points.name: 〜てみる (try doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add てみる (te miru, literally 'do and see') after the te-form of a verb to mean 'try doing X to see what happens'. It expresses doing something as an experiment or attempt.

Example from this song: 出してみた (dashite mita) = 'tried putting out / tried expressing' — from 出す (dasu, 'to put out') → 出して (dashite, te-form) + みた (mita, past of miru, 'tried')

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べてみる (tabete miru, 'try eating it')
• 聞く (kiku, 'to ask') → 聞いてみる (kiite miru, 'try asking')
• 着る (kiru, 'to wear') → 着てみる (kite miru, 'try wearing it')

Note: てみる doesn't mean 'try hard' — it means 'give it a try to see the result'. For 'try hard / attempt', use ようとする (yō to suru).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 出す (dasu, 'to put out') → 出して (dashite, te-form) + みた (mita, 'tried') → 出してみた (dashite mita, 'tried putting out')

grammar_points.name: 〜たら (if/when)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add たら (tara) to the past tense (た-form) of a verb to create a conditional — 'if/when X happens'. It's the most versatile conditional in Japanese.

Example from this song: しゃべりかけたら (shaberikake tara) = 'when I tried to talk to you' — from しゃべりかける (shaberikakeru, 'to start talking to') → しゃべりかけたら (shaberikake tara, 'when I tried to talk to')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行ったら (ittara, 'if/when you go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたら (tabetara, 'if/when you eat')
• 雨 (ame, 'rain') → 雨だったら (ame dattara, 'if it rains')

Note: たら can express both hypothetical ('if') and temporal ('when') conditions. It often implies discovering something unexpected: 家に帰ったら猫がいた (ie ni kaettara neko ga ita, 'when I got home, there was a cat').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: しゃべりかける (shaberikakeru, 'to start talking to') → しゃべりかけたら (shaberikake tara, 'when I tried to talk to')

grammar_points.name: 〜ばかり (only; always doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ばかり (bakari) after a verb in て-form or dictionary form to indicate doing something repeatedly or exclusively, often with a slightly negative nuance — 'always doing X' or 'nothing but X'.

Example from this song: The song describes being stuck in a pattern of repetitive behavior — doing the same thing ばかり.

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べてばかり (tabete bakari, 'always eating')
• 遊ぶ (asobu, 'to play') → 遊んでばかり (asonde bakari, 'always playing')
• 文句 (monku, 'complaint') → 文句ばかり (monku bakari, 'nothing but complaints')

Note: ばかり has multiple uses: after た-form = 'just did' (食べたばかり, tabeta bakari, 'just ate'). After て-form = 'always doing'. After nouns = 'nothing but'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べてばかり (tabete bakari, 'always eating') / 文句 (monku, 'complaint') + ばかり (bakari) → 文句ばかり (monku bakari, 'nothing but complaints')

grammar_points.name: 可能形 (potential form)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change a verb to express ability — 'can do X'. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with られる. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent and add る.

Example from this song: しゃべれた (shabereta) = 'was able to talk' — from しゃべる (shaberu, 'to talk') → しゃべれる (shabereru, 'can talk') → しゃべれた (shabereta, 'was able to talk')

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べられる (taberareru, 'can eat')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行ける (ikeru, 'can go')
• 読む (yomu, 'to read') → 読める (yomeru, 'can read')

Note: For godan verbs: く→ける, す→せる, つ→てる, む→める, ぶ→べる, ぬ→ねる, う→える, る→れる. In casual speech, 食べられる is often shortened to 食べれる (tabereru) — called ら抜き (ra-nuki).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: しゃべる (shaberu, 'to talk') → しゃべれる (shabereru, 'can talk') → しゃべれた (shabereta, 'was able to talk')

grammar_points.name: 〜のさ (explanatory + emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add のさ (no sa) at the end of a sentence to provide an explanation with casual, often masculine emphasis. の (no) is the explanatory particle and さ (sa) adds assertion.

Example from this song: The song uses のさ to assert explanations in a laid-back, confident way — 'that's just how it is, you see'.

More examples:
• そう (sou, 'that's right') → そうなのさ (sou na no sa, 'that's just how it is')
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなのさ (suki na no sa, 'it's that I like it, you see')
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かるのさ (wakaru no sa, 'I understand, you know')

Note: のさ is more casual and assertive than のだ or んだ. It's common in song lyrics and casual male speech. The feminine equivalent would be のよ (no yo).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 好き (suki, 'like') + な (na) + のさ (no sa, 'it's that...') → 好きなのさ (suki na no sa, 'it's that I like it, you see')

grammar_points.name: 〜ている (te iru) — ongoing state

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + いる (iru) expresses either an ongoing action ("is doing ~") or a resulting state ("is in the state of having done ~"). In casual speech, いる (iru) contracts to る (ru). This is one of the most fundamental patterns in Japanese.

Example from this song:
そばにいる (soba ni iru) — "to be by (someone's) side"
いる (iru) here expresses the state of existing/being present near someone.

More examples:
• 今、テレビを見ている (ima, terebi o mite iru) — "I'm watching TV right now"
• ドアが開いている (doa ga aite iru) — "the door is open" (resulting state)
• もう食べてる (mou tabeteru) — "already eating" (casual)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: いる (iru, "to be/exist") — そば (soba, "side") + に (ni, "at") + いる (iru) → そばにいる (soba ni iru, "to be by one's side")

grammar_points.name: 〜から (kara) — because

explanation.en:
How it works:
The particle から (kara) after a clause means "because ~" and gives a reason. The pattern is: Reason clause + から (kara), Result clause. It is one of the first grammar points learners study and is used constantly in everyday Japanese. It can also mean "from" when following a noun (time/place).

Example from this song:
そばにいるから (soba ni iru kara) — "because I'll be by your side"
The title itself uses this pattern — the singer gives the reason for comfort: because I am here.

More examples:
• 疲れたから休む (tsukareta kara yasumu) — "I'll rest because I'm tired"
• 好きだから頑張る (suki da kara ganbaru) — "I'll try hard because I like it"
• 雨だから家にいる (ame da kara ie ni iru) — "I'm staying home because it's raining"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: そばにいる (soba ni iru, "be by your side") + から (kara, "because") → そばにいるから (soba ni iru kara, "because I'll be by your side")

grammar_points.name: 〜だって (datte) — even (casual)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The particle だって (datte) after a noun means "even ~" in casual speech. It is the informal equivalent of でも (demo, "even"). It adds emphasis to something that might be unexpected or difficult. With question words: 誰だって (dare datte, "anyone"), いつだって (itsu datte, "anytime").

Example from this song:
離ればなれの夜だって (hanabanare no yoru datte) — "even on nights when we're apart"
Even during painful separation, the singer's feelings remain unchanged.

More examples:
• 子供だって分かる (kodomo datte wakaru) — "even a child understands"
• どんな時だって味方だよ (donna toki datte mikata da yo) — "I'm on your side no matter when"
• 一人だって大丈夫 (hitori datte daijoubu) — "even alone, it's okay"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 離ればなれの夜 (hanabanare no yoru, "nights apart") + だって (datte, "even") → 離ればなれの夜だって (hanabanare no yoru datte, "even on nights apart")

grammar_points.name: 〜のかな (no kana) — I wonder if

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + のかな (no kana) expresses casual wondering — "I wonder if ~." The の (no) adds explanatory nuance, and かな (kana) expresses uncertainty or self-directed questioning. It is softer and more reflective than a direct question. Very common in song lyrics and inner monologue.

Example from this song:
今もあるのかな (ima mo aru no kana) — "I wonder if it's still there"
The singer gently wonders whether something from the past still exists.

More examples:
• 元気にしてるのかな (genki ni shiteru no kana) — "I wonder if they're doing well"
• これで良かったのかな (kore de yokatta no kana) — "I wonder if this was the right thing"
• 覚えてるのかな (oboeteru no kana) — "I wonder if they remember"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 今もある (ima mo aru, "still exists") + の (no, explanatory) + かな (kana, wondering) → 今もあるのかな (ima mo aru no kana, "I wonder if it's still there")

grammar_points.name: 〜たりする (tari suru) — sometimes / among other things

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb た-form (ta-form) + り (ri) + する (suru) means "do things like ~" or "sometimes ~." It lists actions as examples, implying there are others too. You can list multiple: AたりBたりする (A tari B tari suru, "do things like A and B"). It gives a casual, non-exhaustive feeling.

Example from this song:
わからなくなったりする (wakaranaku nattari suru) — "sometimes I become confused"
The singer admits to occasionally losing their way — it happens from time to time.

More examples:
• 週末は映画を見たり買い物したりする (shuumatsu wa eiga o mitari kaimono shitari suru) — "on weekends I do things like watch movies and go shopping"
• 泣いたり笑ったりする (naitari warattari suru) — "sometimes cry, sometimes laugh"
• 忘れたりしないよ (wasuretari shinai yo) — "I won't do things like forgetting (you)"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: わからなくなる (wakaranaku naru, "become confused") → わからなくなった (wakaranaku natta, past) + り (ri) + する (suru) → わからなくなったりする (wakaranaku nattari suru, "sometimes become confused")

grammar_points.name: 〜ている (te iru) — progressive / ongoing state

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + いる (iru) expresses either (1) an ongoing action — "is doing ~," or (2) a resulting state — "has done ~ (and the result remains)." In casual speech, いる (iru) contracts to る (ru): 食べている (tabete iru) → 食べてる (tabeteru). This is one of the most essential patterns in Japanese.

Example from this song:
いつも笑っている (itsumo waratte iru) — "is always smiling"
Describes a habitual, ongoing state — someone who constantly smiles.

More examples:
• 今、本を読んでいる (ima, hon o yonde iru) — "I'm reading a book right now" (ongoing action)
• 窓が開いている (mado ga aite iru) — "the window is open" (resulting state)
• もう食べてる (mou tabeteru) — "already eating" (casual contraction)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 笑う (warau, "to smile/laugh") → 笑って (waratte, te-form) → 笑っている (waratte iru, "is smiling")

grammar_points.name: 〜てみせる (te miseru) — I'll show you I can!

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + みせる (miseru, "to show") expresses strong determination — "I will definitely do ~ (and prove it)!" or "I'll show you that I can ~!" It is a declaration of resolve. Literally, it means "I will do ~ and show (the result)." This is a powerful, confident expression.

Example from this song:
The singer declares with conviction that they will achieve something and prove it to the world.

More examples:
• 絶対に勝ってみせる (zettai ni katte miseru) — "I will win, I'll show you!"
• 夢を叶えてみせる (yume o kanaete miseru) — "I will make my dream come true, just watch!"
• 最後まで生き延びてみせる (saigo made ikinobite miseru) — "I'll survive to the end, I promise!"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb て-form (te-form) + みせる (miseru, "to show") → "I'll prove I can ~!"

grammar_points.name: 〜ても (te mo) — even if

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + も (mo) means "even if ~" or "even though ~." It states that the result will not change regardless of the condition. For い-adjectives (i-adjectives): drop い (i), add くても (kutemo). For な-adjectives (na-adjectives)/nouns: add でも (demo). This is fundamental for expressing resilience and determination.

Example from this song:
Used to express that obstacles will not stop the singer — even if they fall, they will get back up.

More examples:
• 雨が降っても行く (ame ga futte mo iku) — "even if it rains, I'll go"
• どんなに辛くても (donna ni tsurakutemo) — "no matter how painful"
• 失敗しても諦めない (shippai shitemo akiramenai) — "even if I fail, I won't give up"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb て-form (te-form) + も (mo) → "even if ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru) — to continue doing

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) means "to continue doing ~" or "to keep doing ~." It emphasizes that an action persists without stopping. 続ける (tsuzukeru) conjugates as a normal ichidan verb: 続けた (tsuzuketa, past), 続けている (tsuzukete iru, is continuing).

Example from this song:
The song emphasizes persistent action — continuing to run, continuing to believe, never stopping.

More examples:
• 書き続ける (kaki tsuzukeru) — "keep writing"
• 待ち続けた (machi tsuzuketa) — "kept waiting"
• 歩き続けよう (aruki tsuzukeyou) — "let's keep walking"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru, "to continue") → "keep doing ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜んだろう (n darou) — I wonder / it must be that

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + んだろう (n darou) combines the explanatory の/ん (no/n, "the fact is") with だろう (darou, "probably / I wonder"). It can express (1) wondering — "I wonder if ~" or (2) conjecture — "it must be that ~." It is softer than a direct question and is common in internal monologue and song lyrics.

Example from this song:
The singer wonders about their path — reflecting on what they should do or what might happen.

More examples:
• どうしてだろう (doushite darou) — "I wonder why"
• 幸せなんだろうか (shiawase nan darou ka) — "I wonder if I'm happy"
• きっと大丈夫なんだろう (kitto daijoubu nan darou) — "it must be okay, surely"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb/Adjective plain form + ん (n) + だろう (darou) → "I wonder if ~" / "it must be ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜ず (zu) — without doing (literary negative)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The ending 〜ず (zu) is the classical Japanese negative form, equivalent to modern ないで (naide, "without doing"). To form it: take the ない-form stem and add ず (zu). For する (suru), it becomes せず (sezu). For example: 食べない (tabenai) → 食べず (tabezu). It sounds more literary and formal, making it common in songs and written Japanese.

Example from this song:
The singer describes doing something "without" another action — pressing forward without hesitation, without looking back.

More examples:
• 何も言わず去った (nani mo iwazu satta) — "left without saying anything"
• 休まず働いた (yasumazu hataraita) — "worked without resting"
• 諦めずに頑張る (akiramezu ni ganbaru) — "persevere without giving up"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: Verb ない-form stem + ず (zu) → "without doing ~"

grammar_points.name: 〜まま (mama: as it is; unchanged)

explanation.en:
How it works: まま (mama) expresses a state that remains unchanged. Attach it after の (no) with nouns, or after the plain form of verbs/adjectives, to mean 'as it is' or 'remaining in that state.'

Example from this song: あの頃のまま (ano koro no mama) = 'unchanged from those days' — the side profile in dreams remains exactly as it was back then

More examples:
• ドアを開けたまま (doa o aketa mama, 'with the door left open') — from 開ける (akeru, 'to open')
• このままでいい (kono mama de ii, 'it's fine as it is') — expressing contentment
• 靴のまま入る (kutsu no mama hairu, 'enter with shoes on') — state unchanged

Note: まま after a past-tense verb means something was left in that state. After の, it describes maintaining a noun's condition. It often implies the state was unexpected or noteworthy.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: あの頃 (ano koro, 'those days') + の (no) + まま (mama, 'as is') + で (de) → あの頃のままで (ano koro no mama de, 'unchanged from those days')

grammar_points.name: 〜てしまう (te shimau: end up doing; regrettably)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach しまう (shimau) to a verb's te-form to express completion with regret, or that something happened unintentionally. 'Ended up doing' or 'regrettably did.'

Example from this song: 置いてきてしまった (oite kite shimatta) = 'ended up leaving behind' — from 置いてくる (oite kuru, 'to leave behind and come back') → 置いてきて (oite kite) + しまった (shimatta)

More examples:
• 忘れてしまった (wasurete shimatta, 'unfortunately forgot') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')
• 食べてしまった (tabete shimatta, 'ended up eating it all') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• なくしてしまった (nakushite shimatta, 'lost it accidentally') — from なくす (nakusu, 'to lose')

Note: Casual contractions: てしまう → ちゃう (chau), てしまった → ちゃった (chatta). Also でしまう → じゃう (jau).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 置いてくる (oite kuru, 'to leave behind') → 置いてきて (oite kite) → 置いてきてしまった (oite kite shimatta, 'ended up leaving behind')

grammar_points.name: 〜のなら (no nara: if it's the case that)

explanation.en:
How it works: のなら (no nara) combines the explanatory の (no) with the conditional なら (nara) to mean 'if it's the case that.' It adds an explanatory nuance to the condition.

Example from this song: 取り戻せないのなら (torimodosenai no nara) = 'if it's the case that I can't get it back' — from 取り戻す (tomodosu, 'to get back') → 取り戻せない (torimodosenai, 'can't get back') + のなら

More examples:
• 行くのなら早く (iku no nara hayaku, 'if you're going, go early') — from 行く (iku, 'to go')
• 本当のなら信じる (hontou no nara shinjiru, 'if it's true, I'll believe it')
• 会えるのなら会いたい (aeru no nara aitai, 'if I could meet you, I'd want to') — from 会える (aeru, 'can meet')

Note: のなら is slightly more emphatic than just なら. It implies the speaker is responding to or considering a specific situation or piece of information.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 取り戻せない (torimodosenai, 'can't get back') + のなら (no nara, 'if it's the case that') → 取り戻せないのなら (torimodosenai no nara, 'if I can't get it back')

grammar_points.name: 〜ながらも (nagara mo: even while)

explanation.en:
How it works: ながらも (nagara mo) adds も (mo, 'even') to ながら (nagara, 'while') to express doing two contradictory or contrasting things simultaneously. It emphasizes the contrast between them.

Example from this song: 明け暮れながらも (akekure nagara mo) = 'even while spending days (in that state)' — from 明け暮れる (akekureru, 'to spend one's days')

More examples:
• 知りながらも黙っていた (shiri nagara mo damatte ita, 'kept quiet even while knowing') — from 知る (shiru, 'to know')
• 小さいながらも頑張る (chiisai nagara mo ganbaru, 'try hard despite being small')
• 泣きながらも笑った (naki nagara mo waratta, 'smiled even while crying') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry')

Note: Plain ながら means 'while doing X.' Adding も creates a concessive meaning: 'even while/despite X.' This highlights that the two actions seem contradictory.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 明け暮れる (akekureru, 'to spend one's days') → 明け暮れ (akekure) + ながらも (nagara mo, 'even while') → 明け暮れながらも (akekure nagara mo, 'even while spending days')

grammar_points.name: 〜ておく (te oku: to do in advance; to leave as is)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach おく (oku) to a verb's te-form to express doing something in preparation for the future, or deliberately leaving something in a certain state.

Example from this song: 焼き付けておこう (yakitsukete okou) = 'let me burn it into (my memory) for safekeeping' — from 焼き付ける (yakitsukeru, 'to burn/imprint') → 焼き付けて (yakitsukete) + おこう (okou, volitional of oku)

More examples:
• 買っておく (katte oku, 'buy in advance') — from 買う (kau, 'to buy')
• 窓を開けておいて (mado o akete oite, 'leave the window open') — from 開ける (akeru, 'to open')
• 調べておいた (shirabete oita, 'researched in advance') — from 調べる (shiraberu, 'to investigate')

Note: In casual speech, ておく contracts to とく (toku): 買っとく (kattoku, 'buy in advance'). The volitional form ておこう means 'let me do X in advance.'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 焼き付ける (yakitsukeru, 'to imprint') → 焼き付けて (yakitsukete) → 焼き付けておこう (yakitsukete okou, 'let me imprint it for keeps')

grammar_points.name: 〜ちゃいけない (cha ikenai: must not)

explanation.en:
How it works: ちゃいけない (cha ikenai) is the casual form of てはいけない (te wa ikenai), meaning 'must not' or 'it's not OK to.' It expresses prohibition.

Example from this song: 忘れちゃいけない (wasureccha ikenai) = 'must not forget' — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れては (wasurete wa) → casual: 忘れちゃ (wasureccha) + いけない (ikenai)

More examples:
• 食べちゃいけない (tabeccha ikenai, 'must not eat') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 言っちゃいけない (iccha ikenai, 'must not say') — from 言う (iu, 'to say')
• 泣いちゃダメ (naiccha dame, 'you mustn't cry') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry') — ダメ is another way to say 'not allowed'

Note: The contraction pattern: ては → ちゃ, では → じゃ. So 飲んではいけない (nonde wa ikenai) → 飲んじゃいけない (nonjya ikenai, 'must not drink').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れては (wasurete wa) → 忘れちゃ (wasureccha, casual) + いけない (ikenai, 'must not') → 忘れちゃいけない (wasureccha ikenai, 'must not forget')

grammar_points.name: せっかく〜のに/から (sekkaku: since the effort was made)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place せっかく (sekkaku) before a clause to emphasize that something special or effortful happened, and you should take advantage of it. Pairs with から (kara, 'so') or のに (noni, 'despite').

Example from this song: せっかく晴れたから (sekkaku hareta kara) = 'since it finally cleared up (don't waste it)' — from せっかく (sekkaku, 'with great effort/finally') + 晴れた (hareta, 'cleared up') + から (kara, 'so')

More examples:
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → せっかく来たのに (sekkaku kita noni, 'you came all this way, and yet...')
• 作る (tsukuru, 'to make') → せっかく作ったから (sekkaku tsukutta kara, 'since I went to the trouble of making it')
• 休み (yasumi, 'holiday') → せっかくの休みだから (sekkaku no yasumi da kara, 'since it's a precious day off')

Note: せっかく + から = positive outcome ('since the effort was made, let's enjoy it'). せっかく + のに = wasted effort ('despite the effort, it was wasted'). With nouns: せっかくの + noun.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: せっかく (sekkaku, 'with great effort') + 晴れた (hareta, 'cleared up') + から (kara, 'so') → せっかく晴れたから (sekkaku hareta kara, 'since it finally cleared up')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending for a direct command. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with ろ.

Example from this song: 進め (susume) = 'Move forward!' — from 進む (susumu, 'to advance') → change む to め. Also: 漕げ (koge) = 'Pedal/Row!' — from 漕ぐ (kogu, 'to pedal/row') → change ぐ to げ

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')
• 見る (miru, 'to look') → 見ろ (miro, 'Look!')
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じろ (shinjiro, 'Believe!')

Note: In this uplifting song, the imperatives are encouraging: 'move forward! keep pedaling!' Godan: む→め, ぐ→げ, す→せ, く→け. Ichidan: る→ろ.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 進む (susumu, 'to advance') → 進め (susume, 'Move forward!') / 漕ぐ (kogu, 'to pedal') → 漕げ (koge, 'Pedal!')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていく (te iku: to go on doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ていく (te iku) after the te-form of a verb to express an action continuing into the future — 'keep doing X' or 'gradually X'. It implies movement away from the current state.

Example from this song: 変わっていく (kawatte iku) = 'keeps changing' and 導いていく (michibiite iku) = 'keep guiding' — expressing forward momentum.

More examples:
• 成長する (seichou suru, 'to grow') → 成長していく (seichou shite iku, 'keep growing')
• 離れる (hanareru, 'to separate') → 離れていく (hanarete iku, 'drifting apart')
• 強くなる (tsuyoku naru, 'to become strong') → 強くなっていく (tsuyoku natte iku, 'getting stronger and stronger')

Note: ていく = future/outward direction. てくる = past/inward direction. 寒くなっていく ('it'll keep getting colder' — looking ahead) vs. 寒くなってきた ('it's gotten colder' — looking back).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わって (kawatte, te-form) + いく (iku, 'go') → 変わっていく (kawatte iku, 'keeps changing') / 導く (michibiku, 'to guide') → 導いていく (michibiite iku, 'keep guiding')

grammar_points.name: 〜にしか...ない (ni shika nai: only)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + にしか (ni shika, 'only to') + negative verb to restrict meaning — 'can only [verb] to/for [noun]'. しか always needs a negative.

Example from this song: 僕にしか見れない (boku ni shika mirenai) = 'that only I can see' — from 僕 (boku, 'I') + にしか (ni shika, 'only to') + 見れない (mirenai, 'can't see')

More examples:
• 君 (kimi, 'you') → 君にしかできない (kimi ni shika dekinai, 'only you can do it')
• ここ (koko, 'here') → ここにしかない (koko ni shika nai, 'only exists here')
• 今 (ima, 'now') → 今しかない (ima shika nai, 'it's now or never')

Note: にしか emphasizes exclusivity with an emotional weight — it's not just 'only' but 'ONLY this and nothing else'. In this song, it's empowering: something unique to 'me' that no one else can see.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 僕 (boku, 'I') + にしか (ni shika, 'only to') + 見れない (mirenai, 'can't see') → 僕にしか見れない (boku ni shika mirenai, 'only I can see')

grammar_points.name: 〜そうだ (sou da: seems like)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach そう (sō) to the verb stem (masu-stem) to express that something appears about to happen based on visual evidence — 'it looks like it will X'.

Example from this song: 途切れそうだ (togiresō da) = 'seems about to break off' — from 途切れる (togireru, 'to be interrupted') → 途切れ (togire, stem) + そうだ (sō da, 'seems like')

More examples:
• 降る (furu, 'to rain') → 降りそうだ (furisō da, 'looks like it'll rain')
• 壊れる (kowareru, 'to break') → 壊れそうだ (kowaresō da, 'looks about to break')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣きそうだ (nakisō da, 'looks about to cry')

Note: This そう is based on appearance/observation. Different from hearsay そうだ (after dictionary form): 雨が降るそうだ (ame ga furu sō da, 'I heard it will rain'). For adjectives: drop い, add そう: 美味しい → 美味しそう (oishisō, 'looks delicious').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 途切れる (togireru, 'to break off') → 途切れ (togire, stem) + そうだ (sō da, 'seems like') → 途切れそうだ (togiresō da, 'seems about to break off')

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて (nante: such a thing as)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add なんて (nante) after a noun or phrase to express surprise, dismissal, or contempt — 'something like X' or 'such a thing as X'. The nuance depends on context.

Example from this song: 地図なんて見ない (chizu nante minai) = 'I won't look at something like a map' — from 地図 (chizu, 'map') + なんて (nante, 'such a thing as') + 見ない (minai, 'won't look at')

More examples:
• テスト (tesuto, 'test') → テストなんて簡単だ (tesuto nante kantan da, 'a test? That's easy!')
• 別れ (wakare, 'farewell') → 別れなんて嫌だ (wakare nante iya da, 'I hate something like goodbyes')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → そんなこと言うなんて (sonna koto iu nante, 'I can't believe you'd say such a thing')

Note: なんて is dismissive: 地図なんて = 'a mere map' — implying it's unnecessary. In this song, it shows confidence: 'who needs a map?' It can express pleasant surprise too: 合格するなんて (goukaku suru nante, 'to think I passed!').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 地図 (chizu, 'map') + なんて (nante, 'such a thing as') + 見ない (minai, 'won't look at') → 地図なんて見ない (chizu nante minai, 'won't bother looking at a map')

grammar_points.name: 〜ば いい (if you do... it's fine)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine the ば-conditional with いい (ii, 'good'). This gives soft advice — 'you should just do X' or 'it would be good if you did X'.

Example from this song: 進めばいい (susumeba ii) = 'just move forward and it'll be fine' — from 進む (susumu, 'to advance') → 進めば (susumeba, ば-conditional) + いい (ii, 'good')

More examples:
• 聞く (kiku, 'to ask') → 聞けばいい (kikeba ii, 'you should just ask')
• 休む (yasumu, 'to rest') → 休めばいい (yasumeba ii, 'you should just rest')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やればいい (yareba ii, 'you should just do it')

Note: This is gentle advice, not a strong command. It's like saying 'just do X, it'll work out'. The tone can range from encouraging to slightly dismissive depending on context. どうすればいい？ (dou sureba ii?, 'What should I do?') is a very common question.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 進む (susumu, 'to advance') → 進めば (susumeba, conditional) + いい (ii, 'good') → 進めばいい (susumeba ii, 'just move forward')

grammar_points.name: 〜はず (should be)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place はず (hazu) after a verb (dictionary or past form), adjective, or noun + の. It expresses expectation — 'should be' or 'is supposed to'. It indicates confidence that something is true.

Example from this song: 飛べるはず (toberu hazu) = 'should be able to fly' — from 飛べる (toberu, 'can fly') + はず (hazu, 'should')

More examples:
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来るはず (kuru hazu, 'should come')
• 安い (yasui, 'cheap') → 安いはず (yasui hazu, 'should be cheap')
• 学生 (gakusei, 'student') → 学生のはず (gakusei no hazu, 'should be a student')

Note: はず expresses the speaker's confident expectation based on logic or information. はずがない (hazu ga nai) = 'there's no way' (strong denial). そんなはずはない (sonna hazu wa nai, 'that can't be right').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 飛べる (toberu, 'can fly') + はず (hazu, 'should') → 飛べるはず (toberu hazu, 'should be able to fly')

grammar_points.name: 〜ないでいて (keep not doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the ない-form, add で (de), then いて (ite, te-form of いる). This requests someone to maintain a negative state — 'keep not doing X' or 'stay in the state of not having done X'.

Example from this song: 閉ざさないでいて (tozasanaide ite) = 'keep it from closing / stay open' — from 閉ざす (tozasu, 'to close off') → 閉ざさない (tozasanai, negative) + でいて (de ite, 'keep being')

More examples:
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れないでいて (wasurenaide ite, 'keep not forgetting / don't forget')
• 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わらないでいて (kawaranaide ite, 'keep not changing / stay the same')
• 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up') → 諦めないでいて (akiramenaide ite, 'keep not giving up')

Note: This is more specific than just ないで (naide, 'don't'). The いて adds 'stay in that state' — it's a request for ongoing non-action, not just a one-time prohibition.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 閉ざす (tozasu, 'to close off') → 閉ざさない (tozasanai, negative) + でいて (de ite, 'keep being') → 閉ざさないでいて (tozasanaide ite, 'keep it from closing')

grammar_points.name: 〜合う (mutual action)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add 合う (au, 'to meet/match'). This creates a compound verb expressing mutual or reciprocal action — 'do X to/with each other'.

Example from this song: 与え合う (atae au) = 'give to each other' — from 与える (ataeru, 'to give') → 与え (atae, masu-stem) + 合う (au). Also 信じ合う (shinji au) = 'believe in each other'.

More examples:
• 助ける (tasukeru, 'to help') → 助け合う (tasuke au, 'help each other')
• 愛する (aisuru, 'to love') → 愛し合う (aishi au, 'love each other')
• 話す (hanasu, 'to talk') → 話し合う (hanashi au, 'discuss together')

Note: 合う as an auxiliary always implies reciprocity or mutuality. It's a beautiful and very Japanese concept — emphasizing togetherness and shared action.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 与える (ataeru, 'to give') → 与え (atae, masu-stem) + 合う (au, 'each other') → 与え合う (atae au, 'give to each other')

grammar_points.name: 〜としても (even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add としても (to shitemo) after a verb to express a strong concessive — 'even if' or 'even assuming that'. It's more emphatic than simple ても.

Example from this song: つまずいたとしても (tsumazuita to shitemo) = 'even if you stumble' — from つまずいた (tsumazuita, 'stumbled') + としても (to shitemo, 'even if')

More examples:
• 失敗する (shippai suru, 'to fail') → 失敗したとしても (shippai shita to shitemo, 'even if I fail')
• 嫌だ (iya da, 'dislike') → 嫌だとしても (iya da to shitemo, 'even if I hate it')
• できない (dekinai, 'can't') → できないとしても (dekinai to shitemo, 'even if I can't')

Note: としても is more hypothetical and emphatic than ても. It often introduces a scenario the speaker acknowledges but pushes past. 仮に (kari ni, 'supposing') often precedes it for extra emphasis.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: つまずく (tsumazuku, 'to stumble') → つまずいた (tsumazuita, past) + としても (to shitemo, 'even if') → つまずいたとしても (tsumazuita to shitemo, 'even if you stumble')

grammar_points.name: 〜ように (just like)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place ように (you ni) after a verb to create a simile — 'just like' or 'as if'. It compares an action or state to another.

Example from this song: 虹が架かるように (niji ga kakaru you ni) = 'just like a rainbow spans (the sky)' — from 虹が架かる (niji ga kakaru, 'a rainbow spans') + ように (you ni, 'just like')

More examples:
• 鳥が飛ぶ (tori ga tobu, 'a bird flies') → 鳥が飛ぶように (tori ga tobu you ni, 'just like a bird flies')
• 水が流れる (mizu ga nagareru, 'water flows') → 水が流れるように (mizu ga nagareru you ni, 'just like water flows')
• 風のように (kaze no you ni, 'like the wind')

Note: ように has multiple uses: simile ('like'), purpose ('so that'), and wish ('I hope'). Context determines meaning. With ますように at the end of a sentence, it becomes a prayer or wish.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 虹が架かる (niji ga kakaru, 'a rainbow spans') + ように (you ni, 'just like') → 虹が架かるように (niji ga kakaru you ni, 'just like a rainbow spans')

grammar_points.name: 〜ても (te mo) — even if / even though

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + も (mo) means "even if ~" or "even though ~." It expresses that the outcome will not change regardless of the condition. For い-adjectives (i-adjectives): drop い (i), add くても (kutemo). For nouns/な-adjectives: でも (demo).

Example from this song:
叩き付けられても (tatakitsukerarete mo) — "even if beaten down"
No matter how many times the singer is knocked down, they refuse to give up.

More examples:
• 雨が降っても行く (ame ga futte mo iku) — "even if it rains, I'll go"
• どんなに辛くても諦めない (donna ni tsurakutemo akiramenai) — "no matter how painful, I won't give up"
• 嫌われても構わない (kirawarete mo kamawanai) — "I don't care even if I'm hated"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 叩き付けられる (tatakitsukerareru, "to be beaten down") → 叩き付けられて (tatakitsukerarete, te-form) + も (mo) → 叩き付けられても (tatakitsukerarete mo, "even if beaten down")

grammar_points.name: 〜わけがない (wake ga nai) — there's no way / impossible

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb plain form + わけがない (wake ga nai) means "there's no reason that ~" or "it can't possibly be that ~." It is a strong denial of possibility. わけ (wake) means "reason/logic," so わけがない (wake ga nai) literally means "there is no logic for ~." Often softened with など (nado): わけなどはない (wake nado wa nai).

Example from this song:
あきらめられるわけなどはなく (akiramerareru wake nado wa naku) — "there's no reason I could give up"
The singer emphatically states that giving up is logically impossible.

More examples:
• そんなことあるわけがない (sonna koto aru wake ga nai) — "there's no way that's true"
• 忘れるわけがない (wasureru wake ga nai) — "there's no way I'd forget"
• 彼が犯人のわけがない (kare ga hannin no wake ga nai) — "there's no way he's the culprit"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: あきらめられる (akiramerareru, "can give up") + わけ (wake, "reason") + など (nado, "such as") + は (wa) + ない (nai) → あきらめられるわけなどはない (akiramerareru wake nado wa nai, "there's no way I could give up")

grammar_points.name: 〜ようと (you to) — no matter what / regardless

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb volitional form + と (to) or とも (tomo) means "no matter what ~" or "regardless of ~." It expresses that whatever may happen, the result will be the same. The volitional form sets up the hypothetical, and と (to) dismisses its relevance. This is a formal, determined expression.

Example from this song:
待ち受けていようと (machiukete iyou to) — "no matter what awaits"
Whatever challenges may lie ahead, the singer faces them undeterred.

More examples:
• 何があろうと (nani ga arou to) — "no matter what happens"
• 誰が反対しようと (dare ga hantai shiyou to) — "no matter who opposes"
• どんな困難が来ようとも (donna konnan ga koyou tomo) — "no matter what difficulty comes"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 待ち受けている (machiukete iru, "is awaiting") → 待ち受けていよう (machiukete iyou, volitional) + と (to) → 待ち受けていようと (machiukete iyou to, "no matter what awaits")

grammar_points.name: 〜ば (ba) — conditional (if)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The 〜ば (ba) conditional means "if ~." For godan verbs: change -u to -e + ば: ある (aru) → あれば (areba). For ichidan verbs: drop る + れば: 食べる (taberu) → 食べれば (tabereba). For い-adjectives: drop い + ければ. This conditional focuses on the condition being the key factor for the result.

Example from this song:
あれば (areba) — "if there is"
If a certain thing exists, everything else follows from it.

More examples:
• 時間があれば行く (jikan ga areba iku) — "if I have time, I'll go"
• 安ければ買う (yasukereba kau) — "if it's cheap, I'll buy it"
• 頑張れば夢は叶う (ganbareba yume wa kanau) — "if you try hard, dreams come true"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: ある (aru, "to exist") → あれば (areba, conditional, "if there is")

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru) — to keep doing

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) means "to continue doing ~" or "to keep doing ~." It emphasizes unbroken persistence. 続ける (tsuzukeru) conjugates as an ichidan verb: 続けた (tsuzuketa, past), 続けている (tsuzukete iru, is continuing).

Example from this song:
廻り続ける (mawari tsuzukeru) — "keep spinning"
The world keeps spinning — an image of perpetual motion and resilience.

More examples:
• 歌い続ける (utai tsuzukeru) — "keep singing"
• 走り続けた (hashiri tsuzuketa) — "kept running"
• 信じ続けよう (shinji tsuzukeyou) — "let's keep believing"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 廻る (mawaru, "to spin") → 廻り (mawari, masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) → 廻り続ける (mawari tsuzukeru, "keep spinning")

grammar_points.name: 〜にも負けず (ni mo makezu) — without losing to / undaunted by

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Noun + にも (ni mo) + 負けず (makezu) means "without losing to ~" or "undaunted by ~." 負ける (makeru) means "to lose," and 負けず (makezu) is its classical negative form (ず = without). This expression is famous from Miyazawa Kenji's poem "Ame ni mo Makezu" ("Not losing to the rain"). It conveys endurance and resilience.

Example from this song:
雨にも負けず (ame ni mo makezu) — "not losing to the rain"
A declaration of perseverance against all natural forces and hardships.

More examples:
• 風にも負けず (kaze ni mo makezu) — "not losing to the wind"
• 困難にも負けず前に進む (konnan ni mo makezu mae ni susumu) — "moving forward without losing to difficulties"
• 病気にも負けず頑張った (byouki ni mo makezu ganbatta) — "persevered without losing to illness"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 雨 (ame, "rain") + に (ni) + も (mo, "even") + 負けず (makezu, "without losing") → 雨にも負けず (ame ni mo makezu, "not losing to the rain")

grammar_points.name: 〜ても (temo: even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ても (temo) after the te-form of a verb to create a concessive — 'even if X happens'. The result doesn't change regardless of the condition.

Example from this song: 描いても (egaitemo) = 'even if I draw/imagine' — from 描く (egaku, 'to draw') → 描いて (egaite, te-form) + も (mo, 'even') = 描いても (egaitemo). Also: 掴んでも (tsukandemo) = 'even if I grab' and 躓いても (tsumazuitemo) = 'even if I stumble'

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べても (tabetemo, 'even if I eat')
• 高い (takai, 'expensive') → 高くても (takakutemo, 'even if it's expensive')
• 雨 (ame, 'rain') → 雨でも (ame demo, 'even if it rains')

Note: For verbs, use te-form + も. For い-adjectives, change い to くても. For な-adjectives/nouns, use でも. ても shows resilience — the outcome stays the same no matter what.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 描く (egaku, 'to draw') → 描いて (egaite) + も (mo, 'even') → 描いても (egaitemo, 'even if I draw') / 掴む (tsukamu, 'to grab') → 掴んでも (tsukandemo, 'even if I grab')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていく (te iku: keep doing; gradually)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ていく (te iku, literally 'do and go') after the te-form of a verb to express an action that continues moving away from the present state — 'keep doing' or 'gradually change'.

Example from this song: 遠ざかっていく (toozakatte iku) = 'keeps getting farther away' — from 遠ざかる (toozakaru, 'to move away') → 遠ざかって (toozakatte, te-form) + いく (iku, 'going')

More examples:
• 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わっていく (kawatte iku, 'keeps changing / gradually changes')
• 消える (kieru, 'to disappear') → 消えていく (kiete iku, 'fading away')
• 強くなる (tsuyoku naru, 'to become strong') → 強くなっていく (tsuyoku natte iku, 'keep getting stronger')

Note: ていく describes movement AWAY from now (into the future). Compare with てくる (te kuru), which describes movement TOWARD now (from the past). 寒くなっていく = 'it keeps getting colder' (future). 寒くなってきた = 'it has gotten cold' (until now).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 遠ざかる (toozakaru, 'to move away') → 遠ざかって (toozakatte, te-form) + いく (iku, 'go') → 遠ざかっていく (toozakatte iku, 'keeps getting farther away')

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru: keep doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach 続ける (tsuzukeru, 'to continue') to the verb stem (masu-stem) to express doing something continuously over time — 'keep doing X'.

Example from this song: 探し続ける (sagashi tsuzukeru) = 'keep searching' — from 探す (sagasu, 'to search') → 探し (sagashi, stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru, 'to continue')

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走り続ける (hashiri tsuzukeru, 'keep running')
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じ続ける (shinji tsuzukeru, 'keep believing')
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩き続ける (aruki tsuzukeru, 'keep walking')

Note: The verb stem is the ます-form minus ます: 探します → 探し. 続ける itself can be conjugated: 探し続けた (kept searching), 探し続けている (has been searching).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 探す (sagasu, 'to search') → 探し (sagashi, stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru, 'to continue') → 探し続ける (sagashi tsuzukeru, 'keep searching')

grammar_points.name: 〜でしかない (de shika nai: can only be)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + でしかない (de shika nai) to express limitation — 'can only be X' or 'nothing more than X'. しか always pairs with a negative.

Example from this song: 僕でしかない (boku de shika nai) = 'can only be me / I'm nothing more than myself' — from 僕 (boku, 'I') + で (de) + しか (shika, 'only') + ない (nai, 'not')

More examples:
• 夢 (yume, 'dream') → 夢でしかない (yume de shika nai, 'it's nothing but a dream')
• 始まり (hajimari, 'beginning') → 始まりでしかない (hajimari de shika nai, 'it's only the beginning')
• 人間 (ningen, 'human') → 人間でしかない (ningen de shika nai, 'merely human')

Note: でしかない expresses humble limitation — accepting what you are or what something is. It can be self-deprecating or philosophical depending on context.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 僕 (boku, 'I') + で (de) + しか (shika, 'only') + ない (nai, 'not') → 僕でしかない (boku de shika nai, 'can only be me')

grammar_points.name: 〜であろうと (de arou to: whether...or)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + であろうと (de arou to) to express 'whether it be X (or Y)'. It's a formal conditional showing indifference to conditions — the result holds regardless.

Example from this song: 架空であろうと現実だろうと (kakuu de arou to genjitsu darou to) = 'whether it be fiction or reality' — expressing that it doesn't matter which one it is.

More examples:
• 雨 (ame, 'rain') → 雨であろうと (ame de arou to, 'whether it be rain')
• 誰 (dare, 'who') → 誰であろうと (dare de arou to, 'whoever it may be')
• 何 (nani, 'what') → 何であろうと (nani de arou to, 'whatever it may be')

Note: であろうと is the formal equivalent of でも (demo). It's used in literary, poetic, or dramatic contexts. The pattern A であろうと B であろうと means 'whether A or B'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 架空 (kakuu, 'fiction') + であろうと (de arou to, 'whether it be') + 現実 (genjitsu, 'reality') + だろうと (darou to, 'or') → 架空であろうと現実だろうと ('whether fiction or reality')

grammar_points.name: 〜なくても (nakutemo: even without)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the negative form of a verb or adjective (ない), change to なくて (nakute), then add も (mo, 'even'). This means 'even without X' or 'even if there isn't X'.

Example from this song: 地図なんかなくても (chizu nanka nakutemo) = 'even without a map or anything' — from 地図 (chizu, 'map') + なんか (nanka, 'or anything') + なくても (nakutemo, 'even without')

More examples:
• お金 (okane, 'money') → お金がなくても (okane ga nakutemo, 'even without money')
• 分からない (wakaranai, 'don't understand') → 分からなくても (wakaranakutemo, 'even if you don't understand')
• 完璧 (kanpeki, 'perfect') → 完璧じゃなくても (kanpeki ja nakutemo, 'even if it's not perfect')

Note: なんか before なくても adds dismissive emphasis — 'something like a map' implies maps are unnecessary. The pattern is very empowering in this context.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 地図 (chizu, 'map') + なんか (nanka, 'such a thing') + なくても (nakutemo, 'even without') → 地図なんかなくても (chizu nanka nakutemo, 'even without a map')
