grammar_points.name: 〜として (assuming; as)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add として (toshite) after a noun to mean 'as (a role/capacity)' or to set up a hypothetical frame. It establishes the perspective or role through which something is considered.

Example from this song: The song uses として to frame scenarios hypothetically — 'assuming this is the case' or 'as if this were so'.

More examples:
• 先生 (sensei, 'teacher') → 先生として (sensei toshite, 'as a teacher')
• 友達 (tomodachi, 'friend') → 友達として (tomodachi toshite, 'as a friend')
• 日本人 (nihonjin, 'Japanese person') → 日本人として (nihonjin toshite, 'as a Japanese person')

Note: として can also mean 'even (one)' in negative sentences: 一人として来なかった (hitori toshite konakatta, 'not even one person came').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 先生 (sensei, 'teacher') + として (toshite, 'as') → 先生として (sensei toshite, 'as a teacher')

grammar_points.name: 〜みたいだ (it seems like; it's like)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add みたいだ (mitai da) after a noun, verb, or adjective to express resemblance or conjecture — 'it seems like X' or 'it's like X'. This is the casual equivalent of ようだ.

Example from this song: The song uses みたいだ to compare feelings and situations to something familiar, creating vivid imagery.

More examples:
• 夢 (yume, 'dream') → 夢みたいだ (yume mitai da, 'it's like a dream')
• 死んだ (shinda, 'died') → 死んだみたいだ (shinda mitai da, 'it seems like it died')
• 春 (haru, 'spring') → 春みたいだ (haru mitai da, 'it's like spring')

Note: Before a noun, use みたいな: 夢みたいな世界 (yume mitai na sekai, 'a world like a dream'). Before a verb, use みたいに: 鳥みたいに飛ぶ (tori mitai ni tobu, 'fly like a bird').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 夢 (yume, 'dream') + みたいだ (mitai da, 'seems like') → 夢みたいだ (yume mitai da, 'it's like a dream')

grammar_points.name: 〜出す (to start doing; to burst out)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach 出す (dasu, 'to put out') to the verb stem (masu-stem) to express a sudden or explosive beginning of an action — 'burst out doing' or 'start to do'.

Example from this song: 抜け出す (nukedasu) = 'to break out / escape' — from 抜ける (nukeru, 'to slip through') → 抜け (nuke, stem) + 出す (dasu, 'to burst out'). Also: 逃げ出す (nigedasu) = 'to run away' — from 逃げる (nigeru, 'to flee') → 逃げ (nige, stem) + 出す (dasu)

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走り出す (hashiridasu, 'to start running suddenly')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣き出す (nakidasu, 'to burst into tears')
• 笑う (warau, 'to laugh') → 笑い出す (waraidasu, 'to burst out laughing')

Note: 〜出す emphasizes the sudden, often unstoppable nature of the action starting. Compare with 〜始める (hajimeru), which is a neutral 'begin to'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 抜ける (nukeru, 'to slip through') → 抜け (nuke, stem) + 出す (dasu, 'burst out') → 抜け出す (nukedasu, 'to break out') / 逃げる (nigeru, 'to flee') → 逃げ出す (nigedasu, 'to run away')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to create a direct command. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with ろ. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent.

Example from this song: 覚ませ (samase) = 'Wake up!' — from 覚ます (samasu, 'to wake/awaken') → change す (su) to せ (se)

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べろ (tabero, 'Eat!')
• 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand') → 立て (tate, 'Stand!')

Note: For godan verbs: す→せ, く→け, む→め, つ→て, ぬ→ね, ぶ→べ, う→え, る→れ. For ichidan verbs: る→ろ. This is very direct — use with caution in real life, but it's extremely common in songs and anime.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 覚ます (samasu, 'to awaken') → 覚ませ (samase, 'Wake up!')

grammar_points.name: 〜のか (rhetorical question)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add のか (no ka) at the end of a sentence to create an emotionally charged question, often rhetorical. の adds an explanatory tone, and か marks the question. Together they express doubt, frustration, or deep wondering.

Example from this song: The song uses のか to question reality with emotional weight — 'Is it really...?' or 'Can it be that...?'

More examples:
• 何 (nani, 'what') → 何なのか (nan na no ka, 'what is it, really?')
• できる (dekiru, 'can do') → できるのか (dekiru no ka, 'can it really be done?')
• 本当 (hontō, 'true') → 本当なのか (hontō na no ka, 'is it really true?')

Note: In casual male speech, のか often drops to のか without rising intonation, making it sound reflective rather than questioning. It adds more emotional weight than plain か alone.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: できる (dekiru, 'can do') + のか (no ka, rhetorical question) → できるのか (dekiru no ka, 'can it really be done?')

grammar_points.name: 〜に変わる (to change into)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + に (ni, 'into') + 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') to express transformation from one thing to another. The particle に marks what something changes into.

Example from this song: 声が耳鳴りに変わった (koe ga miminari ni kawatta) = 'the voice changed into a ringing in the ears' — from 声 (koe, 'voice') + が (ga, subject) + 耳鳴り (miminari, 'ringing') + に (ni, 'into') + 変わった (kawatta, 'changed')

More examples:
• 雨が雪に変わる (ame ga yuki ni kawaru, 'the rain changes to snow')
• 緑が赤に変わる (midori ga aka ni kawaru, 'green changes to red')
• 笑顔が涙に変わった (egao ga namida ni kawatta, 'the smile turned to tears')

Note: 変わる (kawaru) is intransitive (changes by itself). 変える (kaeru) is transitive (someone changes it). 色を変える (iro wo kaeru, 'to change the color').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 声 (koe, 'voice') + が (ga) + 耳鳴り (miminari, 'ringing') + に (ni, 'into') + 変わった (kawatta, 'changed') → 声が耳鳴りに変わった (koe ga miminari ni kawatta, 'the voice changed into ringing')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていますか (te imasu ka - are you doing?)

explanation.en:
A polite progressive question asking whether someone is currently doing something or in an ongoing state.

How it works:
Take the て-form (te-form) of a verb, add います (imasu, polite "to be"), then か (ka, question particle).

Example from this song:
君は覚えていますか (kimi wa oboete imasu ka, "Do you remember?")

More examples:
- 今何をしていますか (ima nani o shite imasu ka, "What are you doing now?")
- 日本語を勉強していますか (nihongo o benkyou shite imasu ka, "Are you studying Japanese?")
- まだ待っていますか (mada matte imasu ka, "Are you still waiting?")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 覚える (oboeru) → 覚えて (oboete, te-form) + います (imasu) + か (ka) → 覚えていますか (oboete imasu ka)

grammar_points.name: 〜はずのない (hazu no nai - not supposed to)

explanation.en:
Expresses that something was not supposed to happen, that it goes against expectations. はず (hazu) means "supposed to" and のない (no nai) negates it.

How it works:
Verb dictionary form + はず (hazu) + の (no) + ない (nai). It modifies a noun: "a [noun] that was not supposed to [verb]."

Example from this song:
来るはずのない朝 (kuru hazu no nai asa, "A morning that was never supposed to come")

More examples:
- 失敗するはずのないテスト (shippai suru hazu no nai tesuto, "A test that was not supposed to be failed")
- ここにあるはずのない鍵 (koko ni aru hazu no nai kagi, "A key that shouldn’t be here")
- 泣くはずのない彼が泣いた (naku hazu no nai kare ga naita, "He cried, though he wasn’t supposed to")

grammar_points.name: 〜出す (dasu - to begin)

explanation.en:
An auxiliary verb indicating the sudden start of an action. When attached to a verb stem, it means "to start [doing something]" or "to burst into [doing something]."

How it works:
Take the masu-stem of a verb and add 出す (dasu).

Example from this song:
二人歩き出す (futari arukidasu, "The two of us start walking")

More examples:
- 雨が降り出した (ame ga furidashita, "It started to rain")
- 急に笑い出した (kyuu ni waraidashita, "Suddenly burst out laughing")
- 走り出す (hashiridasu, "to start running")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 歩く (aruku) → 歩き (aruki, masu-stem) + 出す (dasu) → 歩き出す (arukidasu, "to start walking")

explanation.en:
Expresses supposition or probability: "probably" or "I think." It is the polite form of だろう (darou).

How it works:
Attach でしょう (deshou) after the plain form of a verb, adjective, or noun.

Example from this song:
忘れたのでしょう (wasureta no deshou, "You’ve probably forgotten")

More examples:
- 明日は雨でしょう (ashita wa ame deshou, "It will probably rain tomorrow")
- 彼は来ないでしょう (kare wa konai deshou, "He probably won’t come")
- 大丈夫でしょう (daijoubu deshou, "It’s probably fine")

grammar_points.name: 〜なかった (nakatta - could not / did not)

explanation.en:
The past negative form of verbs, meaning "could not" or "did not." One of the most fundamental conjugations in Japanese.

How it works:
Take the ない-form (nai-form) of a verb, replace ない (nai) with なかった (nakatta).

Example from this song:
果たせなかった約束 (hatasenakatta yakusoku, "Promises we could not fulfill")

More examples:
- 行けなかった (ikenakatta, "could not go")
- 食べなかった (tabenakatta, "did not eat")
- 間に合わなかった (ma ni awanakatta, "did not make it in time")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 果たす (hatasu) → 果たせる (hataseru, potential) → 果たせない (hatasenai) → 果たせなかった (hatasenakatta, "could not fulfill")

grammar_points.name: 〜ぜ (masculine emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ぜ (ze) at the end of a sentence for emphatic, masculine assertion. It expresses determination, excitement, or confidence. Think of it as a punchy 'I tell ya!' or 'let's do this!'

Example from this song: The song uses ぜ throughout to convey high energy and determination — a very common particle in rock and punk songs.

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くぜ (iku ze, 'I'm going!')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やるぜ (yaru ze, 'I'll do it!')
• いい (ii, 'good') → いいぜ (ii ze, 'It's good, man!')

Note: ぜ is masculine casual speech. The feminine equivalents would be わ (wa) or の (no). In anime and songs, ぜ is extremely common for energetic male characters. It's stronger than よ (yo) but not as rough as ぞ (zo).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 行く (iku, 'to go') + ぜ (ze, emphasis) → 行くぜ (iku ze, 'I'm going!')

grammar_points.name: 〜たら (conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add たら (tara) after the past tense form (た-form) of a verb to create a conditional — 'if/when X happens'.

Example from this song: 引き寄せたら (hikiyosetara) = 'if you pull it close' — from 引き寄せる (hikiyoseru, 'to pull close') → 引き寄せた (hikiyoseta, past) + ら (ra) = 引き寄せたら (hikiyosetara)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたら (tabetara, 'if you eat')
• 会う (au, 'to meet') → 会ったら (attara, 'if you meet')
• 暑い (atsui, 'hot') → 暑かったら (atsukattara, 'if it's hot')

Note: たら is the most versatile conditional in Japanese. It works with verbs, adjectives, and nouns. For nouns/な-adjectives: だったら (dattara). It's especially natural for one-time or future events.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 引き寄せる (hikiyoseru, 'to pull close') → 引き寄せた (hikiyoseta, past) + ら (ra) → 引き寄せたら (hikiyosetara, 'if you pull it close')

grammar_points.name: 〜より (comparison)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place より (yori) after the thing being compared to express 'more than X' or 'rather than X'. The pattern is: A より B が [adjective] = 'B is more [adj] than A'.

Example from this song: The song uses より to express preferences and comparisons — choosing one path over another.

More examples:
• 昨日 (kinou, 'yesterday') → 昨日より元気 (kinou yori genki, 'healthier than yesterday')
• 誰 (dare, 'anyone') → 誰よりも (dare yori mo, 'more than anyone')
• 言葉 (kotoba, 'words') → 言葉より行動 (kotoba yori koudou, 'actions over words')

Note: より can also mean 'from' in formal writing: 東京より (Toukyou yori, 'from Tokyo'). Adding も after より intensifies the comparison: 誰よりも強い (dare yori mo tsuyoi, 'stronger than anyone').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 昨日 (kinou, 'yesterday') + より (yori, 'than') → 昨日より (kinou yori, 'more than yesterday')

grammar_points.name: 〜だって (even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add だって (datte) after a noun, pronoun, or phrase to mean 'even' or 'even if'. It can also mean 'because' at the start of a sentence.

Example from this song: The song uses だって to express 'even if' — showing that regardless of circumstances, the resolve remains unchanged.

More examples:
• 僕 (boku, 'I') → 僕だって (boku datte, 'even I')
• 何 (nani, 'what') → 何だって (nan datte, 'anything at all')
• 子供 (kodomo, 'child') → 子供だって (kodomo datte, 'even a child')

Note: だって has three uses: 1) 'even' after nouns (僕だって, 'even I'), 2) 'because' at the start (だって寒いもん, datte samui mon, 'because it's cold!'), 3) 'even if' after verbs in past tense (言ったって, ittatte, 'even if you say').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 僕 (boku, 'I') + だって (datte, 'even') → 僕だって (boku datte, 'even I')

grammar_points.name: 〜のさ (explanatory + masculine emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add のさ (no sa) at the end of a sentence to explain something with a casual, confident tone. の (no) provides explanation, さ (sa) adds masculine assertion.

Example from this song: The song uses のさ to assert its philosophy with rock-band confidence — 'that's just how it is, man'.

More examples:
• そう (sou, 'so') → そうなのさ (sou na no sa, 'that's just the way it is')
• 強い (tsuyoi, 'strong') → 強いのさ (tsuyoi no sa, 'I'm strong, you know')
• 知ってる (shitteru, 'I know') → 知ってるのさ (shitteru no sa, 'I know, you see')

Note: のさ is softer than んだぜ but still masculine and assertive. Common in song lyrics for declaring truths or personal philosophies. The feminine equivalent is のよ (no yo).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: そう (sou, 'so') + なのさ (na no sa, 'it's that') → そうなのさ (sou na no sa, 'that's just how it is')

grammar_points.name: 〜っと (onomatopoeia emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: The っと (tto) ending is added to adverbs and mimetic words (onomatopoeia) to emphasize the manner or feeling of an action. The small っ adds a sharp, crisp quality.

Example from this song: The song uses words like そっと (sotto, 'gently/quietly') and ギュッと (gyutto, 'tightly/squeezing') — mimetic adverbs with っと that vividly describe how actions are performed.

More examples:
• じっと (jitto, 'still/staring intently')
• ぐっと (gutto, 'with force / holding back emotions')
• パッと (patto, 'suddenly/brightly')
• ふわっと (fuwatto, 'softly/floatily')

Note: Japanese has a rich system of mimetic words (擬態語, gitaigo). The っと pattern makes them feel more immediate and vivid. These words are essential for natural-sounding Japanese and are very common in everyday speech.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: そっと (sotto, 'gently') / ギュッと (gyutto, 'tightly') / じっと (jitto, 'intently')

grammar_points.name: 〜と言う (quoting with to)

explanation.en:
How it works: と (to) is the quotation particle. Place it after what someone said or thought, followed by 言う (iu, 'to say') or other verbs of expression.

Example from this song: ピエロになると言って (piero ni naru to itte) = 'saying "I'll become a clown"' — from ピエロになる (piero ni naru, 'to become a clown') + と (to) + 言って (itte, te-form of 言う)

More examples:
• 好きだと言った (suki da to itta, 'said "I like you"') — from 好き (suki, 'like')
• 行くと思う (iku to omou, 'I think I'll go') — with 思う (omou, 'to think')
• 大丈夫だと聞いた (daijoubu da to kiita, 'I heard it's OK') — with 聞く (kiku, 'to hear')

Note: と quotes both direct and indirect speech. The quoted part uses plain form. Common verbs after と: 言う (iu, say), 思う (omou, think), 聞く (kiku, hear), 書く (kaku, write).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: ピエロになる (piero ni naru, 'become a clown') + と (to, quotation) + 言って (itte, 'saying') → ピエロになると言って (piero ni naru to itte, 'saying I'll become a clown')

grammar_points.name: 〜みたいに (like; similar to)

explanation.en:
How it works: みたいに (mitai ni) means 'like' or 'similar to.' It's the adverbial form of みたい, used to compare actions or states. Attach it to nouns or plain form verbs.

Example from this song: The song uses みたいに to compare the singer's situation to something familiar — creating a vivid image.

More examples:
• 鳥みたいに飛びたい (tori mitai ni tobitai, 'want to fly like a bird') — from 鳥 (tori, 'bird')
• 子供みたいに遊ぶ (kodomo mitai ni asobu, 'play like a child') — from 子供 (kodomo, 'child')
• 嘘みたいに消えた (uso mitai ni kieta, 'disappeared as if it were a lie') — from 嘘 (uso, 'lie')

Note: みたいに is the casual equivalent of のように (no you ni). Use みたいに in speech and songs, のように in writing and formal contexts. Both mean 'like/as if.'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: noun + みたいに (mitai ni, 'like')

grammar_points.name: 〜たくない (don't want to)

explanation.en:
How it works: たくない (takunai) is the negative of たい (tai, 'want to'). Take the verb stem, add たい, then conjugate it like an i-adjective: たい → たくない.

Example from this song: 帰りたくない (kaeritakunai) = 'don't want to go home' — from 帰る (kaeru, 'to go home') → 帰り (kaeri, stem) + たい (tai) → 帰りたくない (kaeritakunai)

More examples:
• 食べたくない (tabetakunai, 'don't want to eat') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 起きたくない (okitakunai, 'don't want to get up') — from 起きる (okiru, 'to wake up')
• 会いたくない (aitakunai, 'don't want to meet') — from 会う (au, 'to meet')

Note: たい conjugates like an i-adjective: たい → たくない (negative) → たかった (past) → たくなかった (past negative). This makes it very versatile for expressing desires.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 帰る (kaeru, 'to go home') → 帰り (kaeri, stem) + たい (tai, 'want') → 帰りたい (kaeritai) → 帰りたくない (kaeritakunai, 'don't want to go home')

grammar_points.name: 〜ていく (gradual change)

explanation.en:
How it works: ていく (te iku) after a verb's te-form expresses a change that progresses over time into the future.

Example from this song: 外れていく (hazurete iku) = 'gradually coming off / falling apart' — from 外れる (hazureru, 'to come off/deviate') → 外れて (hazurete) + いく (iku)

More examples:
• 増えていく (fuete iku, 'keeps increasing') — from 増える (fueru, 'to increase')
• 離れていく (hanarete iku, 'drifting apart') — from 離れる (hanareru, 'to separate')
• 暗くなっていく (kuraku natte iku, 'getting darker and darker')

Note: ていく emphasizes the direction of change — moving away from the current state into the future. It often has a bittersweet quality when describing loss or fading.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 外れる (hazureru, 'to come off') → 外れて (hazurete) + いく (iku, 'to go') → 外れていく (hazurete iku, 'gradually coming off')

grammar_points.name: 〜のせい (because of; due to)

explanation.en:
How it works: のせい (no sei) means 'because of' or 'due to,' specifically when attributing blame or a negative cause. It implies the cause is at fault.

Example from this song: The song uses のせい to blame something for a negative outcome — 'it's because of (something bad).'

More examples:
• 雨のせいで遅れた (ame no sei de okureta, 'was late because of the rain') — from 雨 (ame, 'rain')
• 君のせいだ (kimi no sei da, 'it's your fault') — from 君 (kimi, 'you')
• 寝不足のせいで (nebusoku no sei de, 'because of lack of sleep')

Note: のせい is for negative causes (blame). For positive causes, use おかげで (okage de, 'thanks to'). 君のせいで泣いた (your fault I cried) vs. 君のおかげで笑えた (thanks to you I could smile).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: noun + の (no) + せい (sei, 'fault/blame') → のせい (no sei, 'because of / it's the fault of')

grammar_points.name: 〜かしら (I wonder, feminine)

explanation.en:
How it works: かしら (kashira) is a feminine sentence-ending particle meaning 'I wonder.' It's the feminine equivalent of かな (kana).

Example from this song: The song uses かしら to express a character's wondering — a soft, introspective question.

More examples:
• 大丈夫かしら (daijoubu kashira, 'I wonder if it's OK')
• 来るかしら (kuru kashira, 'I wonder if they'll come')
• 私、変かしら (watashi, hen kashira, 'am I strange, I wonder?')

Note: かしら is traditionally feminine and sounds elegant/gentle. In modern usage, some people of all genders use it, but it still carries a feminine or refined nuance. In anime, it often marks a refined female character.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: plain form + かしら (kashira, 'I wonder' — feminine)

grammar_points.name: 頂戴 (ちょうだい) please/give me

explanation.en:
How it works: ちょうだい (choudai) is a casual/feminine way to say 'please give me' or 'please do (for me).' It's softer and cuter than ください (kudasai).

Example from this song: The song uses ちょうだい as a soft, intimate request — 'give me' or 'please do.'

More examples:
• お水ちょうだい (omizu choudai, 'give me water, please') — from お水 (omizu, 'water')
• 見せてちょうだい (misete choudai, 'show me, please') — from 見せる (miseru, 'to show')
• もう少し待ってちょうだい (mou sukoshi matte choudai, 'please wait a bit more')

Note: ちょうだい comes from 頂戴 which originally means 'to humbly receive.' As a request form, it's casual and often used by women and children, or in intimate situations. Noun + ちょうだい = 'give me (noun).' Te-form + ちょうだい = 'please do (action).'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: noun + ちょうだい (choudai, 'give me') / verb te-form + ちょうだい (choudai, 'please do')

grammar_points.name: 〜だって (datte: even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add だって (datte) or って (tte) after the past tense of a verb to express 'even if'. After nouns, だって means 'even [noun]'.

Example from this song: 転んだって (korondatte) = 'even if you fall down' — from 転ぶ (korobu, 'to fall') → 転んだ (koronda, past) + って (tte, 'even if')

More examples:
• 失敗する (shippai suru, 'to fail') → 失敗したって (shippai shitatte, 'even if you fail')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣いたって (naitatte, 'even if you cry')
• 何 (nani, 'what') → 何だって (nan datte, 'anything/no matter what')

Note: たって is the casual version of ても (temo). Both mean 'even if': 転んでも = 転んだって. たって/だって is more colloquial and common in hip-hop lyrics like this song.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 転ぶ (korobu, 'to fall') → 転んだ (koronda, past) + って (tte, 'even if') → 転んだって (korondatte, 'even if you fall')

grammar_points.name: 〜ぜ (ze: masculine emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ぜ (ze) at the end of a sentence for strong masculine assertion. It conveys confidence, excitement, and determination. Very common in hip-hop and shonen anime.

Example from this song: いいぜ (ii ze) = 'It's good!' / 行くぜ (iku ze) = 'Let's go!' — ぜ turns statements into confident declarations.

More examples:
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やるぜ (yaru ze, 'I'll do it, yeah!')
• 負けない (makenai, 'won't lose') → 負けないぜ (makenai ze, 'I won't lose!')
• 最高 (saikou, 'the best') → 最高だぜ (saikou da ze, 'It's the best!')

Note: ぜ is strongly masculine and casual. Using it in formal settings would be inappropriate. In this hip-hop track, it perfectly matches the high-energy, confident tone. Strength ranking: ぞ (strongest) > ぜ > よ (mildest).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: いい (ii, 'good') + ぜ (ze, emphasis) → いいぜ (ii ze, 'It's good!') / 行く (iku, 'to go') + ぜ (ze) → 行くぜ (iku ze, 'Let's go!')

grammar_points.name: 〜となる (to naru: to become)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + と (to) + なる (naru, 'to become') to express transformation — something becomes something else. と marks what it transforms into.

Example from this song: 勇気となる (yuuki to naru) = 'becomes courage' — from 勇気 (yuuki, 'courage') + と (to, 'into') + なる (naru, 'to become')

More examples:
• 力 (chikara, 'strength') → 力となる (chikara to naru, 'becomes strength')
• 光 (hikari, 'light') → 光となる (hikari to naru, 'becomes light')
• 問題 (mondai, 'problem') → 問題となる (mondai to naru, 'becomes a problem')

Note: となる is slightly more formal/literary than になる (ni naru). Both mean 'become', but となる often implies a more significant or dramatic transformation. In songs and literature, となる adds weight.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 勇気 (yuuki, 'courage') + と (to, 'into') + なる (naru, 'to become') → 勇気となる (yuuki to naru, 'becomes courage')

grammar_points.name: 〜でしょ (desho: right?; isn't it?)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add でしょ (desho) at the end of a statement to seek confirmation or express assumption — 'right?' or 'isn't it?'. It's the casual form of でしょう (deshou).

Example from this song: 覚悟でしょ (kakugo desho) = 'you're prepared, right?' — from 覚悟 (kakugo, 'readiness/resolve') + でしょ (desho, 'right?')

More examples:
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かるでしょ (wakaru desho, 'you understand, right?')
• 寒い (samui, 'cold') → 寒いでしょ (samui desho, 'it's cold, right?')
• 本当 (hontou, 'true') → 本当でしょ (hontou desho, 'it's true, right?')

Note: With rising intonation, でしょ seeks confirmation. With falling intonation, it asserts 'I told you so'. でしょう (long form) is more polite; でしょ (short) is casual.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 覚悟 (kakugo, 'resolve') + でしょ (desho, 'right?') → 覚悟でしょ (kakugo desho, 'you're prepared, right?')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to create a direct command. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with ろ. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent.

Example from this song: 上げろ (agero) = 'Raise it!' — from 上げる (ageru, 'to raise') → replace る with ろ = 上げろ (agero)

More examples:
• 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand') → 立て (tate, 'Stand up!')
• 見る (miru, 'to look') → 見ろ (miro, 'Look!')
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来い (koi, 'Come!') — irregular

Note: In this hip-hop track, the imperative carries rallying energy — 'raise your voice!' 'stand up!' Ichidan: る→ろ. Godan: final syllable → え-row. Irregulars: する→しろ (shiro), 来る→来い (koi).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 上げる (ageru, 'to raise') → 上げろ (agero, 'Raise it!')

grammar_points.name: 〜だけ (dake: only; just)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add だけ (dake) after a noun, verb, or number to restrict meaning to 'only' or 'just'. It limits the scope to exactly what's mentioned.

Example from this song: 繰り返すだけの (kurikaesu dake no) = 'just/only repeating' — from 繰り返す (kurikaesu, 'to repeat') + だけ (dake, 'only') + の (no, connecting)

More examples:
• 一つ (hitotsu, 'one') → 一つだけ (hitotsu dake, 'just one')
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見るだけ (miru dake, 'just looking')
• 少し (sukoshi, 'a little') → 少しだけ (sukoshi dake, 'just a little')

Note: だけ is neutral — it simply limits. Compare with しか (shika) + negative, which implies disappointment: 一つだけある (hitotsu dake aru, 'there's just one') vs. 一つしかない (hitotsu shika nai, 'there's only one [unfortunately]').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 繰り返す (kurikaesu, 'to repeat') + だけ (dake, 'only') + の (no) → 繰り返すだけの (kurikaesu dake no, 'just repeating')

grammar_points.name: 〜んでしょ (right?)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine the explanatory ん (n) with でしょ (desho, seeking confirmation). This creates a casual way to seek agreement — 'right?' or 'isn't it?'. It's the casual form of のでしょう (no deshou).

Example from this song: 忘れてないんでしょ (wasuretenainddesho) = 'you haven't forgotten, right?' — from 忘れてない (wasuretenai, 'haven't forgotten') + んでしょ (ndesho, 'right?')

More examples:
• 知っている (shitteiru, 'know') → 知ってるんでしょ (shitterundesho, 'you know, right?')
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなんでしょ (suki nandesho, 'you like it, right?')
• 行きたい (ikitai, 'want to go') → 行きたいんでしょ (ikitaindesho, 'you want to go, right?')

Note: んでしょ is softer than でしょ alone and adds emotional depth. It's very common in anime dialogue when a character confronts another about their true feelings.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れてない (wasuretenai, 'haven't forgotten') + んでしょ (ndesho, 'right?') → 忘れてないんでしょ (wasuretenaindesho, 'you haven't forgotten, right?')

grammar_points.name: 〜ばっか / ばかり (just)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place ばかり (bakari) or its casual form ばっか (bakka) after a past tense verb to mean 'just did' or after a noun to mean 'only/nothing but'. It indicates exclusivity or recency.

Example from this song: 始まったばっか (hajimatta bakka) = 'just started' — from 始まった (hajimatta, 'started') + ばっか (bakka, 'just')

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたばかり (tabeta bakari, 'just ate')
• 文句 (monku, 'complaints') → 文句ばかり言う (monku bakari iu, 'do nothing but complain')
• 来た (kita, 'came') → 来たばっかり (kita bakkari, 'just arrived')

Note: た + ばかり = 'just did' (recency). ばかり with nouns = 'only/nothing but'. ばっか/ばっかり are casual contractions. 遊んでばかりいる (asonde bakari iru, 'do nothing but play').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 始まる (hajimaru, 'to start') → 始まった (hajimatta, past) → 始まったばっか (hajimatta bakka, 'just started')

grammar_points.name: 〜きれない (can't completely)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add きれない (kirenai). This means 'can't do X completely' — the action can't be finished or fully accomplished.

Example from this song: 隠しきれない (kakushi kirenai) = 'can't fully hide' — from 隠す (kakusu, 'to hide') → 隠し (kakushi, masu-stem) + きれない (kirenai)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べきれない (tabe kirenai, 'can't eat it all')
• 数える (kazoeru, 'to count') → 数えきれない (kazoe kirenai, 'too many to count')
• 伝える (tsutaeru, 'to convey') → 伝えきれない (tsutae kirenai, 'can't fully express')

Note: The positive きる (kiru) means 'to do completely': 走りきる (hashiri kiru, 'run the whole distance'). Negative きれない means the completion is impossible.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 隠す (kakusu, 'to hide') → 隠し (kakushi, masu-stem) + きれない (kirenai, 'can't completely') → 隠しきれない (kakushi kirenai, 'can't fully hide')

grammar_points.name: 〜出す (begin to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add 出す (dasu, 'to put out'). As an auxiliary, it means 'to suddenly begin doing'. It emphasizes the abruptness of the start.

Example from this song: 動き出す (ugoki dasu) = 'begin to move' — from 動く (ugoku, 'to move') → 動き (ugoki, masu-stem) + 出す (dasu)

More examples:
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走り出す (hashiri dasu, 'suddenly start running')
• 降る (furu, 'to fall — rain') → 降り出す (furi dasu, 'suddenly start raining')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣き出す (naki dasu, 'burst into tears')

Note: Compare with はじめる (hajimeru, 'begin to') which is a gradual, expected start. 出す implies suddenness and often surprise. 急に笑い出した (kyuu ni warai dashita, 'suddenly burst out laughing').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 動く (ugoku, 'to move') → 動き (ugoki, masu-stem) + 出す (dasu, 'to begin') → 動き出す (ugoki dasu, 'begin to move')

grammar_points.name: Japanese-English code-switching

explanation.en:
How it works: Code-switching means mixing two languages within a song or conversation. Many J-rock and J-pop songs blend Japanese and English lyrics freely, using English for emphasis, coolness, or to highlight key phrases.

Example from this song: The song mixes Japanese lyrics with English words and phrases, a common technique in J-rock. English words are often used for song titles, hooks, and emotional peaks.

More examples of anime songs with code-switching:
• FLOW - GO!!! (Naruto) — mixes English shouts with Japanese verses
• LiSA - Crossing Field — includes English phrases
• UVERworld - D-technoLife (Bleach) — English choruses

Note: When English appears in Japanese songs, it's often written in katakana: ディスタンス (disutansu, 'distance'). Learning to recognize these katakana English words helps with reading and listening.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: N/A — code-switching is a sociolinguistic phenomenon, not a grammar conjugation

grammar_points.name: 〜まで (made: until)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add まで (made) after a noun or verb to mark an endpoint — 'until X'. It indicates the limit of an action's duration or reach.

Example from this song: 届くまで (todoku made) = 'until it reaches' — from 届く (todoku, 'to reach') + まで (made, 'until')

More examples:
• 終わる (owaru, 'to end') → 終わるまで (owaru made, 'until it ends')
• 朝 (asa, 'morning') → 朝まで (asa made, 'until morning')
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かるまで (wakaru made, 'until you understand')

Note: まで with verbs uses the dictionary form: 届くまで. With nouns, it attaches directly: 朝まで. まで can also mean 'as far as' for distance: 駅まで (eki made, 'as far as the station').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 届く (todoku, 'to reach') + まで (made, 'until') → 届くまで (todoku made, 'until it reaches')

grammar_points.name: 〜なくちゃ (nakucha: must; have to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Shorten なくてはいけない (nakute wa ikenai, 'must do') to the casual なくちゃ (nakucha). This expresses obligation or necessity in a conversational way.

Example from this song: 信じられなくちゃ (shinjirarena kucha) = 'I have to be able to believe' — from 信じられる (shinjirareru, 'can believe') → 信じられない (shinjiranai, negative) → 信じられなくちゃ (shinjirarena kucha, 'must be able to believe')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かなくちゃ (ikanakucha, 'I have to go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べなくちゃ (tabenakucha, 'I have to eat')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しなくちゃ (shinakucha, 'I have to do it')

Note: Contraction chain: なくてはいけない → なくては → なくちゃ → なきゃ (even shorter). All mean 'must/have to'. なくちゃ is the most common casual form. It's warm and conversational.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 信じられる (shinjirareru, 'can believe') → 信じられない (shinjiranai, negative) → 信じられなくちゃ (shinjirarena kucha, 'must be able to believe')

grammar_points.name: 〜ても (temo: even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ても (temo) after the te-form of a verb to express 'even if X happens'. The outcome doesn't change regardless of the condition.

Example from this song: 回り道をしても (mawarimichi wo shitemo) = 'even if I take a detour' — from 回り道をする (mawarimichi wo suru, 'to take a detour') → しても (shitemo, 'even if doing')

More examples:
• 雨が降る (ame ga furu, 'it rains') → 雨が降っても (ame ga futtemo, 'even if it rains')
• 失敗する (shippai suru, 'to fail') → 失敗しても (shippai shitemo, 'even if I fail')
• 難しい (muzukashii, 'difficult') → 難しくても (muzukashikutemo, 'even if it's difficult')

Note: For verbs: te-form + も. For い-adjectives: くても. For な-adjectives/nouns: でも. This pattern shows resilience and determination — 'no matter what happens, I'll keep going'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 回り道をする (mawarimichi wo suru, 'to take a detour') → 回り道をして (shite, te-form) + も (mo, 'even') → 回り道をしても (mawarimichi wo shitemo, 'even if I take a detour')

grammar_points.name: 〜より (yori: rather than; compared to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place より (yori) after what you're comparing to — 'more than X' or 'rather than X'. It sets up the comparison baseline.

Example from this song: 逃げるよりマシ (nigeru yori mashi) = 'better than running away' — from 逃げる (nigeru, 'to run away') + より (yori, 'rather than') + マシ (mashi, 'better')

More examples:
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩くより走る方がいい (aruku yori hashiru hou ga ii, 'running is better than walking')
• 昨日 (kinou, 'yesterday') → 昨日より今日 (kinou yori kyou, 'today more than yesterday')
• 何もしない (nanimo shinai, 'doing nothing') → 何もしないより (nanimo shinai yori, 'rather than doing nothing')

Note: より + マシ is a powerful combination meaning 'better (of two bad options)'. The full comparison pattern: A より B の方が [adjective] = 'B is more [adj] than A'.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 逃げる (nigeru, 'to run away') + より (yori, 'rather than') + マシ (mashi, 'better') → 逃げるよりマシ (nigeru yori mashi, 'better than running away')

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru: keep doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach 続ける (tsuzukeru, 'to continue') to the verb stem (masu-stem) to express ongoing, persistent action — 'keep doing X'.

Example from this song: 叫び続ける (sakebi tsuzukeru) = 'keep shouting' — from 叫ぶ (sakebu, 'to shout') → 叫び (sakebi, stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru, 'to continue')

More examples:
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じ続ける (shinji tsuzukeru, 'keep believing')
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩き続ける (aruki tsuzukeru, 'keep walking')
• 待つ (matsu, 'to wait') → 待ち続ける (machi tsuzukeru, 'keep waiting')

Note: The stem is found by dropping ます: 叫びます → 叫び. 続ける is one of the most common compound verb suffixes in Japanese, expressing determination and persistence — key themes in anime songs.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 叫ぶ (sakebu, 'to shout') → 叫び (sakebi, stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru, 'to continue') → 叫び続ける (sakebi tsuzukeru, 'keep shouting')

grammar_points.name: 〜ば (ba: if; conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to form the conditional 'if'. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent and add ば. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with れば.

Example from this song: 振り向けば (furimukeba) = 'if you look back' — from 振り向く (furimuku, 'to look back') → change く to け + ば = 振り向けば (furimukeba)

More examples:
• 聞く (kiku, 'to listen') → 聞けば (kikeba, 'if you listen')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べれば (tabereba, 'if you eat')
• 良い (yoi, 'good') → 良ければ (yokereba, 'if it's good')

Note: The ば-conditional implies 'if A, then B naturally follows'. It works well with general truths and natural consequences. く→けば, す→せば, む→めば, つ→てば, る→れば, ぶ→べば, う→えば.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 振り向く (furimuku, 'to look back') → 振り向けば (furimukeba, 'if you look back')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (meireikei - imperative)

explanation.en:
How it works: The imperative form creates direct commands. For godan verbs (-u verbs), change the final vowel to -e. For ichidan verbs (-ru verbs), replace る with ろ.

Example from this song: 目覚めろ (mezamero) = 'wake up!' — from 目覚める (mezameru, 'to awaken'), an ichidan verb → drop る, add ろ. Also: 燃やせ (moyase) = 'set ablaze!' — from 燃やす (moyasu, 'to burn'), a godan verb → す becomes せ

More examples:
• 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand') → 立て (tate, 'stand up!')
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見ろ (miro, 'look!')
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来い (koi, 'come!') — irregular

Note: This form is very strong and direct, common in anime, songs, and sports cheering. Irregular verbs: する (suru) → しろ (shiro), 来る (kuru) → 来い (koi).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 目覚める (mezameru, 'to awaken') → 目覚めろ (mezamero, 'wake up!') / 燃やす (moyasu, 'to burn') → 燃やせ (moyase, 'set ablaze!')

grammar_points.name: 〜ても (temo - even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ても (temo) after a verb's te-form to express 'even if' or 'even though.' The result doesn't change regardless of the condition stated.

Example from this song: 焦がれても (kogarete mo) = 'even if I yearn' — from 焦がれる (kogareru, 'to yearn for') → 焦がれて (kogarete) + も (mo)

More examples:
• 雨が降っても行く (ame ga futte mo iku, 'I'll go even if it rains') — from 降る (furu, 'to rain')
• 失敗しても大丈夫 (shippai shite mo daijoubu, 'even if you fail, it's OK') — from 失敗する (shippai suru, 'to fail')
• 高くても買う (takakute mo kau, 'I'll buy it even if it's expensive') — i-adjective form

Note: For verbs → te-form + も. For i-adjectives → change い to くても. For na-adjectives/nouns → でも.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 焦がれる (kogareru, 'to yearn') → 焦がれて (kogarete) → 焦がれても (kogarete mo, 'even if yearning')

grammar_points.name: 〜のは〜だ (no wa ~ da - emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: This cleft sentence structure emphasizes one part of the sentence. Verb + のは (no wa) turns the action into a topic, and だ (da) identifies it. Pattern: 'The thing that does X is Y.'

Example from this song: 僕を強くするのは仲間の絆 (boku o tsuyoku suru no wa nakama no kizuna) = 'what makes me strong is the bond with my companions' — the のは highlights 'the thing that makes me strong'

More examples:
• 好きなのは音楽だ (suki na no wa ongaku da, 'what I like is music') — emphasizing the object
• 大切なのは気持ちだ (taisetsu na no wa kimochi da, 'what's important is feelings') — emphasizing importance
• 教えてくれたのは先生だ (oshiete kureta no wa sensei da, 'the one who taught me was the teacher') — emphasizing the person

Note: の nominalizes the verb clause (turns it into a noun phrase). This structure is used when you want to say 'the one who / the thing that / what...'

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 僕を強くする (boku o tsuyoku suru, 'makes me strong') + のは (no wa) + 仲間の絆 (nakama no kizuna, 'bond with companions')

grammar_points.name: 意志形 〜よう (volitional form)

explanation.en:
How it works: The volitional form expresses intention ('let's do') or suggestion. For godan verbs, change the final -u to -ou. For ichidan verbs, replace る with よう.

Example from this song: つなごう (tsunagou) = 'let's connect (hands)' — from つなぐ (tsunagu, 'to connect') — godan verb, ぐ (gu) → ごう (gou)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べよう (tabeyou, 'let's eat')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行こう (ikou, 'let's go')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しよう (shiyou, 'let's do it') — irregular

Note: For godan verbs, the vowel shift is: u→ou, ku→kou, su→sou, tsu→tou, nu→nou, bu→bou, mu→mou, ru→rou, gu→gou. Irregular: する → しよう, 来る (kuru) → 来よう (koyou).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: つなぐ (tsunagu, 'to connect') → つなごう (tsunagou, 'let's connect')

grammar_points.name: 〜ば (ba conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: The ば (ba) conditional means 'if' or 'when.' For godan verbs, change the final -u vowel to -e and add ば. For ichidan verbs, drop る and add れば.

Example from this song: 来れば (kureba) = 'if/when it comes' — from 来る (kuru, 'to come') — irregular: く → くれ + ば

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行けば (ikeba, 'if you go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べれば (tabereba, 'if you eat')
• 安い (yasui, 'cheap') → 安ければ (yasukereba, 'if it's cheap') — i-adjective: い → ければ

Note: The ば conditional often implies a general truth or natural consequence: 'if X happens, then Y naturally follows.' Irregular: する → すれば (sureba), 来る → 来れば (kureba).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来れば (kureba, 'if/when it comes')

grammar_points.name: 〜なら (nara conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: なら (nara) means 'if it is the case that.' It's used when the condition is based on new information or a hypothetical situation. Just add なら after a plain form verb, noun, or adjective.

Example from this song: 求めるなら (motomeru nara) = 'if you seek (it)' — from 求める (motomeru, 'to seek')

More examples:
• 暇なら来て (hima nara kite, 'if you're free, come over') — from 暇 (hima, 'free time')
• 行くなら早く (iku nara hayaku, 'if you're going, go early') — from 行く (iku, 'to go')
• 学生なら安い (gakusei nara yasui, 'if you're a student, it's cheap') — noun + なら

Note: なら is often used to give advice or make suggestions based on what someone just said. It differs from ば (ba) in that なら focuses on the situation/topic rather than a cause-and-effect relationship.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 求める (motomeru, 'to seek') + なら (nara, 'if') → 求めるなら (motomeru nara, 'if you seek')

grammar_points.name: 〜フリをする (furi wo suru: to pretend)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use [state/action] + フリをする (furi wo suru) to express pretending — 'to act as if' or 'to pretend to be'. フリ means 'pretense' or 'act'.

Example from this song: 気にならないフリして (ki ni naranai furi shite) = 'pretending not to care' — from 気にならない (ki ni naranai, 'don't care') + フリ (furi, 'pretense') + して (shite, 'doing')

More examples:
• 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知らないフリをする (shiranai furi wo suru, 'to pretend not to know')
• 寝る (neru, 'to sleep') → 寝たフリをする (neta furi wo suru, 'to pretend to be sleeping')
• 元気 (genki, 'fine') → 元気なフリをする (genki na furi wo suru, 'to pretend to be fine')

Note: フリ is often written in katakana to stand out, though 振り is the kanji form. This pattern beautifully captures the song's theme of hiding true feelings — putting on an act to mask vulnerability.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 気にならない (ki ni naranai, 'don't care') + フリ (furi, 'pretense') + して (shite, 'doing') → 気にならないフリして (ki ni naranai furi shite, 'pretending not to care')

grammar_points.name: 〜のに (noni: even though)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add のに (noni) at the end of a clause to express frustration or disappointment that reality contradicts expectation — 'even though X' or 'despite X'.

Example from this song: 溢れるのに見えない (afureru noni mienai) = 'even though it overflows, I can't see it' and 伝えたいのに (tsutaetai noni) = 'even though I want to convey it (I can't)'

More examples:
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなのに (suki na noni, 'even though I like it...')
• 頑張った (ganbatta, 'tried hard') → 頑張ったのに (ganbatta noni, 'even though I tried hard...')
• 約束した (yakusoku shita, 'promised') → 約束したのに (yakusoku shita noni, 'even though you promised...')

Note: のに carries emotional weight — frustration, sadness, or mild complaint. After な-adjectives and nouns: なのに. After verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly. Often the sentence trails off: ...のに (implying the unfair result).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 溢れる (afureru, 'to overflow') + のに (noni, 'even though') → 溢れるのに (afureru noni, 'even though it overflows') / 伝えたい (tsutaetai, 'want to convey') + のに (noni) → 伝えたいのに (tsutaetai noni, 'even though I want to convey it...')

grammar_points.name: 〜ちゃう (chau: end up doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Replace てしまう (te shimau) with ちゃう (chau) in casual speech to express unintentional completion, often with a sense of regret — 'end up doing X'.

Example from this song: 忘れちゃう (wasurechau) = 'end up forgetting' — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れて (wasurete, te-form) + しまう (shimau) → 忘れちゃう (wasurechau)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べちゃう (tabechau, 'end up eating it all')
• 壊す (kowasu, 'to break') → 壊しちゃう (kowashichau, 'accidentally break it')
• 好きになる (suki ni naru, 'to fall in love') → 好きになっちゃう (suki ni nacchau, 'end up falling in love')

Note: ちゃう is one of the most common casual forms in Japanese. Past: ちゃった. For で-forms: でしまう → じゃう. 飲んじゃう (nonjau). In this song, forgetting captures the bittersweet tone of the farewell.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れて (wasurete, te-form) + しまう (shimau) → 忘れちゃう (wasurechau, 'end up forgetting' — casual)

grammar_points.name: 〜たくない (takunai: don't want to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the たい (tai, 'want to') form and make it negative by changing い to くない (kunai). Since たい conjugates like an い-adjective, its negative is たくない.

Example from this song: 見たくない (mitakunai) = 'don't want to see' — from 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見たい (mitai, 'want to see') → 見たくない (mitakunai, 'don't want to see')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行きたくない (ikitakunai, 'don't want to go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたくない (tabetakunai, 'don't want to eat')
• 会う (au, 'to meet') → 会いたくない (aitakunai, 'don't want to meet')

Note: たい conjugates exactly like an い-adjective: たい (want), たくない (don't want), たかった (wanted), たくなかった (didn't want). In this farewell song, 見たくない expresses the pain of not wanting to witness the goodbye.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見たい (mitai, 'want to see') → 見たくない (mitakunai, 'don't want to see')

grammar_points.name: 〜なりに (nari ni: in one's own way)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add なりに (nari ni) after a noun or pronoun to express 'in one's own way' or 'to the best of one's ability' — doing something within one's own capacity or style.

Example from this song: 私なりに (watashi nari ni) = 'in my own way' — from 私 (watashi, 'I/me') + なりに (nari ni, 'in one's own way')

More examples:
• 自分 (jibun, 'oneself') → 自分なりに (jibun nari ni, 'in my own way')
• 子供 (kodomo, 'child') → 子供なりに (kodomo nari ni, 'in a child's own way')
• 彼 (kare, 'he') → 彼なりに (kare nari ni, 'in his own way')

Note: なりに implies doing the best you can with what you have. 子供なりに頑張った (kodomo nari ni ganbatta, 'tried hard in a child's own way') acknowledges effort within limitations. It's humble and genuine.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 私 (watashi, 'I') + なりに (nari ni, 'in one's own way') → 私なりに (watashi nari ni, 'in my own way')

grammar_points.name: 〜気がする (ki ga suru: have a feeling that)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use [clause] + 気がする (ki ga suru, literally 'a feeling does') to express a vague intuition or feeling — 'I have a feeling that X' or 'it feels like X'.

Example from this song: そんな気がする (sonna ki ga suru) = 'I have that kind of feeling' — from そんな (sonna, 'that kind of') + 気がする (ki ga suru, 'have a feeling')

More examples:
• 会ったことがある (atta koto ga aru, 'have met') → 会ったことがある気がする (atta koto ga aru ki ga suru, 'I feel like I've met you before')
• 忘れている (wasurete iru, 'am forgetting') → 何か忘れている気がする (nanika wasurete iru ki ga suru, 'I have a feeling I'm forgetting something')
• うまくいく (umaku iku, 'go well') → うまくいく気がする (umaku iku ki ga suru, 'I have a feeling it'll work out')

Note: 気がする is for uncertain, gut feelings — lighter than 思う (omou, 'to think'). It's perfect for intuitive or emotional moments, which is why it fits so well in this song's reflective farewell.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: そんな (sonna, 'that kind of') + 気がする (ki ga suru, 'have a feeling') → そんな気がする (sonna ki ga suru, 'I have that kind of feeling')

grammar_points.name: 〜たらいいのに (tara ii noni - if only)

explanation.en:
Expresses a wish for something that is unlikely or impossible. "If only [X would happen]..." It carries a feeling of longing or frustration.

How it works:
Take the たら (tara, conditional) form of a verb and add いいのに (ii noni, "it would be nice, but...").

Example from this song:
君の事嫌いになれたらいいのに (kimi no koto kirai ni naretara ii noni, "If only I could grow to dislike you")

More examples:
- 飛べたらいいのに (tobetara ii noni, "If only I could fly")
- もっと時間があったらいいのに (motto jikan ga attara ii noni, "If only there were more time")
- 日本語が上手だったらいいのに (nihongo ga jouzu dattara ii noni, "If only my Japanese were better")

grammar_points.name: 〜てしまう (te shimau - end up doing)

explanation.en:
Expresses an unintended or regrettable action. "End up doing [X]" or "accidentally do [X]." Often carries a nuance of "oops" or helplessness.

How it works:
Take the て-form (te-form) of a verb and add しまう (shimau). Casual contraction: ちゃう (chau).

Example from this song:
きっとまた思い出してしまうよ (kitto mata omoidashite shimau yo, "I’ll surely end up remembering again")

More examples:
- 全部食べてしまった (zenbu tabete shimatta, "I ended up eating everything")
- 電車に乗り遅れてしまった (densha ni noriokurete shimatta, "I accidentally missed the train")
- また泣いちゃった (mata naichatta, "I ended up crying again" - casual)

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 思い出す (omoidasu) → 思い出して (omoidashite) + しまう (shimau) → 思い出してしまう (omoidashite shimau)

grammar_points.name: 〜なきゃよかった (nakya yokatta - wish I hadn’t)

explanation.en:
Expresses regret about something that already happened: "I wish I hadn’t [done X]." なきゃ is a casual contraction of なければ (nakereba).

How it works:
Take the ない-form (nai-form) of a verb, contract it to なきゃ (nakya), then add よかった (yokatta, "it would have been better").

Example from this song:
こんな気持ち知らなきゃよかった (konna kimochi shiranakya yokatta, "I wish I’d never known these feelings")

More examples:
- 行かなきゃよかった (ikanakya yokatta, "I wish I hadn’t gone")
- 食べなきゃよかった (tabenakya yokatta, "I wish I hadn’t eaten that")
- 言わなきゃよかった (iwanakya yokatta, "I wish I hadn’t said that")

Expresses contrast with frustration or disappointment: "even though [X], [Y happened]." It implies the speaker expected a different outcome.

How it works:
Attach のに (noni) after the plain form of a verb or adjective.

Example from this song:
もう二度と会えることもないのに (mou nidoto aeru koto mo nai noni, "Even though we can never meet again")

More examples:
- 約束したのに来なかった (yakusoku shita noni konakatta, "Even though we promised, they didn’t come")
- 勉強したのにテストに落ちた (benkyou shita noni tesuto ni ochita, "Even though I studied, I failed")
- 高いのに美味しくない (takai noni oishikunai, "Even though it’s expensive, it’s not good")

Limits to "only" or "just." With 一人 (hitori), it means "all by oneself." It can also mean "since [doing X], nothing else happened."

How it works:
Attach きり (kiri) after a noun or counter.

Example from this song:
一人きりで見上げる花火 (hitori kiri de miageru hanabi, "Fireworks I look up at all alone")

More examples:
- 二人きりになりたい (futari kiri ni naritai, "I want to be alone together")
- あれっきり会っていない (arekkiri atte inai, "Haven’t met since then")
- 一回きりのチャンス (ikkai kiri no chansu, "A one-time-only chance")

explanation.en:
Expresses doing something repeatedly or excessively, often with a slightly negative nuance. It means "always doing [X]" or "nothing but [X]."

How it works:
Attach ばかり (bakari) after the て-form (te-form) of a verb. It emphasizes that the person does nothing else.

Example from this song:
逃げてばかりで (nigete bakari de, "Always running away")

More examples:
- 遊んでばかりいる (asonde bakari iru, "All you do is play")
- 文句を言ってばかりだ (monku o itte bakari da, "You do nothing but complain")
- テレビを見てばかりで勉強しない (terebi o mite bakari de benkyou shinai, "You only watch TV and don't study")

Expresses purpose: "in order to" or "for the sake of." It states the goal behind an action.

How it works:
Place ために (tame ni) after the dictionary form of a verb or a noun + の (no).

Example from this song:
なりたい自分になるために (naritai jibun ni naru tame ni, "In order to become the person I want to be")

More examples:
- 試験に受かるために勉強する (shiken ni ukaru tame ni benkyou suru, "I study in order to pass the exam")
- 健康のために運動する (kenkou no tame ni undou suru, "I exercise for my health")
- 夢を叶えるために頑張る (yume o kanaeru tame ni ganbaru, "I do my best in order to make my dream come true")

Used as a soft negative request ("don't [do X]") or to express doing something without another action.

How it works:
Take the ない-form (nai-form) of a verb, replace ない with ないで (naide). As a request, it means "please don't."

Example from this song:
怖がらないで (kowagaranaide, "Don't be afraid")

More examples:
- 泣かないで (nakanaide, "Don't cry")
- 心配しないで (shinpai shinaide, "Don't worry")
- 朝ごはんを食べないで学校に行った (asagohan o tabenaide gakkou ni itta, "I went to school without eating breakfast")

grammar_points.name: 〜きれない (kirenai - unable to completely)

explanation.en:
Expresses the inability to complete an action fully. 切る (kiru) as an auxiliary means "to do completely," so 切れない (kirenai) means "cannot finish doing."

How it works:
Take the masu-stem of a verb and add 切れない (kirenai). It means "cannot completely [do X]."

Example from this song:
諦めきれずに (akirame kirezu ni, "Unable to fully give up")

More examples:
- 食べきれない量の料理 (tabekirenai ryou no ryouri, "an amount of food too much to finish eating")
- 言いきれない (iikirenai, "cannot say it all")
- 数えきれないほど (kazoekirenai hodo, "too many to count")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 諦める (akirameru) → 諦め (akirame, masu-stem) + 切れる (kireru) → 諦めきれない (akiramekirenai) → 諦めきれずに (akiramekirezu ni, "unable to completely give up, and...")

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru - keep doing)

explanation.en:
An auxiliary verb meaning "to continue doing." It attaches to the masu-stem of another verb to express an ongoing action.

How it works:
Take the masu-stem of a verb and add 続ける (tsuzukeru).

Example from this song:
まだ走り続けたいの (mada hashiri tsuzuketai no, "I still want to keep running")

More examples:
- 歩き続ける (aruki tsuzukeru, "to keep walking")
- 待ち続けた (machi tsuzuketa, "kept waiting")
- 努力し続ければ夢が叶う (doryoku shi tsuzukereba yume ga kanau, "If you keep making effort, your dream will come true")

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 走る (hashiru) → 走り (hashiri, masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) → 走り続けたい (hashiri tsuzuketai, "want to keep running")

grammar_points.name: 〜みたいに (mitai ni) — like ~

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Noun + みたいに (mitai ni) means "like ~" and is the casual equivalent of のように (no you ni). みたい (mitai) expresses resemblance, and に (ni) turns it into an adverb. Before a noun, use みたいな (mitai na): 夢みたいな話 (yume mitai na hanashi, "a story like a dream"). It sounds more conversational and informal.

Example from this song:
太陽みたいに (taiyou mitai ni) — "like the sun"
The singer compares someone to the sun — warm, bright, and life-giving.

More examples:
• 子供みたいに笑う (kodomo mitai ni warau) — "laugh like a child"
• 映画みたいな恋 (eiga mitai na koi) — "a romance like a movie"
• 夢みたいだ (yume mitai da) — "it's like a dream"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 太陽 (taiyou, "sun") + みたいに (mitai ni) → 太陽みたいに (taiyou mitai ni, "like the sun")

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru) — to keep doing

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) means "to keep doing ~" or "to continue doing ~." It emphasizes persistence and endurance. Combined with ている (te iru): 続けている (tsuzukete iru, "has been continuing"). Casual: 続けてる (tsuzuketeru).

Example from this song:
走り続けてる (hashiri tsuzuketeru) — "keeps running" (casual)
The singer describes someone who never stops running — relentless determination.

More examples:
• 信じ続ける (shinji tsuzukeru) — "keep believing"
• 10年間書き続けている (juu-nenkan kaki tsuzukete iru) — "has been writing for 10 years"
• 歩き続けよう (aruki tsuzukeyou) — "let's keep walking"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 走る (hashiru, "to run") → 走り (hashiri, masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) → 走り続ける (hashiri tsuzukeru, "keep running") → 走り続けてる (hashiri tsuzuketeru, casual progressive)

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて (nante) — such a thing as / how surprising that

explanation.en:
How it works:
なんて (nante) expresses surprise, disbelief, or dismissiveness about something. After a verb or noun, it means "such a thing as ~" (often dismissive) or "how ~ !" (expressing surprise). It can belittle something or express amazement depending on context.

Example from this song:
あきらめるなんて (akirameru nante) — "such a thing as giving up"
The singer dismisses the very idea of giving up — it is unthinkable.

More examples:
• 嘘なんて信じない (uso nante shinjinai) — "I don't believe such a thing as lies"
• こんなに美しいなんて (konna ni utsukushii nante) — "how beautiful!"
• 失敗するなんて思わなかった (shippai suru nante omowanakatta) — "I never thought I'd fail"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: あきらめる (akirameru, "to give up") + なんて (nante, "such a thing as") → あきらめるなんて (akirameru nante, "such a thing as giving up")

grammar_points.name: 〜たって (tatte) — even if (casual)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb た-form (ta-form) + って (tte) is a casual form of ても (temo), meaning "even if ~." It sounds tougher and more defiant. For nouns: なくたって (nakutatte, "even without"). This form is very common in song lyrics and casual speech.

Example from this song:
負けたって (maketatte) — "even if you lose"
なくたって (nakutatte) — "even without"
The singer encourages perseverance regardless of setbacks.

More examples:
• 失敗したって気にしない (shippai shitatte ki ni shinai) — "even if I fail, I don't care"
• 金がなくたって幸せだ (kane ga nakutatte shiawase da) — "even without money, I'm happy"
• 笑われたって構わない (warawaretatte kamawanai) — "I don't mind even if I'm laughed at"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 負ける (makeru, "to lose") → 負けた (maketa, past) + って (tte) → 負けたって (maketatte, "even if you lose")

grammar_points.name: 〜てくる (te kuru) — approaching / coming toward

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + くる (kuru) expresses something coming toward the speaker or the present moment. It can mean: (1) an action approaching — 伝わってくる (tsutawatte kuru, "comes through / reaches me"), (2) a change developing up to now — 暗くなってきた (kuraku natte kita, "it's gotten dark"), (3) going and coming back — 買ってくる (katte kuru, "go buy and come back").

Example from this song:
伝わってくる (tsutawatte kuru) — "comes through / reaches me"
The feelings or message travels toward the singer and arrives.

More examples:
• 雨が降ってきた (ame ga futte kita) — "it started raining" (change approaching now)
• お腹が空いてきた (onaka ga suite kita) — "I'm getting hungry" (gradual change)
• コンビニで買ってくる (konbini de katte kuru) — "I'll go buy it at the convenience store (and come back)"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 伝わる (tsutawaru, "to be transmitted") → 伝わって (tsutawatte, te-form) + くる (kuru, "to come") → 伝わってくる (tsutawatte kuru, "comes through / reaches me")

grammar_points.name: 受身形 (ukemi-kei) — passive form 〜られる/〜れる

explanation.en:
How it works:
The passive form means the subject receives an action. For godan (u-verb) verbs: change -u to -a + れる (reru). For ichidan (ru-verb) verbs: drop る (ru) + られる (rareru). Japanese passive often implies adversity — something unwanted happening to the subject.

Example from this song:
言われる (iwareru) — "to be told"
引き離される (hikihanasareru) — "to be pulled apart"
Both express being on the receiving end of actions imposed by others.

More examples:
• 先生に褒められた (sensei ni homerareta) — "was praised by the teacher"
• 雨に降られた (ame ni furareta) — "got rained on" (adversity)
• 彼に嘘をつかれた (kare ni uso o tsukareta) — "was lied to by him"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 引き離す (hikishanasu, "to pull apart") → 引き離される (hikihanasareru, passive, "to be pulled apart")

grammar_points.name: 〜ようで (you de) — as if / it seems like

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb plain form + ようで (you de) means "as if ~" or "it seems like ~ and..." The で (de) is the て-form of だ (da), allowing this simile to connect to another clause. It describes the appearance or impression of something while continuing the sentence.

Example from this song:
しみ込むようで (shimi komu you de) — "as if soaking in"
The feeling is described as seeping deeply into the singer's heart.

More examples:
• 夢のようで信じられない (yume no you de shinjirarenai) — "it's like a dream and I can't believe it"
• 終わりのないようで疲れた (owari no nai you de tsukareta) — "it seemed endless and I got tired"
• 時間が止まったようで静かだった (jikan ga tomatta you de shizuka datta) — "it was as if time stopped and it was quiet"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: しみ込む (shimikomu, "to soak in") + ようで (you de, "as if ~ and") → しみ込むようで (shimikomu you de, "as if soaking in")

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru) — to keep doing

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) means "to keep doing ~" or "to continue doing ~." It emphasizes persistence and duration without interruption. 続ける (tsuzukeru) itself conjugates normally as an ichidan verb.

Example from this song:
降り続ける (furi tsuzukeru) — "keep falling" (rain)
The rain does not stop — it keeps falling continuously.

More examples:
• 歩き続ける (aruki tsuzukeru) — "keep walking"
• 信じ続けた (shinji tsuzuketa) — "kept believing"
• 叫び続ける (sakebi tsuzukeru) — "keep shouting"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 降る (furu, "to fall/rain") → 降り (furi, masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) → 降り続ける (furi tsuzukeru, "keep falling")

grammar_points.name: 〜んだよ (n da yo) — explanatory + emphasis

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + んだよ (n da yo) combines the explanatory んだ (n da) with the emphatic particle よ (yo). It means "you see, it's that ~" or "the thing is ~!" It is used to explain something to the listener with conviction, insistence, or emotional emphasis. Very common in casual speech and songs.

Example from this song:
あるんだよ (aru n da yo) — "there are, you see!" / "they exist, I tell you!"
The singer emphatically asserts that something real exists.

More examples:
• 本当なんだよ (hontou nan da yo) — "it's true, I'm telling you!"
• 好きなんだよ (suki nan da yo) — "I like you, you know!"
• 頑張ってるんだよ (ganbatteru n da yo) — "I AM trying hard, you see!"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: ある (aru, "to exist") + ん (n, explanatory) + だ (da) + よ (yo, emphasis) → あるんだよ (aru n da yo, "there are, you see!")

grammar_points.name: 〜というの (to iu no) — are you saying that / the fact that

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Clause + というの (to iu no) means "are you saying that ~?" (questioning) or "the fact that ~" (nominalizing). It wraps an entire statement into something that can be questioned or discussed. In questions, it often carries surprise or disbelief.

Example from this song:
行くというの (iku to iu no) — "are you saying you'll go?" / "you're going, you say?"
The singer questions someone's claim with surprise or disbelief.

More examples:
• 知らないというの？ (shiranai to iu no?) — "are you saying you don't know?"
• 嘘だというのか (uso da to iu no ka) — "are you saying it's a lie?"
• 彼が来るというのは本当？ (kare ga kuru to iu no wa hontou?) — "is it true that he's coming?"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 行く (iku, "to go") + という (to iu, "saying that") + の (no, nominalizer) → 行くというの (iku to iu no, "you're saying you'll go?")

grammar_points.name: 〜ていける (te ikeru) — can keep doing / can go on

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + いける (ikeru) means "can keep doing ~" or "can go on doing ~." It combines ていく (te iku, progressive into the future) with the potential form いける (ikeru, "can go"). It expresses confidence that something can be sustained or continued.

Example from this song:
変えていける (kaete ikeru) — "can keep changing"
The singer believes they have the power to continue transforming things.

More examples:
• 一人でもやっていける (hitori demo yatte ikeru) — "I can manage even alone"
• この調子で続けていける (kono choushi de tsuzukete ikeru) — "can keep going at this pace"
• 二人なら乗り越えていける (futari nara norikoete ikeru) — "together we can keep overcoming"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 変える (kaeru, "to change") → 変えて (kaete, te-form) + いける (ikeru, "can go") → 変えていける (kaete ikeru, "can keep changing")

grammar_points.name: 〜んじゃないの (n ja nai no) — isn't it that / could it be

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + んじゃないの (n ja nai no) is a casual way to suggest or gently accuse — "isn't it that ~?" or "could it be ~?" It wraps a statement into a soft question or challenge. It can be confrontational or genuinely questioning, depending on tone.

Example from this song:
怖いんじゃないの (kowai n ja nai no) — "aren't you actually scared?"
The singer challenges someone, suggesting they are hiding their fear.

More examples:
• 本当は知ってるんじゃないの (hontou wa shitteru n ja nai no) — "don't you actually know?"
• 好きなんじゃないの (suki nan ja nai no) — "isn't it that you like them?"
• 嫌なんじゃないの (iya nan ja nai no) — "don't you actually dislike it?"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 怖い (kowai, "scary") + ん (n) + じゃないの (ja nai no, "isn't it?") → 怖いんじゃないの (kowai n ja nai no, "aren't you actually scared?")
